en: Source: AVS01-10.noacc [The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence.
What four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth.
These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence.”
Atharvavedasaṃhitā; Śaunaka Recension Based on the Edition of [Roth and Whitney]
The Hymns of the Atharvaveda (Śaunaka),
transliterated by Chatia Orlandi, Pisa 1991, with a collation of the edition by Roth/Whitney.
Edited by Vladimir Petr and Petr Vavroušek. Preliminary final editorial revision: Jost Gippert. Frankfurt am Main, 31 January 1997.
(1.1.1’) Those who move thrice-sevenfold, bearing all forms—
(1.1.1.c) may the Lord of Speech today bestow their strengths upon my bodies. (1.1.2’) Return again, O Lord of Speech, together with the divine mind.
(1.1.2.c) O Lord of Wealth, cause [the two] to rest within me; let what is heard abide in me alone.
(1.1.3’) Right here, let the Lord of Speech bind both [ends] together like the two ends of a bowstring with a cord; let what is heard abide in me alone.

(1.1.4’) Invoked is the Lord of Speech; may the Lord of Speech invoke us. (1.1.4.c) May we be united with what we have heard; may I not be deprived of what I have heard. 4 (1.2.1’) We know Parjanya, the father of the arrow, the one who provides abundant nourishment.
(1.2.1.c) We know indeed his mother, the Earth, of vast form. (1.2.2’) O bowstring, bend around us; make our bodies like stone.
(1.2.2.c) Make us firm and wide; drive away hostilities and enmities.
When the cows embrace the tree, they praise the quivering arrow, the skillful *ṛbhu*.
O Indra, ward off from us the shaft, the missile!
Just as the point of the arrow stands between heaven and earth, so [ward it off].
(1.2.4.c) Thus let the disease and the discharge come to an end; let the *muñja* grass stand here!

(1.3.1’) We know the father of the arrow, Parjanya, who possesses a hundred virile powers. (1.3.1.c) With him I bring well-being to your body; let your outflow be upon the earth, and let your residue be outside, [like] hair!

(1.3.2’) We know the father of the arrow, Mitra, possessed of a hundred virile powers; with him I shall bring well-being to your body. Let your discharge be upon the earth; let your residue be upon the sacrificial grass.
(2) (1.3.3’) We know the father of the arrow, Varuṇa, possessed of a hundred virile powers.

(1.3.3.c) With that, I shall bring well-being to your body; let your outflow be upon the earth; let it be outside you, [not] on the grass! (1.3.5’) We know the father of the arrow, Sūrya, who possesses a hundredfold virility. (1.3.5.c) With him, I shall bring well-being to your body. Let your outflow be upon the earth; let it be outside you, *bāl*. ‖5‖ (1.3.6’) That which has settled within the entrails, in the two kidneys, or in the bladder—
(1.3.6.c) Thus let your urine be released outside, O child—thus for all.
(1.3.7’) I split open your urethra as one opens the dam of a river;
(1.3.7.c) thus let your urine be released outside, O child—thus for all.

(1.3.8’) Your bladder-opening is loosened, like that of the ocean, the great sea. (1.3.8.c) Thus let your urine be released outward—*bāl iti sarvakam*. (1.3.9’) Just as an arrow flies forth when discharged from the bow, so [let it go].
(1.3.9.c) Thus let your urine be released outward, O Bāla; thus for all [the others].
(1.4.1’) The waters go along their paths, the sisters of those performing the sacrifice, (1.4.1.c) mingling their milk with honey.
(1.4.2’) Those waters which are near the sun, or those with which the sun is joined—
may they speed our sacrifice.
(1.4.3’) I invoke the divine waters where our cattle drink.
(1.4.3.c) An oblation is to be prepared for the rivers.
(1.4.4’) Within the waters is immortality; within the waters is healing.
By means of the praises of the waters, may you horses become swift; may you cows become rich in vigor. (1.4.4.c) 4.
O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss; grant us strength for great joy and vision.
Grant us a share here of that most auspicious sap of yours.
Like longing mothers, [be gracious to us]. (1.5.2.c) We come gladly to you for whose abode you quicken us;
O Waters, give us life. (1.5.3.c)
(1.5.4’) Rulers of precious things, governing the people—
(1.5.4.c) I beg the Waters for healing.
(1.6.1’) May the divine Waters be auspicious for our aid and for our drinking.
(1.6.1.c) May they flow toward us for peace and well-being.
1 (1.6.2’) Soma has told me that within the waters are all healing remedies, and Agni, who brings welfare to all. 2
O Waters, bestow healing medicine as a protection for my body, so that I may long behold the sun.
(1.6.3) May the waters of the desert be auspicious to us, and may the waters of the marshes also be auspicious. (1.6.4)
(1.6.4.c) May the waters dug from the earth be auspicious to us, and may those brought in jars be auspicious;
(1.6.4.e) may the waters of the rainy season be propitious to us.
(1.7.1’) O Agni, bring hither the sorcerer and the Kimīdin who praises [thee].

(1.7.1.c) For you, O God, when praised, have become the slayer of the Dasyu. (1.7.2’) O Agni, Supreme Lord, Knower of Beings, Master of the Body, consume the fat offering and cause the sorcerers to wail. (1.7.2.c) O Agni, eater of the Taula plant, rend asunder the Yātudhānas.
(1.7.3’) Let the sorcerers cry out, the devouring Kimīdins;
(1.7.3.c) then, O Agni, may you and Indra accept this our oblation.
(1.7.4’) May Agni take hold first; may Indra, the mighty-armed, drive them away.
(1.7.4.c) Let every sorcerer come and say, "I am this one!
(1.7.5.a) We shall see your power, O Jātavedas; proclaim to us the sorcerers, O you who have the eye of man!
(1.7.5.c) Scorched by you from of old, let them all come hither, declaring themselves: "Here we are! (1.7.5.d) 5.
(1.7.6’) Grasp hold, O Jātavedas! You were born for our sake.
(1.7.6.c) Having become our messenger, O Agni, cause the sorcerers to wail aloud!
(1.7.7’) You, O Agni, bring the bound sorcerers here!
(1.7.7.c) Then may Indra shatter their heads with his thunderbolt.
(1.8.1’) May this oblation carry away the sorcerers like foam on the water. (1.8.1.c) Whether it was a woman or a man who performed this here, let that person be struck down.
This one has come praising;
welcome him. O Bṛhaspati and Agni-Soma, having brought him under your control, pierce him through.
O Soma-drinker, slay the progeny of the sorcerer and lead them away.
(1.8.3.c) Cast down the upper eye of him who praises you, and also the lower one!
(1.8.4’) O Agni Jātavedas, where you know the secret births of these devouring demons who dwell in hiding,
do you, strengthened by our prayer, strike them down— slay a hundred of them, O Agni!
(1.9.1’) May the Vasus, Indra, Pūṣan, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni bestow wealth upon this man.
(1.9.1.c) May the Ādityas and all the gods establish him in the higher light.
1 (1.9.2’) May there be light in his direction—Sūrya, Agni, or even gold.

(1.9.4’) From them I have taken the sacrifice, the splendor, the increase of wealth, and the thoughts, O Agni.
(1.9.4.c) May our rivals be lower than we; may we cause this [sacrificer] to ascend to the highest heaven.
(1.10.1’) This Asura of the gods shines forth, for the desire of King Varuṇa is indeed true.
(1.10.1.c) Therefore, exulting in the sacred word (*brahman*), I lead this man out from the fierce wrath.
1 (1.10.2’) Homage be to thee, O King Varuṇa, and to thy wrath; for thou, O fierce one, perceivest every offense.
2 I release him along with thousands of others; may he live a hundred autumns under thy protection. 2
Whatever falsehood you have spoken with your tongue, or much crookedness—
from King Varuṇa, whose law is truth, I release you.
I release you from Vaiśvānara, from the great ocean around.
(1.10.4.c) Speak to our kinsmen with power; fashion for us a sacred prayer.

(1.11.1’) O Pūṣan, let Aryaman, the wise ordainer, perform the *vaṣaṭ* call for you at this birth. Let the women, who have given birth in accordance with the cosmic order (*ṛta*), move forward; let her joints relax so that she may give birth.
The four quarters of heaven and the four of the earth—the gods have brought together this embryo; may they unfold it for birth.
May Sūṣā unfold it; we cause the womb to open wide.
(1.11.3.c) O you who bring forth easily, loosen it; release it, O you who are whole.
(1.11.4.a) It has not struck against the flesh, nor against the fat, nor against the marrow. (1.11.4.c) Let the speckled afterbirth go away to the dog to eat; let the afterbirth fall away.
I split open your urethra, I split open the womb, and I split open the two labia.
I split apart mother and son; let the child fall away from the placenta along with the afterbirth.
As the wind, as the mind, as birds fly, so [let it pass].
(1.11.6.c) Even so, O ten-month-old one, fly forth together with the afterbirth; let the afterbirth fall away.
(1.12.1’) Born from the womb, the first, the ruddy bull, born of the wind and the cloud, he comes thundering with rain.
(1.12.1.c) May he, who strode out the single [world] in three ways, protect our bodies as he moves straight forward, breaking [the obstacles].
Resting limb upon limb with your radiance, we shall worship you with oblation while paying homage.
We shall worship with oblation those who have joined the joints together, he who has grasped the joints of this [body], the grasper.
Release him from headache and from cough; joint after joint, that which has entered into him, release it.
(1.12.3.c) May that vigor which is born of the clouds and born of the wind attend upon the trees and the mountains.
3 (1.12.4.a) May there be well-being for my outer limb; may there be well-being for my inner limb. (1.12.4.c) May there be well-being for my four limbs; may there be well-being for my entire body. 4
Homage be to you, O lightning; homage be to you, O thunder!
Homage be to you, O stone, with which you strike the ill-sacrificer.
Homage to you, O Son of the Slopes, from whom you gather heat!
Be gracious to our bodies; grant well-being to our offspring.
O Son of the Slopes, let there be homage indeed unto you! We offer homage to your weapon and to your heat.
We know your supreme abode which is hidden in secret; you are the navel placed within the ocean.
(1.13.4’) You whom all the gods created, making you a bold arrow for the purpose of striking— as such, being praised in our assembly, be gracious to us; homage be to you, O Goddess!
(1.14.1’) I shall draw forth fortune and splendor from her, like a garland from a tree.
(1.14.1.c) Like a mountain with a vast base, may he remain long among his ancestors.
(1.14.2’) O King Yama, let this maiden, your bride, be deposited for you;
let her be bound in the house of her mother, and likewise in that of her brother and her father.
(1.14.3) This is your family-guardian, O King; we entrust her to you.
May she sit long among the ancestors, until the top of her head is covered in white hair. (1.14.4) By the sacred word of Asita, of Kaśyapa, and of Gaya—may it be yours.
(1.14.4.c) Like sisters [guarding] a treasure-chest, I bind your vulva.
(1.15.1’) May the rivers flow together; may the winds and the birds come together.
(1.15.1.c) May they take pleasure in this sacrifice of mine from of old; I offer with an oblation that flows together.
Come here indeed to my call; come here to these libations and cause this song of praise to increase.
Let every animal come here; let whatever wealth exists remain in this place. Those perennial, inexhaustible springs that flow from the rivers—
With all these outpourings, we cause wealth to flow together for me.
(1.15.3.c) Those which flow forth from clarified butter, from milk, and from water—with all those outpourings, we cause wealth to flow together for me. (1.15.4)
The devourers who rose up against the pen on this night of the new moon—may Agni, the fourth slayer of demons, speak for our protection.
Varuṇa has spoken against the lead; Agni protects against the lead.
(1.16.2.c) Indra gave me this lead; it is indeed the dispeller of malevolent spirits.
(1.16.3’) This overcomes *viṣkandha*; this drives away the devourers (*attriṇaḥ*).
(1.16.3.c) By means of this, I have overcome all the offspring of the *piśācī*.
Whether you kill our cow, or our horse, or our man—
(1.16.4.c) we pierce you with lead so that he shall not be a slayer of our heroes.
(1.17.1) Those women who go there, the veins clothed in red garments—
(1.17.1.c) Let the female relatives stand like brotherless women, their luster destroyed.
||1|| (1.17.2’) Stand, O lower one; stand, O upper one; and you too, stand, O middle one! (1.17.2.c) Let the littlest one stand, and let this great vein stand firm. ||2||
Of the hundred arteries and the thousand veins, these middle ones have stood firm; together the ends have come to rest.
The great, sand-filled quiver has encompassed you all.
(1.17.4.c) Stand still; let him tremble! ‖4‖ (1.18.1’) Out we drive misfortune, out the shameful thing, out the enemy we drive away.
(1.18.1.c) And those things which are auspicious, those we bring for our progeny; we lead the enemy away. ‖1‖
Savitar has driven it out from the kindling-wood, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman have driven it out from his feet and from his hands;
Anumati, bestowing [favor], has driven it out for us—these gods have impelled it for our good fortune.
Whatever terrible thing is in your self, in your body, or in your hair, or in your appearance—
(1.18.3.c) All that we drive away with our speech; may the divine Savitṛ impel you [to destruction].
3 (1.18.4’) The one with the foot of a hyena, the one with the footprint of a bull, the one who dwells among cattle, and the destroyer;
(1.18.4.c) the one who swallows and the one who licks—these we cause to perish away from us. 4
May those who pierce from afar find us not; may those who pierce from close by find us not.
O Indra, strike down the arrows far away from us in all directions.
Let the arrows fly away from us in every direction—those which are shot and those which remain in the quiver.

O divine arrows of man, pierce through my enemies! (1.19.2.c) Whether he be our own kin, a stranger, a fellow clansman, or a foreigner who assails us—may Rudra pierce all these enemies of mine with his arrow. (1.19.3)
(1.19.4) Whether he be an enemy or no enemy, whoever hates us and seeks to harm us—(1.19.4c) may all the gods destroy him; let the sacred prayer (*brahman*) be my inner armor.
(1.20.1) O divine Soma, be one who does not spill the vessel; O Maruts, be gracious to us at this sacrifice.
Let not the overpowering one find us, nor the curse; let not the crooked, hateful things find us.
(1.20.1.c) Whatever deadly weapon of the malevolent ones is raised today against us—O Mitra and Varuṇa, keep that far away from us! (1.20.2.c)
Drive away from here and from there whatever death, O Varuṇa;
extend wide protection, grant us ample shelter, and drive away death. Such is your command: great indeed you are, the unconquered subduer of enemies.
(1.20.4.c) He whose friend is never slain nor ever conquered;

(1.21.1’) May Indra—the giver of well-being, lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, dispeller of foes, the controller, the bull, the drinker of Soma, and the granter of fearlessness—go before us. (1.21.1.c) May he lead us.
O Indra, strike down our enemies; humble those who attack us. Send into the lowest darkness him who seeks to harm us.
Strike away the demon, strike away the enemies; break apart the jaws of Vṛtra.

(1.21.3.c) O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, turn away the wrath of the enemy who assails us. (1.21.4.a) O Indra, avert the mind of the hater; avert the weapon of him who seeks to overcome us. (1.21.4.c) Grant us great protection, extend it far and wide; drive away the weapon.
(1.22.1’) May the heart-pain and the jaundice depart after the sun.
(1.22.1.c) With the color of a red bull, with that we enclose you.
(1.22.2’) We enclose you with red colors for the sake of long life.
(1.22.2.c) So that this one may be free from blemish and likewise free from disease.
(1.22.3’) The ruddy cows that have the gods as their deity, and those which are ruddy—form by form, age by age—with them we enclose you.
(1.22.3.c) Form by form, age by age, with them we enclose you.
We transfer your yellowness onto the parrots, onto the *ropaṇākā* birds; and so we deposit your yellowness upon the *hāridrava* birds.
(1.22.4) O herb, you are born by night—fair, dark, and black. (1.23.1)
O Dyer, dye this away—the leprosy and whatever grayness there is!
O Pṛṣat, drive away and destroy the leprosy and the grayness from here! Let your own natural color enter you; cast off the white parts!
Black is your dissolution, black is your abode;
O herb, you are black. Drive away, O speckled one, the white leprosy from here—both that which is born of the bone and that which is born of the skin.
(1.23.4.c) By means of the sacred word (*brahman*), I have caused the white mark of the deed committed by the Dūṣīs to vanish.
(1.24.1’) The Suparṇa was born first; you were his bile.

The daughter of Asura first prepared this remedy for vitiligo; it is the destroyer of vitiligo. It has destroyed the vitiligo and made the skin uniform in color. Uniform is the name of your mother, and Uniform is the name of your father.
(1.24.3.c) O herb, you are the maker of beauty; make this [person] beautiful. (1.24.4.a) The Śyāmā plant, which produces beauty, has been brought forth from the earth.
(1.24.4.c) Accomplish this well; restore their forms and fashion them.

When Agni, having entered the waters, burned them—where those upholders of the cosmic order (dharmadhṛtaḥ) offered their salutations—it is there they say is your highest birthplace. Knowing this, O Takman, spare us!
Whether you are the flame, or the glowing heat, or you move within the wood-chips, or wherever your place of origin may be.

(1.25.2.c) You are named Hrūḍu, O god of the green [fever]; being fully aware, spare us from *takman*. (1.25.3’) Whether you are sorrow, or intense affliction, or the son of King Varuṇa; (1.25.3.c) You are named Hrūḍu, O god of the green [fever]; being fully aware, spare us from *takman*.
Homage to the cold fever, homage to the glowing heat; I pay homage to the fever that comes on the next day, on both days, and to the third-day fever—homage be to it!
O gods, let that weapon be far away from us!
Far away be the stone that you hurl!
May he be our friend; may Indra, Bhaga, and Savitṛ of wondrous bounty be our generous givers.
O Maruts, sons of the mountain’s daughter, you whose skins are like the sun—grant us wide-reaching protection.
3 Make us well-prepared; be gracious; have mercy upon our bodies.
(1.26.4.c) Grant joy to our offspring!
(1.27.1’) Those [serpents] on the far shore of the *pr̥dāku*, the thrice-seven, are devoid of birth-membranes.
With their birth-membranes we wipe away the eyes of the evil-intentioned highwayman. (1.27.1.c) With their birth-membranes we wipe away the eyes of the evil-intentioned highwayman.
Let her go forth in all directions, cutting [them down] like one bearing a *pināka* bow; let the malevolent ones, unsuccessful in their aims, be scattered in every way by the *punarbhū*.
The many could not prevail; the small ones did not dare to attack.

(1.27.3.c) Like the joints of a bamboo, the malevolent ones are unsuccessful on all sides. (1.27.4’) O feet, move forward! Carry [him] away to the house of the donor. Let Indrāṇī go first, unconquered and unharmed, before [the others].
The divine Agni has arrived, the slayer of demons, the driver away of disease;
burning away the double-dealing Yātudhānas and the Kimīdins. Burn against the Yātudhānas, O God; burn against the Kimīdins!
(1.28.2.c) O you whose path is black, burn up those sorceresses who come against us!
2 (1.28.3.a) She who cursed with a curse, she who laid on a deadly spell, (1.28.3.c) she who set her mind upon seizing the essence—may she devour her own offspring! 3
Let the sorceresses devour their own son, their sister, and even their grandson;
then, with disheveled hair, let the sorceresses strike one another down, and let the Arāyīs be torn asunder.
With the *abhīvarta* amulet by which Indra grew in power—
With that, O Brahmanaspati, cause us to prosper for the sake of sovereignty.
Overpowering our rivals, overpower those who are hostile to us; overcome the one who attacks us, overcome him who seeks to harm us.
Thee, O Lord, Savitar has strengthened; Soma has strengthened thee; all beings have strengthened thee, so that thou mayest be victorious.
(1.29.4) The victorious, overpowering amulet is the destroyer of rivals.

(1.29.4.c) Let it be bound for my kingdom, for the defeat of my rivals. (1.29.5’) Yonder sun has risen; so too has this word of mine, so that I may be a slayer of enemies, without rivals, a destroyer of rivals. (1.29.5.c) So that I may be a slayer of enemies, without rivals, a destroyer of rivals. (1.29.5.c) So that I may be a slayer of enemies, without rivals, a destroyer of rivals. (1.29.5.c) So that I may be a slayer of enemies, without rivals,
The bull, the destroyer of rivals, the unassailable Aṣṭra—may I, like him, rule over these heroes and over this people.
O All-Gods, O Vasus, protect this man; and you, O Ādityas, remain watchful over him.

(1.30.1.c) Let neither one of my own kin nor one of a different kin, nor any human slaughter, fall upon me. 1 (1.30.2’) O gods who are fathers, and you who are sons—being of one mind, hear this which is spoken by me!
(1.30.2.c) I entrust him to you all; carry him safely to old age. 2
(1.30.3’) O gods who abide in heaven, who on earth, who in the intermediate space, in the plants, in the cattle, and within the waters:

(1.30.3.c) grant him old age and long life; let him spare another hundred deaths. (1.30.4’) Those gods to whom there are fore-offerings or after-offerings, both those who partake of oblations and those who eat what is not offered:

(1.30.4.c) You whose five quarters have been apportioned—those of you who sit at the sacrificial session, I dedicate them for this man. (1.31.1’) To the guardians of the quarters, the four immortal ones;
(1.31.1.c) to these overseers of all that has come into being, we offer this oblation.
(1.31.2’) You who are the four guardians of the quarters, O gods—may you release us from the snares of Nirṛti, from distress, from every distress.
(1.31.3’) Unlame, I worship you with an oblation; uncrippled, I offer you with clarified butter.
(1.31.3.c) He who is the guardian of the quarters, the fourth god—may he bring us well-being here.
(1.31.4’) May there be well-being for our mother and for our father; may there be well-being for our cattle, for all living beings, and for men.
May everything be auspicious and easy for us to find; may we long behold the sun.
O people, know this: he shall proclaim a great sacred formulation (*brahman*).
It is not on earth nor in heaven—that by which the plants breathe. Their station is in the intermediate space, like that of those who have grown weary.
Whether there is a standing place for this being, or not, for that wise Ordainer— (2) When you two fashioned the trembling worlds and the earth,
that remains moist today forever, like the currents of the ocean. (3)
The one [is] all-encompassing; that [other] rests upon the other.
To Heaven, the all-knowing, and to Earth, I have paid homage.
Golden-hued, pure, and purifying are those [waters] in whom Savitṛ was born, and in whom Agni was born.
(1.33.1.c) Those golden waters that have conceived Agni as their embryo—may they be auspicious and gentle to us.
1 (1.33.2’) Those in whose midst King Varuṇa moves, beholding the truth and falsehood of men—those golden waters that have conceived Agni as their embryo—may they be auspicious and gentle to us. 2

Those whose portion the gods enjoy in heaven, those who exist manifoldly in the intermediate space, those golden ones who have taken Agni as their embryo—may those waters be auspicious and pleasant to us.
Behold me with a gracious eye, O Waters; touch my skin with your gracious body.
(1.33.4.c) May those waters, dripping with clarity, pure and purifying, be auspicious and pleasant to us.
4 (1.34.1’) This plant is born of honey; we dig thee up with honey.
(1.34.1.c) Thou art produced from honey; do thou make us full of honey. 1
At the tip of my tongue is honey; at the root of my tongue is the sweet-leafed plant. Truly, you abide in my will; you conform to my thought. Sweet is my stepping forth; sweet is my departure.
(1.34.3.c) With my voice I speak sweetly; may I become full of sweetness, like one who beholds sweetness. (1.34.4’) I am sweeter than sweetness, more honeyed than those who possess honey.
(1.34.4.c) Surely you would choose me alone, as one chooses a honey-sweet branch.
I have come around you with a surrounding stalk of sugarcane, so that there may be no enmity;
so that you may be loving toward me, and so that you may not turn away from me.
When the Dākṣāyaṇas, being well-disposed, bound the gold upon Śatānīka—
I bind this upon you for life, for splendor, for strength, and for long life lasting a hundred autumns.
(1.35.1.c) Neither demons nor malevolent spirits prevail against him; for this is the first-born vigor of the gods.
He who wears the gold of Dakṣa’s lineage secures for himself a long life among the living. (1.35.2.c)
The brilliance of the waters, the light, the vigor, and the strength of the trees—may we deposit these heroic powers in him, even as Indra deposits his senses; may he, growing strong, bear that gold.
With the seasons of the common months, I fill you with the milk of the year.
(1.35.4.c) May Indra and Agni, and all the gods, grant their approval to this, being free from anger.
‖4‖ (2.1.1’) Vena beheld that which is supreme, hidden in the cave, where all becomes one in form.
(2.1.1.c) The dappled cow yielded this [milk] as she was born; the hosts who found the light of heaven raised their voices in response. ‖1‖
(2.1.2’) Let him who knows the immortal proclaim that supreme abode of the Gandharva which is hidden in the cave;
(2.1.2.c) three steps of his are placed in the secret place—he who knows them shall be the father of the Father.
(2.1.3’) He is our father, our progenitor, and he is our kinsman; he knows all the abodes and all the worlds.
(2.1.3.c) He who alone is the name-giver of the gods—to him all the worlds go for inquiry.
(2.1.4’) In an instant I have gone around heaven and earth; I have approached the first-born of Order (*ṛta*).
(2.1.4.c) Like speech in a speaker, he stands firm among the worlds; he is the one who bestows [wealth], for he is indeed this Agni.
I have gone around all beings so as to behold the outstretched thread of *ṛta*,
where the gods, having attained immortality, took their stand upon a common womb.
The celestial Gandharva, who is the lord of the world, the one alone to be revered among the people and worthy of praise.
(2.2.1.c) I seek you with a prayer, O divine god; homage be unto you! In heaven is your dwelling place.
(2.2.2’) Touching the sky, worthy of sacrifice, sun-skinned, he drives away the fury of the divine.
(2.2.2.c) May he be gracious, the Gandharva who is the lord of the world—the one and only one to be revered, most kindly.
(2.2.3’) With these blameless ones he has come together; even among the Apsarases there was a Gandharva.
(2.2.3.c) They say the ocean is their dwelling place, from which they go forth and return again immediately.
(2.2.4’) O you who belong to the clouds and the stars, you who attend upon Viśvāvasu the Gandharva!

(2.2.4.c) To you, O goddesses, I offer this homage. (2.2.5’) Those who are gliding, who dwell in darkness, who desire the dice, and who delude the mind—to those *gandharvas* and *apsarases* I have paid homage. (2.2.5.c) To them I have offered reverence.
(2.3.1’) That which flows down from the mountain in a rushing torrent—
(2.3.1.c) that I prepare for you as medicine, a most effective remedy, so that you may be well.
(2.3.2’) Indeed, O body, how many are those hundred remedies of yours?

(2.3.2.c) Of these, you are the highest, free from discharge and free from disease. ||2|| (2.3.3’) The Asuras dig this great wound-deep below; (2.3.3.c) That is the remedy for discharge; that has destroyed the disease. ||3||
The ants bring forth the healing medicine from the ocean;
it is the remedy for the discharge, and it has allayed the disease. This great healer of wounds has been brought forth from the earth.
(2.3.5.c) That is the medicine for the discharge; that has destroyed the disease. (2.3.6’) May the waters and the plants be auspicious and propitious to us.
May Indra’s thunderbolt strike down the demons; may the arrows, once released, fall upon the demons from afar. (2.3.6.c) 6.
For long life and for great joy, always striving and exerting ourselves,
we wear the *jaṅgiḍa* amulet that destroys *viṣkandha*.
The *jaṅgiḍa* [protects] from the crushing bite, from falling apart, from *viṣkandha*, and from the burning fever.
(2.4.2.c) May the jewel of a thousand powers protect us on every side.
(2.4.3’) This [jewel] overcomes the *viṣkandha* demon; this drives away the devourers (*attriṇas*). (2.4.3.c) This *jaṅgiḍa*, the possessor of all healing medicines, may it protect us from distress.
With the jewel given by the gods, the *jaṅgiḍa*,
which brings delight, we overcome *viṣkandha* and all demonic powers through our exertion.
May both the hemp and the *jaṅgiḍa* protect me from *viṣkandha*.
(2.4.5.c) One is brought from the forest, another from the products of cultivation and juices.
(2.4.6’) This amulet is a destroyer of witchcraft, and likewise a destroyer of enemies; moreover, may the powerful Jaṅgiḍa prolong our lifespans. (2.4.6.c) May it extend our years.
O Indra, take pleasure; come hither, O hero, with your two bay steeds!
Drink of the pressed soma, longing here for the honeyed draught, you who are lovely and eager for exhilaration.
O Indra, fill your belly anew with the honey, as if from heaven.
(2.5.2.c) As the sun approaches this pressed juice, so have the exhilarations of the well-spoken hymns come unto thee.

|| 2 || (2.5.3’) Indra, the swift-conquering friend, who struck down Vṛtra like one striking down those who go astray; || 2.5.3.c) he shattered Vala like Bhṛgu; in the intoxication of Soma, he overcame his enemies. || 3 ||
(2.5.4’) Let the pressed juices enter you; O Indra, fill your belly! O Śakra, understand through our prayer; come to us!

(2.5.4.c) Hear my call, enjoy my songs, O Indra; exhilarate yourself here with your own companions for great delight! 4 (2.5.5’) Now I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra, those which the wielder of the thunderbolt performed for the first time.

(2.5.5.c) He slew the serpent; he pierced the waters and cleft open the bellies of the mountains. (2.5.6’) He slew the serpent as he lay coiled upon the mountain; Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned for him the thunderbolt that roars like heaven.
Like lowing cows, the flowing waters went straight down to the ocean. (2.5.6.c) Like lowing cows, the flowing waters went straight down to the ocean.
Acting like a bull, he chose the Soma; at the Trikadruka rites, he drank of the pressed juice.
Maghavan took up his missile, the thunderbolt; he slew this first-born of the serpents.
O Agni, may the seasons and the years increase you, as do the seers and those things that are true.
(2.6.1.c) Shine forth together with the divine light; illuminate all four quarters.
(2.6.2’) O Agni, be kindled and cause this man to prosper; rise up for great good fortune.
(2.6.2.c) Let those who attend upon you, O Agni, not come to harm; let your priests be glorious, and let no others be so.

(2.6.3’) These Brahmins choose you, O Agni; be auspicious to us in our dwelling, O Agni. (2.6.3.c) Be a slayer of rivals, O Agni, a conqueror of those who plot against us; watch over your own household, never being heedless.
(2.6.4’) With your own sovereign power, O Agni, take hold; with Mitra, O Agni, strive to establish friendship.
(2.6.4.c) Standing in the midst of your kinsmen, O Agni, worthy of invocation among kings, shine brightly here!

(2.6.5’) Beyond the attacks, beyond the oppressors, beyond the thoughtless, and beyond the enemies— (2.6.5.c) For you, O Agni, cross over all difficulties; therefore, grant us wealth together with heroic sons!
Born of the gods, a plant that hates evil and wards off curses,
she has looked upon all my curses as water looks upon impurity.
Whatever curse comes from a rival wife, and whatever curse comes from a sister-in-law— [may they be removed].
(2.7.2.c) Whatever Brahman curses out of anger, may all that be beneath our feet.
(2.7.3’) Its root is extended down from heaven; it is raised up above the earth.
With that thousand-jointed [plant], protect us on every side. (2.7.3.c) With that thousand-jointed [plant], protect us on every side.
Protect me, protect my offspring, and protect whatever wealth we possess.
Let not the enemy overcome us; let not our adversaries prevail over us.
May the curse return to its curser, he who has cursed us with a well-aimed intent. May it be with him.
(2.7.5.c) With the mantra of the eye, we crush even the ribs of the evil-hearted one.
(2.8.1’) Up have risen the two blessed stars named Vicṛtau; may they release the lowest and the highest bond of the kṣetriya disease.
(2.8.1.c) May they release the lowest and the highest bond of the kṣetriya disease. 1.
(2.8.2’) May the night dawn so that it is not to be drunk; may the attacking [diseases] depart. May the plant that destroys *kṣetriya* drive away the *kṣetriya*.
(2.8.3’) With the husk of brown barley with white stalks, and with the reddish-brown powder of sesame—
(2.8.3.c) O plant that destroys *kṣetriya*, may it drive away the *kṣetriya* disease!
‖3‖ (2.8.4’) Homage to your plowshares, homage to your poles and yokes! (2.8.4.c) O plant that destroys *kṣetriya*, may it drive away the *kṣetriya* disease! ‖4‖
Homage to those with drooping eyes; homage to those who are to be addressed.
Homage to the Lord of the Field! O herb that destroys *kṣetriya*, may it drive away the *kṣetriya* disease.
O ten-armed tree, release this man from the *rakṣas* and from the *grāhi* who has seized him in his joints.
(2.9.1.c) And so, O Lord of the Forest, lead him up to the world of the living.
(2.9.2’) He has come; he has risen up; he has joined the company of the living. (2.9.2.c) He has become the father of sons and the most blessed among men.
(2.9.3’) This one has gone up to the study of the Vedas; he has gone up to the cities of the living.
(2.9.3.c) For he has a hundred physicians and a thousand plants.
(2.9.4’) The gods have found your healing power, as have the sacred formulations and the plants.
(2.9.4.c) All the gods have found a resting place for you upon the earth.
(2.9.5.a) He who made it shall undo it; he indeed is the most skilled physician. (2.9.5.c) He alone, the pure one, shall act as a healer and prepare medicines for you.

From the field-disease, from Destruction, from the curse of kinship, and from the malevolent one, I release you from the noose of Varuṇa. By means of the sacred word (*brahman*), I make you sinless; may both Heaven and Earth be auspicious for you.
May Agni be a blessing to you along with the waters; may Soma be a blessing along with the plants.

(2.10.2.c) Thus do I release you from hereditary disease, from Destruction, from the curse of kin, and from malice—from the noose of Varuṇa. (2.10.2.e) By means of the sacred word (*brahman*), I make you sinless; may both Heaven and Earth be auspicious for you.
2. (2.10.3’) May the wind in the mid-air bestow vigor upon you for your peace; may the four quarters of space be auspicious for you.

(2.10.3.c) Thus do I release you from hereditary disease, from Destruction, from the curse of kin, and from malice; I release you from the noose of Varuṇa. (2.10.3.e) By means of the sacred word (*brahman*), I make you sinless; may both Heaven and Earth be auspicious for you.
3. (2.10.4’) These goddesses, the four quarters, whose lord is Vāta—over them the Sun looks on.

(2.10.4.c) Thus do I release you from hereditary disease, from destruction, from the curse of kin, and from malice—from the noose of Varuṇa. (2.10.4.e) By means of this sacred prayer (*brahman*), I make you sinless; may both Heaven and Earth be auspicious for you.
4. (2.10.5’) Within these [plants] I place you against old age; let consumption and destruction depart far away.

(2.10.5.c) Thus do I release you from hereditary disease, from Destruction, from the curse of kin, and from the malevolent one—from the noose of Varuṇa. (2.10.5.e) By means of a sacred prayer (*brahman*), I make you sinless; may both Heaven and Earth be auspicious for you. 5. (2.10.6’) You have been released from consumption, from misfortune, from reproach, and from the malevolent one; and you have been released from the grasp of the Seizer.
(2.10.6.c) Thus do I release you from hereditary disease, from destruction, from the curse of kin, and from malice; I release you from the noose of Varuṇa.

(2.10.6.e) By means of the sacred word (*brahman*), I make you sinless; may both Heaven and Earth be auspicious for you. 6. (2.10.7’) You have found freedom from hostility; you have entered the pleasant world of the well-doer.

(2.10.7.c) Thus do I release you from hereditary disease, from Destruction, from the curse of kin, and from malice—from the noose of Varuṇa. (2.10.7.e) By means of the sacred word (*brahman*), I make you sinless; may both Heaven and Earth be auspicious for you.
7. (2.10.8’) The gods, releasing Sūrya from the grasp of darkness, set him free from sin.
(2.10.8.c) Thus do I release you from hereditary disease, from destruction, from the curse of kin, from malice, and from the noose of Varuṇa.
(2.10.8.e) By means of this sacred prayer (*brahman*), I make you sinless; may both Heaven and Earth be auspicious for you.
8 (2.11.1’) You are the corrupter of the corruptible; you are the missile of the missile; you are the destroyer of the destructible.
(2.11.1.c) Attain what is better; surpass that which is equal.
‖1‖ (2.11.2’) You are the corner-stone; you are the protection; you are the counter-attack.
(2.11.2.c) Attain what is better; surpass that which is equal. ‖2‖
(2.11.3’) Attack him who hates us and whom we hate!
(2.11.3.c) Reach one who is better; surpass your equal!
(2.11.4’) You are a patron; you are the bestower of splendor; you are the protector of the body.
(2.11.4.c) Attain what is better; transcend the equal. (2.11.5’) You are the bright; you are the radiant; you are the heavenly light; you are the light.
(2.11.5.c) Attain what is better; transcend the equal.
Heaven and Earth, the wide mid-air, the two wives of the field, the far-striding and wondrous ones;
and the wide mid-air whose guardian is Vāta—may these burn against you here while I am burning.
O gods who are worthy of sacrifice, listen to this: Bharadvāja recites hymns for my sake.
(2.12.2.c) May he who injures this mind of ours be bound in fetters and cast down into misfortune.
(2.12.3’) O Indra, drinker of Soma, hear this which I call out to you with a grieving heart.
(2.12.3.c) I cut him down like a tree with an axe—he who injures this mind of ours.
With the three groups of eighty Sāmagas, with the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Aṅgirases—may the merit of our sacrifices and pious works protect the ancestors; I bestow that upon him by divine power.
O Heaven and Earth, look upon me with favor; O All-Gods, take hold of me!

(2.12.5.c) May the sin reach the one who acts with ill-will toward the *pitṛ*s of the *Aṅgiras* lineage, who are worthy of the *soma*. (2.12.6’) May burning pains be his who thinks too highly of himself toward us, O Maruts, or who reviles the sacred formulation (*brahman*) as it is being performed. The seven vital breaths and the eight thoughts—these I cut away from you with the sacred word (*brahman*).
By this [means], Agni has been made ready as a messenger to the abode of Yama.
I place your foot upon the kindled Jātavedas.
(2.12.8.c) May Agni pervade the body; may speech enter the vital breath.
‖8‖ (2.13.1’) O Agni, giver of life, choosing old age—O Agni, whose face is clarified butter, whose back is clarified butter!
(2.13.1.c) Having drunk the clarified butter and the sweet, pleasant product of the cow, protect this man as a father protects his sons. ‖1‖
Clothe him, clothe him with splendor; make him free from death in old age, grant him long life.
Bṛhaspati bestowed this garment upon King Soma that he might put it on. You have put on this garment for well-being; you have become the protector of the young cows against imprecation.
(2.13.3.c) Live for a hundred abundant autumns, and clothe yourself in the nourishment of wealth.
3 (2.13.4’) Come, step upon the stone; let your body be as firm as stone.
(2.13.4.c) May all the gods grant you a lifespan of a hundred autumns. 4
(2.13.5’) You whose garment we take as your first clothing—may all the gods protect you!
(2.13.5.c) May many brothers, increasing and well-born, follow after you as you grow.
5 (2.14.1’) [Drive away] the houseless one, the bold, the bowl-like, the one who speaks alone, the one who desires to devour!
(2.14.1.c) And we destroy all the daughters of Caṇḍa, the Sadānvās.
(2.14.2’) We drive you out from the cow-pen, out from the axle, out from the wagon;
(2.14.2.c) O daughters of Maguṇḍī, we banish you from your homes.
(2.14.3) May those *arāyyas* dwell in that house which is below;
may exhaustion settle there, along with all the *yātudhānīs*.
(2.14.4) May Bhūtapati and Indra drive away this mind [of yours], O Sadānvās.
(2.14.4.c) Sitting upon the foundation of the house, may Indra trample them down with his thunderbolt.
(2.14.5’) Whether you belong to those afflicted by field-disease, or whether you are sent by men, (2.14.5.c) or if you are born from the Dasyus— perish from here, O Sadānvās!
(2.14.6’) I have run around their domains like a swift horse to the goal.
(2.14.6.c) I have won all your races; let the Sadānvās perish from here!
(2.15.1’) Just as heaven and earth do not fear and do not come to harm—
(2.15.1.c) Thus, O Prāṇa, do not be afraid for me.
(2.15.2’) Just as day and night do not fear and do not suffer harm,
(2.15.2.c) thus, O Prāṇa, do not be afraid for me.
Just as the sun and the moon neither fear nor suffer harm, so,
O breath, do not fear for me.
Just as the spiritual power (*brahman*) and the ruling power (*kṣatra*) neither fear nor suffer harm, [so may it be for me].
(2.15.4.c) Thus, O Prāṇa, do not be afraid for me.
(2.15.5’) Just as truth and falsehood do not fear and do not come to harm,
(2.15.5.c) thus, O Prāṇa, do not be afraid for me.
As that which has been and that which is to be do not fear nor suffer harm, so, O Prāṇa, do not fear for me.
6 O Prāṇa and Apāna, protect me from death; Svāhā! 1
O Heaven and Earth, protect me with attentive hearing; svāhā!
O Sūrya, protect me with your eye; svāhā!
O Agni Vaiśvānara, protect me with all the gods; svāhā!
O All-sustainer, protect me with all-sustaining nourishment; Svāhā!
(2.17.1) You are vigor; grant me vigor; Svāhā! (2.17.2) You are strength; grant me strength; Svāhā!
(2.17.3) You are strength; grant me strength, svāhā!
(2.17.4) You are life; grant me life, svāhā!
(2.17.5) You are hearing; grant me hearing, svāhā!
(2.17.6) You are sight; grant me sight, svāhā!
(2.17.7) You are protection; grant me protection, svāhā!
(2.18.1) You are the destruction of rivals; grant me the driving away of rivals, svāhā!
(2.18.2) You are the destroyer of rivals; grant me the driving away of rivals, svāhā!
(2.18.3) You are the destroyer of goblins; grant me the driving away of goblins, svāhā! (2.18.4) You are the destroyer of piśācas; grant me the driving away of piśācas, svāhā!
(2.18.5) You are the constant follower; grant me the constant removal [of enemies]. Svāhā!
(2.19.1) O Agni, with that heat which is yours, burn him who hates us and whom we hate. (2.19.2) O Agni, with that fury which is yours, strike him down who hates us and whom we hate.
(2.19.3) O Agni, with that flame which is yours, strike back at him who hates us and whom we hate.
(2.19.4) O Agni, with that glow which is yours, burn him back who hates us and whom we hate.
(2.19.5) O Agni, with that splendor which is yours, render him lusterless who hates us and whom we hate.
O Vāyu, with that heat which is yours, burn him who hates us and whom we hate. O Vāyu, with that flame which is yours, consume him who hates us and whom we hate.
O Vāyu, with that radiance which is yours, scorch him who hates us and whom we hate.

(2.20.4) O Vāyu, with that splendor which is yours, burn against him who hates us and whom we hate. (2.20.5) O Vāyu, with that brilliance which is yours, render him lusterless who hates us and whom we hate. (2.21.1) O Sūrya, with that heat which is yours, burn against him who hates us and whom we hate.
O Sūrya, with that heat which is yours, strike back at him who hates us and whom we hate.
O Sūrya, with that flame which is yours, blaze back at him who hates us and whom we hate.
O Sūrya, with that glow which is yours, scorch him who hates us and whom we hate.

(2.21.5) O Sūrya, with that splendor which is yours, make him lusterless—he who hates us and whom we hate. (2.22.1) O Candra, with that heat which is yours, burn him in return—he who hates us and whom we hate.
(2.22.2) O Candra, with that consuming power which is yours, consume him in return—he who hates us and whom we hate.
O Moon, with that radiance which is yours, shine back against him who hates us and whom we hate. O Moon, with that glow which is yours, burn against him who hates us and whom we hate.
O Moon, with that splendor which is yours, deprive of splendor him who hates us and whom we hate.
O Waters, with that heat which is yours, burn against him who hates us and whom we hate.
O Waters, with that flame which is yours, seize him who hates us and whom we hate.
O Waters, with that radiance which is yours, scorch him who hates us and whom we hate.
O Waters, with that heat which is yours, burn him who hates us and whom we hate. O Waters, with that brilliance which is yours, deprive him of his brilliance who hates us and whom we hate.
O Śerabhaka, O Śerabha, let your sorceries go back, let the missile of the Kimīdin go back!
(2.24.1.c) Eat him from whom you have come; eat him who sent you here. Eat your own flesh!
(2.24.2’) O Śevṛdhaka, O Śevṛdha, let your sorceries go back again, and back the missile of the Kimīdin! (2.24.2.c) Eat him from whom you have come; eat him who sent you here. Eat your own flesh!
(2.24.3) Let your *mrokas* and *anumrokas* go back, O sorcerers; let your missile go back, O *kimīdin*s! Devour him from whom you come; devour him who sent you; devour your own flesh!
(2.24.4) Let your *sarpas* and *anusarpas* go back, O sorcerers; let your missile go back, O *kimīdin*s!
(2.24.4.c) Devour him from whom you come; devour him who sent you; devour your own flesh!
||4|| (2.24.5’) Let your flames go back, O sorceries; let the missile of the Kimīdin go back!
(2.24.5.c) Devour him from whom you come; devour him who sent you; devour your own flesh! ||5||
(2.24.6) Let your sorceries go back to Upabda, and back your missile, O Kimīdin!
Devour him from whom you come; devour him who sent you; devour your own flesh!
(2.24.7) O Arjuni, let your sorceries go back to you, and back your missile, O Kimīdin!
(2.24.7.c) Devour him from whom you have come; devour him who sent you; devour your own flesh!
7 (2.24.8’) O Bharūjis, let your sorceries go back to their source; let the missile of the Kimīdins return!
(2.24.8.c) Devour him from whom you have come; devour him who sent you; devour your own flesh! 8
May the goddess Pṛśniparṇī bring us peace; she has brought peace away from Nirṛti.
For she is mighty, the crusher of the Kaṇvas; I have consumed that powerful one. This Pṛśniparṇī was born first as the conqueror.
By means of you, I sever the head of those with evil names, like that of a bird.
(2.25.2.c) O Pṛśniparṇī, destroy the Arāya, the blood-drinker, and him who seeks to steal our prosperity; destroy the Kaṇva who devours the embryo, and overcome him! (2.25.3)
(2.25.4’) Lead these Kaṇvas, who seek to preserve their lives, into the mountain! (2.25.4.c) O Goddess Pṛśniparṇī, go forth, burning them up like fire!
(2.25.5’) Drive these Kaṇvas, who seek to preserve their lives, away to the far distance!
I have sent the flesh-eaters to that place where the darknesses go.
May the cattle come hither—those which have passed away, whose companion Vāyu has enjoyed;
may Tvaṣṭṛ, who knows their forms, and Savitṛ establish them here in this cow-pen.
(2.26.2) May the cattle flow together into this pen; may Bṛhaspati lead them here, knowing the way.
(2.26.2c) May Sinīvālī lead them to the forefront; O Anumati, restrain those who have arrived.
(2.26.3) May the cattle flow together, may the horses and the men likewise gather together.
(2.26.3.c) Whatever abundance there is in grain, that I offer with the flowing oblation.
(2.26.4’) I pour together the milk of the cows, together with the strength and essence of the clarified butter;
(2.26.4.c) May our heroes be united, and may the cows remain steadfast with me, their lord.
(2.26.5’) I bring the milk of the cows; I have brought grain and juice.
(2.26.5.c) Our heroes have been brought back, as have our wives; here is this home.
(2.27.1’) Let no enemy gain a share; you are the subduer, the conqueror.
(2.27.1.c) O herb, do thou cause the eater and the one who eats in return to abandon [the poison] and make them tasteless.
(2.27.2’) The fair-winged bird found thee; the boar dug thee up with his snout.
(2.27.2.c) O herb, do thou cause the eater and the one who eats in return to abandon [the poison] and make them tasteless.
Indra indeed placed you in his arm to strike down the Asuras.
O Herb, consume the consumer; destroy him and render him sapless! Indra has devoured the *pāṭā* plant to strike down the Asuras.
(2.27.4.c) O herb, do thou consume the consumer; do thou render [him] sapless.
(2.27.5.a) With that [herb], may I overcome my enemies as Indra [overcame] the *sālāvṛkas*.
(2.27.5.c) O herb, do thou consume the consumer; do thou render [him] sapless.
O Rudra, whose remedy is the cooling balm, blue-crested one, performer of deeds!
O Herb, destroy the consumer and the one who consumes; deprive those who are weak of their strength.
Destroy the consumer of him who assails us, even as Indra does.
(2.27.7.c) Speak for us with your powers; bestow upon me a higher state.
(2.28.1’) May this very man increase in old age for you alone; may other deaths, those hundreds of them, not harm him.

Like a well-disposed mother holding her son in her lap, may Mitra, as a friend, protect him from distress. (2.28.1.c) Like a well-disposed mother holding her son in her lap, may Mitra, as a friend, protect him from distress.
May Mitra and Varuṇa, the destroyers of enemies, acting in harmony, ordain for him a death that comes with old age.
Agni, the Hotṛ-priest who knows all sacred ordinances, proclaims the entire lineage of the gods.
You rule over the cattle of the earth—those already born and those yet to be born.
(2.28.3.c) May neither out-breath nor in-breath desert me; may neither friends nor enemies slay me.
(2.28.4.a) May Heaven as father and Earth as mother, acting in harmony, grant you old age as your death.
(2.28.4.c) So that you may live for a hundred winters, protected by out-breath and in-breath in the lap of Aditi.
O Agni, lead this man to long life and splendor; O King Varuṇa, Mitra, grant him dear progeny.
O Aditi, bestow upon him protection like a mother, so that he may reach old age, O All-Gods.
O Gods, [grant him] the essence of the earthly realm, the body of Bhaga, and strength.
May Agni and Sūrya bestow long life upon him; may Bṛhaspati bestow splendor.
(1) O Jātavedas, grant him long life; O Tvaṣṭṛ, bestow progeny upon him.
O Savitṛ, impel for him the increase of wealth; may he live a hundred autumns through you. (2)
Grant us blessings, nourishment, and good offspring; bestow upon us wisdom and wealth, O you two of one mind!
May Indra, conquering with might, win the fields and cast our rivals beneath us. Given by Indra, instructed by Varuṇa, and sent forth by the Maruts, the fierce one has come to us.
(2.29.4.c) O Heaven and Earth, in your lap, let him not hunger, let him not thirst.
4 (2.29.5’) O you who are full of vigor, bestow vigor upon him; O you who are full of milk, bestow milk upon him.
(2.29.5.c) Heaven and Earth have bestowed vigor upon him; all the gods, the Maruts, and the waters [have bestowed] vigor. 5
With auspicious [waters] I satiate your heart; free from disease and full of luster, may you rejoice.
Wearing their wondrous form through magic power, let the two Aśvins, dwelling together, drink this stirred potion.
Indra created this in the beginning when he was pierced; it is this very [potion], the undecaying source of strength and self-sustenance, which belongs to you.
(2.29.7.c) Live through many autumns with her, full of luster; let her not fail you—your physicians have prepared her for you.
(2.30.1’) Just as the wind stirs this blade of grass upon the earth, so do I stir your mind, so that you shall be in love with me, so that you shall never turn away from me.
If you two, O Aśvins, lead us together as those who desire, and carry us together; may your blessings come together, and may your thoughts and your vows be in harmony.
When the fair-winged ones, free from disease, desire to speak, they desire to speak.
Let my vital breath enter there, as an arrow enters its quiver.
That which is within is without; that which is without is within.
O Herb, seize the heart of these maidens of every form!
(2.30.5’) This one has come desiring a husband; I have come desiring a wife. (2.30.5.c) Like a neighing horse, I have come together with good fortune.
5 (2.31.1’) That great stone of Indra, which crushes every worm—
With it I grind the worms together like grains of sesame with a millstone.
(2.31.1.c) I have crushed the seen and the unseen; I have also crushed the *kurūru*. All the *algaṇḍu* and *chaluna* worms—we crush them with our word. (2.31.2)
I slay the *algaṇḍu*s with a great weapon; the tormented have become untormented and sapless.

I drive away the remaining ones, both those that are tamed and those that are untamed, by my word, so that not a single worm shall remain. The worms in the intestines, those in the head, and those in the back—[I destroy] the worms.

(2.31.4.c) We crush the worms with our speech—the burrowing ones that obstruct the sacrifice. (2.31.5’) Those worms which are in the mountains, in the forests, in the plants, in the cattle, and within the waters; those which have entered our bodies—all that brood of worms I destroy. (2.31.5.c) I strike down every single generation of worms. (2.31.5) All those worms which are in the mountains, in the forests, in the plants, in the cattle, and within the waters; those which have entered our bodies—all that brood of worms I destroy. May the rising sun destroy the worms; may he, setting, destroy them with his rays—those worms that dwell within the cow.
The four-eyed worm of every form, the speckled one and the white one.
I crush his ribs and I cut off his head.
Like Atri, like Kaṇva, and like Jamadagni, I slay you worms;
by the sacred spell of Agastya, I grind the worms to powder.
Slain is the king of the worms, and their chief architect is slain;
slain is the worm whose mother is slain, whose brother is slain, and whose sister is slain.
Slain are his kinsmen, and slain are those who dwell around him.
(2.32.5.c) Moreover, all those tiny creatures like worms have been slain. (2.32.6.a) I break off your two horns with which you gore; (2.32.6.c) I split open your pouch that contains your poison.
From your two eyes, from your two nostrils, from your two ears, and from your chin—
I pull out the consumption (*yakṣma*) from your head, from your brain, and from your tongue.
From your necks, from your *uṣṇihā* joints, from your vertebrae, and from your spine—
I drive away from you the consumption residing in the shoulders, from the shoulder-blades, and from the arms.
(2.33.2.c) From your heart, from your lungs, from the gall-bladder, and from both sides;
from the kidneys, from the spleen, and from the liver, we drive away your consumption. (2.33.3)
From your intestines, from your bowels, from your rectum, and from your belly;
from your two sides, from your bladder, and from your navel—I tear away your consumption.
From your two thighs, from your two knees, from your two heels, and from your two foreparts—I tear away your consumption.
I root out from you the consumption that is in the anus, that which is in the hips, and that which is in the groin.
(5) From your bones, from your marrow, from your sinews, and from your vessels—from your hands, from your fingers, and from your nails—I root out the consumption. (6)
In every limb, in every hair, in every joint of yours—
the consumption (*yakṣma*) that dwells in your skin, we root out in all directions with the *vībarha* of Kaśyapa.
He who is the Lord of cattle, Paśupati, of four-footed beasts as well as of those that have two feet—
(2.34.1.c) Let him, now released, go to his sacrificial portion; may the increase of wealth attend the sacrificer!

‖1‖ (2.34.2’) Releasing the seed of the world, O gods, grant a path for the sacrificer! (2.34.2.c) Having been brought forward and having stood ready, let that which was performed go to the beloved domain of the gods. ‖2‖
(2.34.3) Those who, observing with mind and eye, looked on while [the victim] was being bound—
may the god Agni release them first, and may Viśvakarman, bestowing progeny, grant them peace.
(2.34.4) Those domestic animals of every form, which, though diverse in appearance, are manifold yet of one nature—
(2.34.4.c) May the god Vāyu release them first, Prajāpati, bestowing them upon offspring.
4 (2.34.5’) May the ancestors, knowing [you], receive you back, as the vital breath returns from the limbs.
(2.34.5.c) Go to heaven; stand firm with your bodies; go to the world of light by the paths traveled by the gods. 5
Those who, while consuming wealth, did not prosper, and for whom the sacrificial fires on their hearths felt remorse—

may Viśvakarman make that ill-sacrificed offering of theirs a well-sacrificed one for us. The seers have declared the lord of the sacrifice to be guilty of sin, excluded from his offspring, and filled with remorse.
May Viśvakarman release us from those drops of water which we have spilled; may he unite us with them.
(2.35.2.c) Thinking himself one who does not give yet drinking the Soma, the wise man, knowing the sacrifice, has not acted according to the proper time.
Whatever sin he has committed while bound, O Viśvakarman, release him for his well-being. (2.35.3.c)
(2.35.4’) Homage be to these terrible seers, to their vision and the truth of their mind!
O Bṛhaspati, O mighty and glorious one, homage; O Viśvakarman, homage to you! Protect us.
(2.35.5’) The eye and the beginning, the mouth of the sacrifice—I offer it with speech, with hearing, and with mind.
(2.35.5.c) May the gods, being well-disposed, come to this sacrifice spread out by Viśvakarman.

5 (2.36.1’) O Agni, may the *saṃbhala* come to our favor; may this maiden come to us together with fortune (*bhaga*). 1c May she be beloved among suitors, beautiful in assemblies; may there be prosperity for her through her husband. 1d
(2.36.2) That which is favored by Soma, favored by Brahman, gathered together by Aryaman, the fortune of the god Dhātṛ—by means of its truth, I perform this finding of a husband.
(2.36.3) O Agni, may this woman find a husband; for King Soma makes her fortunate.
(2.36.3.c) Having given birth to sons, may she become a great queen; having approached her husband, may the fortunate woman shine forth.
(2.36.4’) Just as this handsome, beloved ass has become a pleasant seat for the generous lord among wild beasts, so may this woman be pleasing to Bhaga—dear to her husband and never causing him harm.
Mount the full boat of Bhaga, which does not sink;
by means of it, cross over to the bridegroom who is desired.
O Lord of Wealth, cry out; make the bridegroom well-disposed toward you.
Perform every circumambulation to the right for him who is the desirable husband.
(6) This gold, this bdellium, this ox, and furthermore Bhaga—these have given you over to husbands, so that he may find you according to his desire. (7)
(2.36.7.e) May Savitṛ lead you; may he who is desirable as a husband lead you.
(3.1.1’) May Agni, the wise one, advance against our enemies, burning away the curse and the enemy.
(3.1.1.c) May he, Jātavedas, confound the army of the foes and render them handless. 1.
(3.1.2’) O you fierce Maruts, you stand ready for such a task as this; go forth, crush them, and overcome them!
(3.1.2.c) These suppliants have not been crushed, O Vasus; for Agni, the wise one, shall come forward as their messenger.
2 O Maghavan, against the army of our enemies that acts as a foe toward us—
(3.1.3.c) O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, you and Agni, burn her up! 3 (3.1.4.a) Urged on by you, O Indra, let your two bay steeds go forward; let your thunderbolt go forth, crushing the enemies.
(3.1.4.c) Slay those who face you, those who follow behind, and those who flee away; make their resolve truly subject to yours! 4
O Indra, confound the army of our enemies;
with the speed of fire and wind, destroy them, scattering them in all directions!
Let Indra confound the army, and let the Maruts slay it with their might!
(3.1.6.c) May Agni restore our eyes; may he who was defeated return again. ||6|| (3.2.1’) May Agni, our wise messenger, come toward us, burning away the curse and the enemy.
(3.2.1.c) May he, Jātavedas, confound the minds of our adversaries and render them handless. ||1||
(3.2.2’) This Agni has confounded those thoughts which were in your hearts.
(3.2.2.c) May he blow you away from your dwelling; may he blow you away from every side. (3.2.3’) O Indra, confounding their thoughts, come hither and act according to our intention.
(3.2.3.c) By the rushing force of fire and wind, scatter them in all directions! 3 (3.2.4’) Let their intentions go astray, and let their thoughts be confounded!
(3.2.4.c) Furthermore, whatever is now in their hearts—that of you I utterly destroy! 4
Bewildering the minds of these men, O Apvā, seize their limbs and pass by!
Advance against them; burn them up with anguish in their hearts! Strike down the enemies with a seizing darkness; pierce the foes!
O Maruts, that army of the adversaries which comes against us, vying with us in its might—
(3.2.6.c) Pierce him with lawless darkness, so that they may not know one another. (3.3.1’) He has bellowed; the skillful one has been present here. O Agni, open wide the two far-reaching worlds.
(3.3.1.c) Let the Maruts, possessors of all wealth, harness you. By means of homage, lead that one for whom the oblation is offered.
(3.3.2’) May the ruddy ones bring hither from afar the sage Indra for friendship, when the gods, through the Sautrāmaṇī, have dared to offer the Gāyatrī, the Bṛhatī, and the hymn to him.
(3.3.3’) O King Varuṇa, let him call you from the waters; let Soma call you from the mountains.
(3.3.3.c) May Indra call you from these subjects; becoming a falcon, fly to these people!
‖3‖ {4} (3.3.4’) Let the falcon carry the offering back from the other’s field, where it was wandering, excluded in another’s domain.
(3.3.4.c) O Aśvins, make a path easy for you; O kinsmen, enter into this one together! ‖4‖ {5}
(3.3.5’) Let the rival clans summon you; let the allies rain [favor] upon you.
(3.3.5.c) O Indra and Agni, all the gods have established security for you within the clan.
5 {6} (3.3.6’) Whether it be a kinsman or a stranger who disputes your invocation—
(3.3.6.c) Having turned him away, O Indra, send this one here instead.
(3.4.1’) May the kingdom come to you together with splendor; go forth! As the lord of the people and sole sovereign, rule over them.
(3.4.1.c) O King, let all the quarters invoke you; being worthy of approach and homage, be established here.
(3.4.2’) May the people choose you for sovereignty; may these five divine quarters choose you.
(3.4.2.c) Rest upon the height, upon the summit of the kingdom; from there, as a mighty one, distribute wealth among us!
(3.4.3’) May your kinsmen come toward you with oblations; may Agni, the swift messenger, move about together with them.
(3.4.3.c) May his wives and sons be well-disposed; may that fierce one look upon abundant tribute.

(3.4.4’) Let the Aśvins, both Mitra and Varuṇa, and all the gods and the Maruts call upon you first. Then direct your mind toward the granting of wealth; thereafter, O fierce one, distribute riches among us.
(3.4.4.c) Then direct your mind toward the granting of wealth; thereafter, O fierce one, distribute riches among us.
(3.4.5’) Run forth from the farthest distance! May both Heaven and Earth be auspicious for you.

(3.4.5.c) Thus has this King Varuṇa spoken; he has called you, so come hither to him. 5 (3.4.6’) O Indra, O Indra, go away from men, for you have become acquainted with Varuṇa and are in agreement with him.
(3.4.6.c) He here has called you to your own dwelling; he shall sacrifice to the gods, and he shall arrange the people.
(3.4.7’) The wealthy Pathyās, manifold and diverse in form, have all come together and made for you a wider space.
(3.4.7.c) Let them all, being in agreement, call you hither; O fierce one, being well-disposed, choose the tenth [day] here.
(3.5.1’) This leaf-amulet has come hither, powerful with power, crushing rivals.
(3.5.1.c) May the vigor of the gods and the sap of the plants quicken me with splendor, never failing.
(3.5.2’) O leaf-amulet, bestow sovereignty upon me; bestow wealth upon me.
(3.5.2.c) May I be the innate, most excellent one in the protection of the kingdom.
(3.5.3’) That secret, beloved amulet which the gods placed within the tree—
(3.5.3.c) may the gods grant that to us, together with long life, so that we may wear it.
The leaf of Soma has come hither with power; given by Indra, instructed by Varuṇa, may it be dear to me, shining brightly for long life through a hundred autumns.
The amulet of leaves has ascended upon me for great safety.
(3.5.5.c) So that I may be superior to Aryaman and to his associates.
(3.5.6’) O Parṇa, you who are wise craftsmen, chariot-makers, smiths, and thinkers—make me superior to all those people around me. (3.5.6.c) Make me the overlord of all these folk.
(3.5.7) Those kings who are appointed as rulers, the charioteers, and the village headmen— O Parṇa, do thou place all these people around me as my attendants.
(3.5.8) Thou art Parṇa, the protector of the body, sharing a common origin with me, a hero with me, a hero.
(3.5.8.c) By the splendor of the year, by that I bind you, O amulet!
||8|| (3.6.1’) A male born from a male, the *aśvattha* tree from the *khadira*— (3.6.1.c) may it slay my enemies, those whom I hate and those who hate me! ||1||
(3.6.2’) O Aśvattha, crush those enemies who are fiercely agitated by their own oppression;
strike with Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, and with Mitra and Varuṇa.
(3.6.3’) Just as you, O Aśvattha, were shattered within the great ocean—
(3.6.3.c) Thus, crush all those whom I hate and those who hate me!
(3.6.4’) O Aśvattha tree, you who move as one who conquers, like a bull that has triumphed— (3.6.4.c) through you may we overcome our rivals!
(3.6.5’) May Nirṛti bind them with the unloosable nooses of Death! (3.6.5.c) O Aśvattha, [bind] my enemies—those whom I hate and those who hate me!
(3.6.6’) Just as you, O Aśvattha, climbing the lords of the forest, bring them low.
(3.6.6.c) Thus, shatter the head of my enemy on every side and overcome him!
(3.6.7’) Let them float downward, like a boat severed from its mooring; for those driven away by the *vaibādha* [weapon], there is no returning again.
(3.6.7.c) For those driven away by the *vaibādha*, there is no returning again.
(3.6.8’) We drive away the enemies with our mind, with our thought, and with our sacred prayer; (3.6.8.c) we drive away the enemies with a branch of the *aśvattha* tree.
(3.7.1’) Upon the head of the swift-moving antelope is the healing medicine.
(3.7.1.c) He has driven away the hereditary disease with its horns, scattering it in all directions. ||1|| (3.7.2’) After you, the tawny bull has stepped with his four feet.
(3.7.2.c) O two horns, unfasten that which is knotted within his heart—the hereditary disease. ||2||
(3.7.3) That which shines down like a four-sided roof-cover—
by that we cause all *kṣetriya* disease to perish from your limbs.
(3.7.4) Those two auspicious stars in heaven named Vicṛtī, which are there...
(3.7.4.c) May [the waters] release from the kṣetriya disease the lowest bond and the highest.
4 (3.7.5’) The waters indeed are healers; the waters drive away disease.
(3.7.5.c) The waters are the healers of all; may they release you from the kṣetriya disease. 5
Whatever *kṣetriya* has entered you while the pressing was being performed—I know the remedy for that; I cause the *kṣetriya* to perish from you.
At the departure of the stars, and at the departure of the dawns.
(3.7.7.c) May all that is ill-omened depart from us; may the *kṣetriya* disease be driven away!
(3.8.1’) May Mitra come, conforming to the seasons, causing the earth to settle with the rays of light. Then may Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Agni bestow upon us a vast kingdom to be settled. 1.
May Mitra come, conforming to the seasons, causing the earth to settle with the rays of light. Then may Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Agni bestow upon us a vast kingdom to be settled. 1.
May Dhātṛ, Rāti, and Savitṛ enjoy this; may Indra and Tvaṣṭṛ welcome my speech.

I invoke the goddess Aditi, mother of heroes, so that I may stand in the midst of my kinsmen as their leader. With prostrations, I invoke Soma and Savitṛ, and all the Ādityas, for the sake of superiority.
(3.8.3.c) This Agni has shone forth, kindled for a long time by his kinsmen who do not oppose him.
‖3‖ (3.8.4’) Stay right here; do not go away! May the noble protector, the lord of prosperity, drive you hither.
(3.8.4.c) For this desire, may all the gods come together toward you, O longing ones. ‖4‖
We bend your minds together, your vows together, and your intentions together.
Those who are of divergent vows, we cause them all to bend toward you.
I seize your minds with my mind; follow my thought with your thoughts.
(3.8.6.c) I place your hearts under my control; follow the path along which I have gone! (6) (3.9.1’) Karśapha and Viśapha: Heaven is your father, Earth is your mother.
(3.9.1.c) Just as the gods have decreed, so do you bring it back again! (1)
(3.9.2’) Without spittle they have held it fast; even so was that deed performed by Manu. (3.9.2.c) I make the *viṣkandha* impotent, like the castrating of bulls.
(3.9.3’) Upon a reddish-brown cord, the wise bind that hook.
(3.9.3.c) May Bandhura make Śravasyu, Śuṣma, and Kāvava eunuchs. (3.9.4.a) With that by which you who seek glory move about like gods through the power of Asuras,
(3.9.4.c) as a monkey is a source of ruin to dogs, so may Bandhura and Kāvava be ruined.
(3.9.5’) For I shall revile you for your malice; I shall corrupt the descendant of Kābu. (3.9.5.c) Like swift chariots, you shall rush forth by means of curses.
(3.9.6’) One hundred and one *viṣkandha* demons are stationed throughout the earth.
(3.9.6.c) They first extracted from them for you the amulet that destroys *viṣkandha*.
(3.10.1’) She who first dawned became a milch-cow for Yama;
may she, rich in milk, yield for us [milk] throughout each succeeding year.
The night which the gods welcome as she approaches like a milch-cow,
she who is the consort of the year— may she be auspicious to us.
O Night, you whom we worship as the image of the year.
(3.10.3.c) Endow us with long-lived offspring and with the increase of wealth.
3 (3.10.4’) She is indeed that one who first shone forth; she moves, having entered into these other [waters].
(3.10.4.c) Within her are great powers; the bride has won them, the mother of the ninefold [world]. 4
The pressing-stones of wood have raised their voice, preparing the oblation that belongs to the year.
O Ekāṣṭakā, may we be possessed of good offspring and brave sons; may we be masters of riches.
O Jātavedas, accept these offerings at the footprint of Iḍā, which is dripping with clarified butter and crawling about.
(3.10.6.c) May the delight of those seven domestic animals of every form abide with me.
(3.10.7.a) O Night, bring me nourishment and abundance; may we remain in the good favor of the gods.
(3.10.7.c) Fly away, O ladle, full of food; fly back again, well-filled!
(3.10.7.e) Enjoying all sacrifices, bring us nourishment and vigor.
(3.10.8’) This year has come, O Ekāṣṭakā, you who are its mistress. As such, endow our offspring with long life and unite them with the increase of wealth.
(3.10.9’) Sacrifice to the seasons, to the lords of the seasons, and to the seasonal periods;
(3.10.9.c) to the years, the full years, and the months—sacrifice to the Lord of Being.
(3.10.10’) For the seasons, for the seasonal periods, for the months, and for the full years, [I take] you.
(3.10.10.c) I sacrifice to Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Samṛdh, and the Lord of Beings.
||10|| (3.10.11’) Sacrificing with the *iḍā* and with clarified butter, we worship the gods;
may we enter homes that are not stingy and are rich in cattle. ||11||
The Ekāṣṭakā, performing austerities, gave birth to a child, Indra, the embodiment of greatness. Through him, the gods overcame their enemies; he became the slayer of the Dasyus, the Lord of Śacī.
O daughter of Prajāpati, you are the daughter of Indra’s son, the son of Soma.
(3.10.13.c) Fulfill our desires; accept our oblation!
‖13‖ (3.11.1’) I release you with this oblation so that you may live, from unknown wasting disease and from royal consumption.
If the Grāhi-demon has seized him, O Indra and Agni, release him from her! ‖1‖
Whether his life-span has been exhausted, or he has passed away, or is already at the very threshold of death— I bring him back from the lap of Destruction, untouched by harm, for a hundred autumns.
With an oblation that possesses a thousand eyes, a hundredfold power, and a hundredfold life, I have brought him back.
(3.11.3.c) May Indra lead him through autumns to the further shore of all misfortune.
3 (3.11.4’) Live for a hundred autumns, growing in strength; live for a hundred winters and a hundred springs!
(3.11.4.c) For a hundred years, may Indra, Agni, Savitṛ, and Bṛhaspati bring him here with this oblation that bestows a hundredfold life. 4
Enter, O out-breath and in-breath, like two oxen into their pen.
Let other deaths pass away—those which they call the hundred others.
Stay right here, O out-breath and in-breath; do not go from us!
(3.11.6.c) Carry this body’s limbs back again unto old age!
(3.11.7’) I entrust you to old age; I commit you to old age.
(3.11.7.c) May auspicious old age lead you; let other deaths pass away—those which they call the other hundred.

(3.11.8’) O you who have been laid hold of by old age, as one binds an ox or a bull with a rope— (3.11.8.c) That death which bound you with a strong noose as soon as you were born— (3.11.8.e) Bṛhaspati has released it for you with the hands of Truth. ||8||
Right here I fix the firm dwelling; may it stand secure, sprinkling with clarity.
O house, may we approach you with all our heroes, with excellent heroes, with unharmed heroes.
Right here, O house, stand firm—rich in horses, rich in cattle, and full of abundance.
(3.12.2.c) Rich in vigor, rich in clarity, rich in milk, rise up for great good fortune!
(3.12.3’) You are a support, O house, with lofty roof-rafters and abundant grain. (3.12.3.c) May the calf come to you, may the boy come, and may the milch-cows come in the evening, lowing softly.
May Savitṛ, Vāyu, Indra, and Bṛhaspati, who knows all, lay down the foundation of this hall.
May the Rudras and Maruts sprinkle it with ghee; may King Bhaga extend our cultivation.
O Mistress of the measurement, be a refuge, a pleasant one; O Goddess, you have been laid down first by the gods.
(3.12.5.c) Wearing grass, you were well-disposed; now grant us wealth together with heroic sons.
(5) (3.12.6’) By means of Truth, ascend the pillar, O mighty beam; shining forth, drive away our enemies.
(3.12.6.c) May those who dwell within you not come to harm; in this house, O hall, may we live for a hundred autumns with all our heroes. (6)
(3.12.7) Here comes the young boy, the calf, together with the moving world; here come the jars of *parisrut* liquor and the vessels of curd.
(3.12.8) O woman, bring forward this full jar, filled with a stream of ghee and prepared with the immortal nectar.
(3.12.8.c) Anoint these drinkers with immortality; may it protect this [house] along with the merit of sacrifices and charitable gifts.
(3.12.9’) I bring forward these waters, free from disease and destroyers of disease; I settle into the house together with Agni and immortality.
(3.12.9.c) I settle into the house together with Agni and immortality. 9.

When you were flowing together there, crying out as the dragon was slain, from that [moment] you have been called by the name "Nadyas" (Rivers); these are your names, O Sindhus. When, sent forth by Varuṇa, you leaped together swiftly, [from that moment you were called rivers].
Indra reached you as you were fleeing; therefore, O Waters, you flowed forth for him.
(3.13.2.c) Flowing according to his will, he indeed opened a path for you;
for Indra, O Goddesses, by means of his powers, [gave] you your name "Vār" (the warder-off). (3.13.3.c)
(3.13.4) "A single god stood over you as you flowed according to your will;
they brought you forth as the great ones—therefore water is called *udaka*.
(3.13.5) "The waters were auspicious, the waters were indeed clarified butter; those waters bear Agni and Soma within them."
(3.13.5.c) May the intense essence of the honeyed [Soma]s, which goes readily to us, come to me with breath and luster.
5 (3.13.6’) Then indeed I see, or else I hear; the sound of them comes to me, their voice. (3.13.6.c) I think that I have partaken of immortality when I was sated by you, O golden-hued ones. 6
(3.13.7’) This, O Waters, is your heart; this is your calf, O you who follow the cosmic order (*ṛtāvarī*).
Come here in this manner, O powerful ones (*śakvarī*), to where I settle you. (3.14.1’) May you be united with a comfortable cow-pen, united with wealth, and united with prosperity.
(3.14.1.c) With that name which was given at birth, we unite you with it.
||1|| (3.14.2’) May Aryaman unite you; may Pūṣan unite you; may Bṛhaspati unite you;
(3.14.2.c) and Indra, the winner of wealth—may whatever riches there are flourish within me. ||2||
Coming together without fear in this stall, you who are covered in dung, bearing the honeyed soma-juice, come hither free from disease.
O cows, stay right here; thrive here like young fawns.
