(3.14.6’) “O cows, be united with me, your lord! This is your stall; here it shall nourish you.
Becoming abundant through the increase of wealth, may we, living and keeping you alive, dwell near you.
(6) (3.15.1’) “I impel Indra the merchant; let him come to us. Let him be our leader.”
Driving away the stingy adversary who lies in wait like a wild beast, may he, the sovereign lord, be a giver of wealth to me.
May those many paths traveled by the gods that traverse the space between heaven and earth favor me with milk and clarified butter, so that having purchased [the goods], I may bring home wealth.
(3.15.3’) O Agni, desiring [success], with fuel and ghee I offer this oblation for speed and strength.
(3.15.3.c) As much as I am able, praising with a prayer, I offer this divine hymn for a hundredfold gain.
3 (3.15.4’) O Agni, forgive us this transgression, this path which we have traveled far.
(3.15.4.c) May our buying be auspicious, as well as our selling and our bargaining; may it make me successful in my trade.
(3.15.4.e) Rejoicing together, may you both accept this oblation; may our movement and our standing still be auspicious.
(3.15.5’) O Gods, with that wealth by which I carry on my buying, desiring wealth with that very wealth—

(3.15.5.c) May that become more for me, not less; O Agni, slayer of the stingy, settle the gods with the oblation. as such, be watchful for us over our offspring, our bodies, our cattle, and our vital breaths.
(3.15.8) May we bring to you all things at all times, O Jātavedas, as one brings fodder to a standing horse.
(3.15.8.c) Rejoicing in the increase of wealth and in nourishment, may we, O Agni, as your neighbors, suffer no harm.
8 (3.16.1’) At dawn we invoke Agni; at dawn Indra; at dawn Mitra and Varuṇa; at dawn the Aśvins.
(3.16.1.c) At dawn Bhaga, Pūṣan, and Brahmaṇaspati; at dawn we invoke Soma and Rudra. 1
We invoke the fierce Bhaga, the winner in the morning, the son of Aditi who is the distributor.
Even the weak man, even the swift one, even the king—each says of him, "May I partake of Bhaga.
O Bhaga, leader; O Bhaga, whose gifts are true; O Bhaga, favor this prayer and grant us wealth.
O Bhaga, further us with cattle and horses; O Bhaga, may we be rich in men through our heroes.
(3.16.3.c) And may we be blessed even now, and at the beginning of the day, and at its midpoint;
and at the rising of the sun, O Maghavan, may we abide in the good favor of the gods. (3.16.4)
(3.16.5’) May the god Bhaga indeed be the Lord; through him may we become possessed of fortune.
(3.16.5.c) O Bhaga, I call upon you with all my heart; as such, O Bhaga, be our leader here.
5 (3.16.6’) Let the dawns incline toward the sacrifices, as [they do] toward the pure station of Dadhikrāvan.
(3.16.6.c) May the horses bring hither to me Bhaga, the finder of wealth, as swift steeds draw a chariot.

(3.16.7’) May the auspicious Dawns ever shine upon us—rich in horses, rich in cattle, and rich in heroes; yielding clarified butter and overflowing on every side. Do you, O gods, protect us always with your blessings. (3.16.7.c) Do you, O gods, protect us always with your blessings.
The seers yoke the ploughs; they stretch out the yokes separately, the wise ones seeking favor among the gods.
Yoke the ploughs, stretch out the yokes; sow the seed here in the prepared womb.
(3.17.2.c) May Virāja’s ploughing be fruitful and bring us abundance; may the sickle come ever closer to the ripened grain.
(3.17.3’) Let the plough, tipped with iron, well-pointed, with Soma as its handle, turn up the earth—cattle and sheep, a wagon for transport, and a stout, prolific mare.
May Indra take hold of the furrow; may Pūṣan protect it.
May she, rich in milk, yield for us [milk] year after year.
May the good ploughshares cleave the earth auspiciously; may the ploughmen follow their draft-animals auspiciously.
(3.17.5.c) O Śunāsīra, being gratified by the oblation, make the plants bear fine fruit for him.
5 (3.17.6’) May the draft-animals be auspicious, may the men be auspicious; may the plough furrow auspiciously.
(3.17.6.c) May the thongs be bound auspiciously; raise the goad auspiciously. 6
O Śuna and Sīra, may you both take pleasure here in my offering;
with that milk which you created in heaven, sprinkle this earth!
O Sītā, we revere you; O auspicious one, turn toward us.

(3.17.8.c) So that you may be well-disposed toward us, so that you may become fruitful for us. (3.17.9’) The furrow, anointed with ghee and honey, approved by all the gods and the Maruts—O Sītā, turn toward us with milk, swelling with vigor and rich in ghee. I dig up this herb, the most powerful of plants,
by which one overcomes a rival wife and by which one wins a husband. O you with upward-pointing leaves, auspicious one, impelled by the gods, victorious one!
(3.18.2.c) Drive my rival wife away; make my husband mine alone.
(3.18.3’) For she has not taken your name, nor does she take delight in this husband of yours.
We send the rival wife far, even to the furthest distance. (3.18.3.c) We cause the rival wife to go to the most remote region.
I am the superior; may I rise above those who are superior.
May my rival be beneath me; may she who is lower remain lower than those who are low. I am the conqueror, and you are the one who conquers.
(3.18.5.c) Having both become powerful, let us two together overcome my rival wife.

(3.18.6’) I have placed you upon the conquering one; I have placed you near the more powerful one. May your mind run toward me like a cow toward her calf; may it run along the path like water toward a cataract.
Sharpened for me is this sacred formulation (*brahman*), sharpened is my vigor and strength;
may the sovereign power (*kṣatra*) of those for whom I am the domestic priest be sharpened, undecaying, and victorious.
May I unite their kingdom, and may I unite their energy, vigor, and strength.
(3.19.2.c) With this oblation, I sever the arms of my enemies.
(3.19.3’) Let them fall low; let those who would attack our patron, our generous lord, be cast down. (3.19.3.c) By means of sacred prayer (*brahman*), I destroy the foes and I raise up my own people.
Sharper than the axe and even sharper than fire, more keen than Indra’s thunderbolt are those for whom I am the domestic priest.
I harness their weapons together; I cause their kingdom to prosper with heroic sons.
(3.19.5.c) May their dominion be invincible and undecaying; may all the gods favor their resolve.
(3.19.6’) O Maghavan, let the strengths of our horses be roused; let the shout of the victorious heroes go forth.
Let the various shouts, tumultuous and accompanied by banners, arise on high.
(3.19.6.e) Let the gods, with Indra as their chief, and the Maruts come with their army!
‖6‖ (3.19.7’) Go forth, conquer, O men! Let your arms be fierce!
(3.19.7.c) With sharp arrows and strong bows, you who possess terrible weapons, let those with fierce arms slay the weak! ‖7‖
(3.19.8’) Loosed, fly away into the range of arrows, sharpened by the sacred word (*brahman*).
Conquer the enemies, fall upon them, and slay their best man after best man; let not one of them escape me.
(3.20.1’) This is your seasonal womb, from which born you shone forth.
Knowing this, O Agni, ascend it, and then increase our wealth for us.
(1) O Agni, speak here to us; turn toward us with a benevolent mind.
Bestow upon us, O Lord of the People; you are the giver of wealth to us. (2)
May Aryaman grant us wealth, may Bhaga, may Bṛhaspati; may the goddesses and Sūnṛtā likewise; may the goddess bestow riches upon me.
We invoke King Soma for our protection, and Agni with our songs of praise.
(3.20.4.c) To Āditya, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Brahmā, and Bṛhaspati.
(3.20.5’) O Agni, with thy fires, increase our prayer and sacrifice;
O God, impel us to bestow wealth upon us for the sake of giving. (3.20.5.c) 5.
We invoke both Indra and Vāyu here, the two who are easy to call upon, so that all people may be well-disposed toward us in our assembly and that they may be desirous of giving to us.
(6) Urge Aryaman, Bṛhaspati, and Indra to grant us gifts. (7)
(3.20.7.c) Vāta, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, and Savitṛ the vigorous;
||7|| (3.20.8’) Now, at the impulse of strength, we have come together within all these worlds.
(3.20.8.c) May he, knowing all, cause him who is unwilling to give to give; and bestow upon us wealth consisting of all heroic sons. ||8||
May the five regions yield for me; may the broad expanses yield according to my strength.
May I attain all my intentions, both with my mind and with my heart.
May I utter speech that wins cattle; may splendor rise up toward me.
(3.20.10.c) May Vāyu encompass [me] from all sides; may Tvaṣṭṛ bestow prosperity upon me.
||10|| (3.21.1’) Those fires that are within the waters, those in Vṛtra, those in man, and those in stones;
(3.21.1.c) he who has entered the plants and he who has entered the trees—to those fires let this be offered as an oblation. ||1||
(3.21.2) That which is within the Soma, that which is within the cattle, that which has entered into birds and that which is in wild beasts;
(3.21.2c) that which has entered into bipeds and that which [has entered] into quadrupeds—may this be offered as an oblation to those Agnis.
(3.21.3) The god who travels on the same chariot with Indra, Vaiśvānara, who is all-bestowing;
(3.21.3.c) To those Agnis whom I invoke as the conqueror in battles—to them let this offering be made.
(3.21.4’) He who is the god of all, whom they call desire, whom they call the giver and the receiver;
he who is wise, powerful, all-encompassing, and invincible—to those Agnis let this offering be made.
(3.21.5’) To you, whom the thirteen Bhauvanas and the five Mānavas have recognized in their minds as the Hotṛ-priest—
to those Agnis, may this offering be made for the sake of splendor, glory, and truthful abundance.
(3.21.6’) To the Ordainer who feeds on bulls and cows, whose back is sprinkled with Soma—
May this be an offering to those Agnis, of whom Vaiśvānara is the eldest.
(3.21.6.c) To those who traverse along heaven, earth, and the intermediate space, who follow the lightning;
to those who are within the quarters or within the wind—to those Agnis, may this be an offering. (3.21.7)
We invoke Savitṛ of the golden hands, Indra, Bṛhaspati, Varuṇa, Mitra, Agni, all the gods, and the Aṅgirases; may they pacify this flesh-eating Agni.
(3.21.9) Agni the flesh-eater is pacified; he who seeks out men is pacified.
And furthermore, that which devours all things, the flesh-eater, I have quelled.
(9) The mountains whose backs are laden with Soma, the waters flowing on their backs, Vāta, Parjanya, and Agni—these have quelled the flesh-eater. (10)
May the great glory, possessing the luster of an elephant, which was produced from the body of Aditi, spread forth.
May all the gods and Aditi, acting in harmony, bestow this upon me.
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, and Rudra take heed.
(3.22.2.c) May the gods, the sustainers of all, anoint me with splendor!
2 (3.22.3’) With that splendor by which the elephant became possessed of splendor, by which the king [became so] among men, and within the waters;
(3.22.3.c) with that splendor by which the gods attained godhood in the beginning—with that, O Agni, make me splendid today! 3
Whatever great luster belongs to you, O Jātavedas, arising from the oblation—
as much as is the luster of the sun and of the elephant of the Asuras— so much luster may the Aśvins, wreathed with lotuses, bestow upon me. 4.
As far as the four quarters extend, and as far as the eye reaches—so far let the sensory power come to me; let that splendor of an elephant be mine.
For the elephant has become the preeminent dweller among well-resting wild beasts.
(3.22.6.c) With his fortune and splendor, I sprinkle myself.
6 (3.23.1’) That by which you became barren—that we cause to perish from you.
(3.23.1.c) Here we set that thing far away from you, elsewhere. 1
(3.23.2’) May a male embryo enter your womb like an arrow into a quiver;
(3.23.2.c) may a heroic son be born here to you, ten months old.
(3.23.3’) Give birth to a male son; may a male be born after him.
May you be the mother of sons already born, and may you give birth to those yet to be born.
By means of those excellent seeds which the bulls produce, may you obtain a son; be a prolific milch-cow.

I prepare for you that which belongs to Prajāpati; let the embryo enter your womb. O woman, may you find a son, and may he be well-disposed toward you, and may you likewise be well-disposed toward him. Of those plants whose father is heaven, whose mother is earth, and whose root is the ocean—
(3.23.6.c) May those divine herbs favor you for the sake of the knowledge of sons.
6 (3.24.1’) The herbs are full of milk; full of milk is my speech.
(3.24.1.c) Therefore, I bring hither from the thousandfold [herbs] that are full of milk. 1
I know him who made [the world] full of milk and abundant grain;
we invoke that god whose name is Saṃbhṛtvan, whoever dwells in the house of the non-sacrificer.
These which are the five directions, the five human tribes—‖2‖
(3.24.3.c) Like rivers that carry away a curse when it has rained, may you bring us abundance here.
(3.24.4’) A fountain with a hundred streams, a thousand streams, inexhaustible—so be this grain of ours, with a thousand streams, inexhaustible. (3.24.4.c) 4.
O you with a hundred hands, gather it; O you with a thousand hands, scatter it!
Bring about the increase of whatever task has been performed here.
The Gandharvas have three measures, and the housewife has four.
Of these, with that which is most full and swelling, we touch you.
Both Upoha and Samūha are your two attendants, O Prajāpati;
may they bring here great swelling, abundance, and inexhaustible prosperity.
Let the pricking one prick thee; do not hold fast upon thy own bed.
With that arrow of desire which is terrible, with that I pierce thee in the heart.
[With] the arrow whose feathers are longing, whose barb is desire, and whose nock is resolve.
Having made it well-bent, let Kāma pierce you in the heart.
That well-bent arrow of Kāma which withers the spleen—
having forward feathers and triple heat— with that I pierce you in the heart.
Pierced by grief, burning with fever, and with a parched mouth, crawl away!
Be gentle, free from anger, devoted solely to me, speaking kindly, and faithful to my will.
You were born from the womb of a noble woman, from the mother and likewise from the father.
(3.25.5.c) Just as you have been in my ritual intention, so do you conform to my thought.
(3.25.6’) O Mitra and Varuṇa, cast away her thoughts from her heart; then, having deprived her of willpower, bring her under my control alone.
(3.25.6.c) Then, having deprived her of willpower, bring her under my control alone.
(3.26.1) O gods named Hetayas who abide in this eastern quarter, Agni is your arrow. Be gracious to us; speak for us; homage to you, svāhā!
(3.26.2) O gods named Aviṣyavas who abide in this southern quarter, Desire is your arrow.
(3.26.2.c) Be gracious to us; speak for us; to you [we offer] homage, to you *svāhā*!
‖2‖ (3.26.3’) O gods named Vairājas who dwell in this western quarter, waters are your arrows. (3.26.3.c) Be gracious to us; speak for us; to you [we offer] homage, to you *svāhā*! ‖3‖

(3.26.4) O gods who abide in this northern quarter, you whose name is Pravidhyanta, the wind is your arrow. Be gracious to us; speak for us; homage to you, svāhā to you! (3.26.5) O gods who abide in this fixed quarter, you whose name is Nilmipa, the plants are your arrows.
(3.26.5.c) Be gracious to us; speak for us; to you we pay homage, to you be *svāhā*!

‖5‖ (3.26.6’) O gods who dwell in this upward direction, whose name is "Possessors of Wealth" (*avasvanta*), Bṛhaspati is your arrow. (3.26.6.c) Be gracious to us; speak for us; to you we pay homage, to you be *svāhā*! ‖6‖
The eastern direction has Agni as its overlord, the black snake as its guardian, and the Ādityas as its arrows.
Homage to them, the overlords; homage to the guardians; homage to the arrows; let there be homage to these!
The southern quarter has Indra as its overlord, Tiraścīrājī as its guardian, and the Fathers as its arrows.
Homage to these overlords, homage to the guardians, homage to the arrows; let there be homage to them!
Whoever hates us and whom we hate, him we place within the jaws of you [arrows]. 2.
The western quarter has Varuṇa as its overlord, the viper as its guardian, and food as its arrows.
Homage to them, the overlords; homage to the guardians; homage to the arrows; let there be homage to these.
The northern direction: Soma is its overlord, the Svaja-serpent its guardian, and the thunderbolt its arrows.
Homage to these overlords, homage to the guardians, homage to the arrows; let there be homage to them!
Whoever hates us and whom we hate, him we place within the jaws of you [all]. 4.
The fixed direction has Viṣṇu as its overlord; Kalmāṣagrīva is its protector; plants are its arrows.
Homage to them, the overlords; homage to the protectors; homage to the arrows; let there be homage to these!
Whoever hates us and whom we hate, him we place within the jaws of you [arrows]. 5.

The upward direction has Bṛhaspati as its overlord; Śvitra is its guardian; rain is its arrows. Homage to them, the overlords; homage to the guardians; homage to the arrows; let there be homage to these!
Whoever hates us and whom we hate, him we place within the jaws of you [all]. 6.
She has become one with each of these creations, wherein the creators of beings produced cows of every form.
Therein is born the female who does not bring forth in season; she, hissing and glowing, destroys the cattle.
Having become a flesh-eater and a devourer, she consumes the cattle.
(3.28.2.c) Moreover, one should give her to a Brahmin; thus she shall be pleasant and auspicious.
(3.28.3’) Be auspicious toward men, toward cattle, and toward horses;
(3.28.3.c) be auspicious toward this entire field, and be auspicious to us here.
(3.28.4) Here is nourishment, here is sap; here become the best of those who win a thousandfold! (3.28.4c) O controller, cause the cattle to thrive!
(3.28.5) Where the benevolent doers of good rejoice, having cast off disease from their own bodies.

(3.28.5.c) That world which Yami has entered—may she not harm our men and cattle! (3.28.6’) Where there is a world for those of good intent, for the doers of good deeds, and for those who have offered the Agnihotra sacrifice—that world which Yami has entered—may she not harm our men and cattle! Whatever sixteenth part of the merit of sacrifices and charitable works the kings distribute, those members of Yama’s assembly take it away.
Therefore, the white-footed sheep, when given, releases one from that [debt]; it is the *svadhā* offering.
Filling all desires, it is the source of prosperity, the power of prosperity, and prosperity itself.
The ram given by Ākūti, the white-footed one, does not fail us.
He who gives a white-footed sheep, commensurate with the world,
ascends to the firmament where no toll is paid for the weak against the stronger.
One who bestows a sheep with five cakes and white feet, which is commensurate with the world,
lives on inexhaustibly in the world of the ancestors.
One who bestows a sheep with five cakes and white feet, which is commensurate with the world...
The giver lives on the inexhaustible [merit] of Sūrya and Māsa. Like a stream, it does not fail; like the great ocean, its water does not fail.
Like two gods dwelling together, the one with white feet does not fail.
Who has given this to whom? Desire has given it to desire. Desire is the giver; desire is the receiver. Desire has entered the ocean.
With desire I receive you; O Desire, this is yours.
(3.29.8’) May the earth receive you; may this great intermediate space [receive you].
(3.29.8.c) Having received [this], may I not be deprived of my breath, my self, or my progeny.
8 (3.30.1’) I create for you a shared heart, a state of concord, and freedom from enmity.

(3.30.1.c) Let each take pleasure in the other, as the cow does for her newborn calf. (3.30.2’) Let the son be devoted to his father and be of one mind with his mother; let the wife speak honeyed and auspicious words to her husband.

Let not brother hate his brother, nor sister her sister; becoming harmonious and of one vow, speak your speech with auspiciousness. [That] by which the gods do not fall apart, nor do they hate one another.
Therefore, we perform this sacred prayer (*brahman*) in your house for the sake of mutual recognition among men.
May you, being superior, wise, and striving for success, move together as companions; speaking kindly to one another, come here. I make you harmonious and of one mind.
Common is the water-trough for you, common your share of food; with one and the same thong I bind you together.
Together, pay homage to Agni as if to a central navel from all sides.
I make you all turn toward one another, of one mind, sharing a single enjoyment through this means of reconciliation.
Like gods guarding the nectar of immortality, may there be goodwill for you every evening and morning. May the gods keep old age away; may you, O Agni, keep it away from ill-will.
May I be separated from all evil and from disease, and united with long life.
May Pavamāna drive away misfortune; may the powerful one [drive away] evil-doing.
May I be separated from all evil and from consumption, and be united with long life.
May the domestic animals be separated from those of the forest; may the waters flow away from thirst.
I have separated myself from all evil, from consumption; I am united with life. May Heaven and Earth depart from me, may the paths in every direction depart;
I have separated myself from all evil, from consumption; I am united with life.
(3.31.5’) “Tvaṣṭṛ yokes the bridal procession for his daughter,” so saying, this entire world moves apart.
(3.31.5.c) May I be separated from all evil, separated from consumption; may I be united with long life. (3.31.6’) Agni restores the breaths; the Moon is joined with breath.
I have separated myself from all evil, from consumption; I am united with life. With breath, the gods sent forth the sun, whose strength is all-pervading;
I have separated myself from all evil, from consumption; I am united with life.
(3.31.8) Of the long-lived ones, the makers of life—live by their breath, do not die!
(3.31.8c) May I be separated from every evil, separated from consumption, and united with life!
(3.31.9) By the breath of those who breathe, live right here; do not die!
I have separated myself from all evil, from consumption, and been united with life.
(9) Up with life, up with life, up with the essence of the plants! I have separated myself from all evil, from consumption, and been united with life. (10)
Through the rain of Parjanya we have risen up as immortals;
I have separated myself from all evil, from consumption, and have united with long life.
The Brahman, first born in the east, Vena has revealed from the radiant horizon.
(4.1.1.c) His foundations, his highest manifestations, the womb of both the existent and the non-existent—you have revealed them for us.
(4.1.2’) Let this ancestral, royal power go forth at the beginning, established in the world for the first-born.
(4.1.2.c) For him, let them prepare this bright, golden vessel, the heated offering, for the first sustenance.
(4.1.3’) He who was born as the knower, his kinship is with this [world]; he proclaims all the generations of the gods.

(4.1.3.c) From the midst of the sacred formulation (*brahman*), he brought forth the sacred formulation; he established himself toward the self-sustaining powers (*svadhā*), both low and high. 3. (4.1.4’) For he knows [it], he stands upon the earth according to cosmic order (*ṛta*); he has propped up the two great worlds, heaven and earth, for the sake of security.

(4.1.4.c) The Great One, once born, propped up the vast heaven and the earthly dwelling-place. (4.1.5’) From the foundation of the earth, Bṛhaspati, the sovereign lord among the gods, attained preeminence by his very birth.
(4.1.5.c) When the bright day was born from the light, then may the inspired sages shine forth in splendor.
(4.1.6’) Surely Kāvya stirs up that ancient majesty of this great god; he was born together with many, even so, when the eastern slope was loosened, he lay there.
(4.1.7’) He who would go with reverence to Bṛhaspati, the father Atharvan, the kinsman of the gods—

(4.1.7.c) You are the progenitor of all, as you are; may the self-dependent seer-god not be deceived. 7 (4.2.1’) He who gives life, who gives strength, whose command all wait upon, whose command the gods obey;
he who rules over these bipeds and quadrupeds—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation? 1
(4.2.2’) He who by his greatness became the sole king of the breathing and blinking world;
(4.2.2.c) whose shadow is immortality and whose [shadow] is death—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
(4.2.3’) He whom the two contending armies invoked when they took their stand and the two worlds, trembling in fear, called upon.

(4.2.3.c) He whose path measures across the realm of dust—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation? (3) (4.2.4’) He to whom belong the vast sky and the great earth, and to whom belongs the wide intermediate space;
(4.2.4.c) he by whose greatness that sun is spread out—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation? (4)
(4.2.5’) He whose greatness all the snowy mountains proclaim, and of whom they say the ocean is but a drop;
(4.2.5.c) he whose two arms are these quarters of space—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
(4.2.6’) In the beginning, the waters, knowing the eternal Law (*ṛta*), bore the universe as an embryo, being immortal and wise.
(4.2.6.c) Upon which goddesses the god was seated—to which god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
(6) (4.2.7’) In the beginning, the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha) came into being; once born, he was the sole Lord of all that exists.
(4.2.7.c) He supported both the earth and the sky—to which god shall we offer worship with our oblation? (7)
The waters, generating the calf, brought forth the embryo in the beginning. And as it was being born, its amnion was golden. To what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
Three have stepped out from here: the tiger, the man, and the wolf.
(4.3.1.c) Apart go the rivers; apart stands the divine tree; let the enemies bend away.
(4.3.2’) Let the wolf go by a distant path, and even further still the thief; (4.3.2.c) let the toothed rope be far away, and let the malevolent one flee far off.
We rend your two eyes and your mouth, O tiger;
then all twenty of your claws. We rend first the tusked tiger.
(4.3.4.c) Moreover, [crush] the thief, and likewise the serpent, the sorcerer, and the wolf.
(4.3.5’) The thief who approaches today departs crushed; let him go by the ruin of his paths; may Indra strike him down with his thunderbolt.
(4.3.5.c) Let him go by the ruin of his paths; may Indra strike him down with his thunderbolt.
(4.3.6’) The teeth of the beast are crushed, and its ribs are shattered.
(4.3.6.c) Let the lizard be your snare; let the beast lie low and hidden.
(4.3.7’) That which is binding is not unbinding, and that which is unbinding is not binding.
(4.3.7.c) Born of Indra, born of Soma, you are the Atharvanic plant that crushes tigers.
(4.4.1’) You whom the Gandharva dug up for Varuṇa when his virility was destroyed— (4.4.1.c) as such, we dig you up, O herb, the stimulator of the penis.
Up has dawned the Dawn; up has the Sun; up has this my word arisen.
Let Prajāpati, the bull, rise up with vigorous strength. Just as when you were growing, [the world] bends down as if scorched by your heat.
(4.4.3.c) Then may this herb make you more vigorous.
(3) (4.4.4’) The vigor of herbs, the essence of bulls— (4.4.4.c) O Indra, lord of the body, bestow upon this man the virility of males. (4)
(4.4.5’) You are the first-born essence of the waters, and likewise of the trees;
(4.4.5.c) you are the brother of Soma, and you are the virile power of the Ṛṣi.
5 (4.4.6’) Today, O Agni; today, O Savitṛ; today, O Goddess Sarasvatī!
(4.4.6.c) Today, O Brahmanaspati, stretch his limbs like a bow. (4.4.7’) I stretch your limbs as one stretches a string upon a bow;
stride forth like a deer toward a red bull, never flagging!
Of the horse, the mule, the goat, and the ram;
and now, O lord of the body, bestow upon this man those vital strengths which belong to the bull.
The bull with a thousand horns who rose up from the ocean—[bestow his strength upon him].
(4.5.1.c) By means of that forceful one, we lull the people to sleep.
(1) (4.5.2’) The wind does not blow over the earth, nor does anyone see anything;
(4.5.2.c) lull all the women and the dogs to sleep as you move about, O friend of Indra! (2)
(4.5.3) Those women who sleep on couches, those who sleep on beds, and those who sleep in litters—(4.5.3c) all those women who possess auspicious fragrances, we cause them to sleep.
(4.5.4) That which stirs, I have seized; I have seized the eye and the breath.
(4.5.4.c) I have seized all their limbs during the deepening of the night.
(4.5.5’) He who sits, he who moves, and he who stands looking about—
of them we set the eyes together, so that they may see as this dwelling-place does.

(4.5.6’) Let the mother sleep; let the father sleep; let the dog sleep; let the lord of the house sleep. (4.5.6.c) Let her kinsmen sleep; let this person around her sleep. 6. (4.5.7’) O Sleep, by means of your instrument of sleep, lull all the people to rest.
(4.5.7.c) May others sleep until the sun rises; may I remain awake until the dawn. Unharmed and undecaying, may I be like Indra.
(4.6.1’) A Brahmin was born first, ten-headed and ten-faced. He drank the Soma first; he rendered the poison sapless.
As far as heaven and earth extend in their breadth, as far as the seven rivers have spread out—
I have uttered from here that speech which destroys poison.
O poison, the fair-winged Garuḍa first swallowed you.
(4.6.3.c) You did not make me emaciated, nor did you make me deformed; thus you became my father.
(4.6.4’) The five-fingered one who sat upon your mouth, even from the curved bow—(4.6.4.c) from the shaft of the support, I have uttered forth the poison. 4.
From the barb I have spoken the poison out, from the ointment and from the feather-case;
from the shaft, from the horn, and from the barb, I have spoken the poison out.
(4.6.5) O arrow, your barb is sapless, and so too is your poison sapless. (4.6.6)
(4.6.6.c) And of the tree that is sapless, let your bow be sapless and sapless.
(4.6.7’) Those who have crushed it, those who have struck it, those who have bitten it, those who have released it—all these have been made castrated; the poison-mountain has been made castrated.
(4.6.7.c) All these have been made castrated; the poison-mountain has been made castrated.
(4.6.8’) Castrated are your diggers; you, O herb, are castrated. (4.6.8.c) Castrated is that mountain, that hill, from which this poison was born.
(4.7.1’) This water shall ward off [the poison] over Varaṇāvatī.
(4.7.1.c) Therein is poured nectar; with that, I ward off your poison.
(4.7.2’) Tasteless is the poison from the east, tasteless is that which comes from the north; (4.7.2.c) even this [poison] from below is rendered powerless by the *karambha* offering.

Having prepared the groats, the oblique *pības-pāka*, the generous gift— O you of evil teeth, it was indeed hunger that made you devour it; you have not destroyed it. O you who are full of intoxication, we cause your rapture to fall like an arrow.
(4.7.4.c) We steady you with our word, as one steadies a moving sacrificial pap. (4.7.5.a) We steady you with our word, as one encloses a village with a rampart.
(4.7.5.c) Stand firm like a tree upon its base; do not be shattered when struck by the axe.
(4.7.6’) They purchased you with winnowing-baskets, with spears, and with skins.
(4.7.6.c) You are bought out, O herb; do not cause pain where you have been dug up.
(4.7.7’) Those who were the first to perform these deeds for you, though they were unattained—
(4.7.7.c) May they not deceive our heroes here; I place this before you.
(4.8.1’) Having come into being among beings, he bestows milk; he has become the overlord of beings.
(4.8.1.c) His death performs the Rājasūya sacrifice; may that king grant his approval for this.
Advance toward us; do not turn back, O fierce one, mindful slayer of rivals!
Stand firm, O increaser of friends; for you the gods have spoken their word.
As he stands firm, all have adorned him; clothed in glory, he moves, self-luminous.
(4.8.3.c) Great is that name of the bull-like Asura; he, possessing all forms, has taken his stand upon the immortal realms.
(4.8.4’) Stride out over the great quarters like a tiger upon a tiger-skin rug!
Let all the people desire you, and the celestial waters rich with milk. (4.8.4.c) Let all the people desire you, and the celestial waters rich with milk.
(4.8.5’) Those waters that rejoice with milk in heaven, or in the intermediate space, or upon the earth—
(4.8.5.c) with the splendor of all those waters, I sprinkle you. (4.8.6’) The divine, milk-rich waters have sprinkled you with splendor here.
(4.8.6.c) As he is the increaser of friends, so may Savitṛ make you.
(4.8.7’) Embracing this tiger, they urge on the lion for great good fortune;
(4.8.7.c) like the sea, they groom him who stands as a well-formed being—the leopard within the waters.
Come, O living one! This eye of the mountain is a protector.
Given by all the gods, it is a fence for the sake of life. You are a protection for men; you are a protection for cattle.
(4.9.2.c) You stand as a protection for the swift, racing horses.
(4.9.3.a) And you, O ointment, are a protection that crushes the sorcerers;
(4.9.3.c) you know the path to immortality, and you are the sustenance of life, and the remedy for yellow ailments.
O ointment, as you creep from limb to limb and joint to joint,
you drive away the consumption (*yakṣma*) from there, like a fierce man who sits in the midst [of his enemies]. Neither a curse, nor a magical spell (*kṛtyā*), nor a consuming fever reaches him.
(4.9.5.c) Viṣkandha does not seize him who applies you, O ointment.
(4.9.6’) From evil incantations, from bad dreams, from ill deeds, and even from impurity;
from the terrible eye of the malevolent, protect us from that, O ointment!
Knowing this, O ointment, I shall speak the truth and not falsehood:
may I win the horse, the cow, and your very self, O man.
The three slaves of the ointment are fever, consumption, and the serpent.
(4.9.8.c) The highest of mountains, your father is named Trikakud. (4.9.9’) The collyrium born from Trikakud, produced from the Himavat,
(4.9.9.c) May it crush all sorcerers and all female sorceresses.
Whether you are called Traikakuda or Yamuna, both names are auspicious for you; with them, O collyrium, protect us!
Born from the wind, from the intermediate space, and from the light of the lightning.
May that gold-born conch, the pearl, protect us from distress.
He who was born from the ocean, foremost among the luminous realms—
having struck down the demons and devourers with the conch, may we prevail.
With the conch, [ward off] disease and lack of understanding; with the conch, also [ward off] the *sadānvās*.
May the conch, the all-healing, and the *kṛśana* gem protect us from distress. (4.10.3) Born in heaven, born of the ocean, brought hither from the river— (4.10.4)
(4.10.4.c) May that gold-born conch, the amulet that prolongs life,
protect us. (4.10.5’) Born from the ocean, born from Vṛtra, the sun-maker amulet— may it protect us on all sides from the weapons of the gods and the asuras.
(4.10.6) You are the one among golden things; from Soma you were born.
(4.10.6c) You are beautiful in the chariot; you are radiant in the quiver. May he prolong our lifespans.
6 (4.10.7) The bone of the gods became a pearl; that moves within the waters, endowed with a living soul.
(4.10.7.c) This I bind upon you for life, for splendor, for strength, for long life lasting a hundred autumns; may Kārśana protect you!
7 (4.11.1’) The ox has supported the earth and the sky; the ox has supported the broad mid-air.
(4.11.1.c) The ox has supported the six wide quarters; the ox has entered the entire world. 1
Indra is the draft-ox; he looks out for the cattle. The Mighty One measures out the three paths.
Milking the past, the future, and the worlds, he fulfills all the ordinances of the gods.
Indra, once born among men, moves as the heated *gharma* vessel, glowing with intense heat.
(4.11.3.c) May he be rich in offspring; let him not sit among the noble ones who, knowing [the value of] the ox, would not eat [of its flesh].
(4.11.4’) The ox yields [milk] in the world of the well-doer; Pavamāna nourishes it from the front.
(4.11.4.c) Parjanya is its udders, the Maruts its teats; sacrifice is its milk, and the sacrificial fee is its milking.
(4.11.5’) He over whom neither the lord of the sacrifice nor the sacrifice itself has power, nor does the giver have power over him, nor the recipient;
he who is the all-conquering, the sustainer of all, the maker of all—tell us of that Gharma which is four-footed.
(4.11.6’) By means of which the gods ascended to heaven, leaving behind their bodies at the navel of immortality.
(4.11.6.c) By that, may we go to the world of the well-done, through the observance of the *gharma* and through austerity, seeking glory.
(4.11.7’) Indra by his form, Agni by his vehicle, Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, Virāj—[all] stepped upon Viśvānara; he stepped upon Vaiśvānara; he stepped upon Anaduhr.
He made it firm; he held it steady.
(7) This is the middle of the ox, where this yoke is placed.
So much is its extent forward as that which is fixed behind. (8)
He who milks the seven milkings of the Vedas that flow according to their tracks, attains both progeny and the world; so the Seven Seers have known.
Treading upon the earth with his feet, he digs up the nourishing moisture with his shanks.
(4.11.10.c) Through toil, the ox and the plowman go toward the sweet drink.
(4.11.11’) They say that these twelve nights belong to Prajāpati as days of observance;
therein he who knows the sacred formulation (brahman) attains it, for that indeed is the vow of the ox. (4.11.11)
She yields in the evening, she yields in the morning, she yields throughout the midday.
Those milkings of his which come together—may we know them to be accompanied by abundance.
You are the healer; you are the healer of the broken bone; you are the healer.

(4.12.1.c) May Arundhatī cause this to grow. (4.12.2’) Whatever is injured in you, whatever is shattered, whatever is crushed within your body—may Dhātṛ, with auspiciousness, join that joint together again, joint by joint. (4.12.2.c) May Dhātṛ, with auspiciousness, join that joint together again, joint by joint. (4.12.2.c) May Dhātṛ, with auspiciousness, join that joint together again, joint by joint. (4.12.3’) May your marrow be joined with marrow, and your joint with joint.
(4.12.3.c) May what is torn away from your flesh grow whole again; may your bone also heal. (4.12.4’) Let marrow be united with marrow; let skin grow together with skin.
(4.12.4.c) Let your blood grow into bone; let your flesh grow with flesh.
(4.12.5’) Let hair be joined with hair; let skin be joined with skin.
(4.12.5.c) Let your blood grow into bone; O herb, mend what is severed.
(4.12.6’) Rise up! Go forth! Run forward! The chariot has good wheels, good felloes, and a good nave; stand upright upon it!
(4.12.7’) Whether he fell into a pit and was crushed, or whether one struck him and killed him—
(4.12.7.c) Like the *Ṛbhus* fitting together the parts of a chariot, joint by joint.
(4.13.1’) O gods, you raise up again that which has been cast down; O gods, you restore again even the one who has committed sin. O gods, you give life once more.
(4.13.2’) These two winds blow from the ocean and from the far distance:
(4.13.2.c) may one blow strength upon you; may the other blow away whatever is diseased. (4.13.3’) O Wind, blow hither healing medicine; O Wind, blow away whatever is diseased.
(4.13.3.c) For you, O possessor of all remedies, go as the messenger of the gods.
||3|| (4.13.4’) May the gods protect him; may the hosts of Maruts protect him;
(4.13.4.c) may all beings protect him, so that he may be free from injury. ||4||
I have come to you with healing remedies and with means for your safety;
I have brought you powerful vigor, and I drive away your disease.
This hand of mine is blessed, this hand of mine is even more blessed.
(4.13.6.c) This is my universal remedy; this is the auspicious touch.
(4.13.7’) With these two hands, ten-fingered, with the tongue as the forerunner of speech— (4.13.7.c) with those two hands that cause no illness, with them we touch you.
For the Unborn was born from the heat of Agni; he beheld his progenitor in the beginning.
By him the gods attained their godhead in the beginning; by him the worthy ones ascended the heights. Step forward with Agni toward the firmament, bearing the fire-pans in your hands.
(4.14.2.c) Having gone to the back of heaven, to the light, be united with the gods.
(4.14.3’) From the back of the earth I have ascended to the intermediate space; from the intermediate space I have ascended to heaven.
(4.14.3.c) From the back of the vault of heaven, I have gone to the light of the sun.
Going to heaven, they look not back; they ascend to the sky and the two worlds—those who, being well-knowing, have extended the sacrifice that flows in every direction.
O Agni, go forward as the first of the deities, the eye of both gods and men!
(4.14.5.c) Desiring to sacrifice, in harmony with the Bhṛgus, may the sacrificers go to heaven in well-being.
5 (4.14.6’) I anoint the goat with milk and ghee—the divine, fair-winged, milk-drinking, great one.
(4.14.6.c) By him may we go to the world of the well-done, ascending to heaven, unto the highest firmament. 6

Lift up this fivefold rice-offering with the five fingers using the ladle; divide this rice into five parts. Place the head of the Unborn One in the eastern direction; place his right side in the southern direction.
Place his buttocks in the western direction; place his left side in the northern direction.

(4.14.8.c) Place the backbone of the goat in the upward direction; place its belly in the fixed quarter. In the middle of the intermediate space, place its waist. (4.14.9’) The goat is cooked; cover it with the cooked skin, it being complete in all its limbs and possessing every form. (4.14.9.c) Let it rise up from here toward the highest firmament; stand firm in the quarters with your four feet.

Let the quarters of the sky rise up, full of moisture; let the clouds, driven by the wind, come together. Let the waters, lowing like the bellowing of a great bull, moist with moisture, satisfy the earth.
Let the powerful ones, the givers of good gifts, look upon us; let the essences of the waters unite with the plants.
(4.15.2.c) May the outpourings of rain glorify the earth; may plants of every form spring up everywhere.
(4.15.3’) Behold the heavens as they sing; let the torrents of water surge forth separately.
(4.15.3.c) May the outpourings of rain glorify the earth; may herbs of every form spring up everywhere.
(4.15.4) Let the hosts of Maruts, sounding like Parjanya, sing their songs for you individually;
let the streams of rain, as they pour down, rain upon the earth.
(4.15.5) O Maruts, raise yourselves up from the ocean; let the brilliant flame send the cloud flying upward.

(4.15.5.c) May the waters, lowing like the great bull as he roars through the wind, satisfy the earth. (4.15.6’) Roar toward us, thunder, and strike the ocean; O Parjanya, drench the earth with milk. Let the rain released by you come down in abundance; let the one who seeks the wind and is emaciated go to his end. (4.15.6.c) 6. May the bounteous ones protect you—the springs and the great serpents.
May the clouds, driven forth by the Maruts, rain down upon the earth.
Let lightning flash in every direction, and let the winds blow from every quarter.
(4.15.8.c) Let the clouds, driven forth by the Maruts, come together over the earth.
(4.15.9’) O bounteous ones, may the waters, the lightning, the cloud, and the rain protect you; may the springs and the serpents also [protect you].
(4.15.9.c) Let the clouds, driven forth by the Maruts, flow over the earth.
Agni, who is in harmony with the bodies of the waters, he who has become the lord of the plants—
may he, Jātavedas, win rain for us, and may he bring forth from the sky immortal life-breath for our offspring.
Prajāpati, driving forth the waters from the ocean and the sea, causes the watery expanse to swell.

(4.15.11.c) May the seed of the virile horse swell; come hither with this thundering sound! (4.15.12’) Pouring out the waters, our father the Asura, let the gargling sounds resound; O Varuṇa, release the downward-flowing waters.
(4.15.12.c) Let the frogs with speckled arms croak along the dry riverbeds.
Having lain dormant for a year, these Brahmins who observe their vows—the frogs—have uttered forth their voice, which is quickened by Parjanya.
13 Speak out, O female frog; croak, O *tāduri*, at the coming of the rain! 14

(4.15.14.c) Float in the middle of the lake, holding out your four feet. (4.15.15’) Khaṇvakhā3i, khaimakhā3i, in the midst of Taduri! (4.15.15.c) Send down the rain, O Fathers; seek the mind of the Maruts.
Pour forth the great reservoir; let it rain down with lightning. Let the wind blow. Let the winds, released in many ways, expand the sacrifice. Let the plants be full of joy.
Their lofty presiding lord beholds them as if from close at hand.

(4.16.1.c) Whosoever thinks he is moving about in secret—all the gods know this. (4.16.2’) He who stands, he who moves, and he who deceives; he who moves in hiding and he who moves openly—when two sit together and whisper counsel, King Varuṇa knows it as the third.
Moreover, this earth belongs to King Varuṇa, and so too does that great heaven with its distant boundaries.
Furthermore, both oceans are the belly of Varuṇa, and even here in this small amount of water he is hidden.
Moreover, whoever should creep beyond the sky to the farthest distance, he shall not be released from King Varuṇa.
(4.16.4.c) His spies move about in the sky; with their thousand eyes, they look down upon this earth. (4.16.5’) King Varuṇa beholds all that which is between the two worlds and that which is beyond.
He has counted the winks of men’s eyes; like a gambler casting dice, he marks them all.

(4.16.6’) O Varuṇa, those snares of yours, seven times seven, which stand released in three groups, full of wrath—let them all cut the one who speaks untruth; let them release him who speaks the truth.
(4.16.7’) Bind him with a hundred snares, O Varuṇa! Let not the speaker of untruth escape you, O Beholder of Men!
(4.16.7.c) Let the rogue remain, having let his belly hang down like an unfastened leather bag being cut away.
(4.16.8’) Varuṇa who is from our own home and he who is from abroad; Varuṇa who is a neighbor and he who is a stranger;
(4.16.8.c) Varuṇa who is divine and he who is human.
With all these nooses I bind you—[Name], son of [Maternal Grandfather], grandson of [Paternal Grandfather].
All of them I assign to you.
We seize you for victory, you who are the sovereign of healing remedies.

I have fashioned you, O herb, with a thousandfold power for the sake of everyone. (4.17.1.c) I have invoked all the herbs—those that conquer truth, those that ward off curses, those that are victorious, and those that heal again—with this prayer: "May they carry us safely across from here. (4.17.2)
She who cursed with a curse, she who placed a deadly poison in the food, she who strove to seize the offspring for the sake of carrying off the essence—may she devour her own child.
3 That which they prepared for you in an unbaked vessel, that which they prepared in the dark-blue and red [vessels]— [may it consume her]. 4

(4.17.4.c) With that *kṛtyā* which they have fashioned against raw flesh, with it, slay the makers of the *kṛtyā*. (4.17.5’) Bad dreams, a miserable life, the *rakṣas*, the monstrous, the *arāyī* demons, all those of evil name and evil speech— we cause them to perish away from us.
The death of hunger, the death of thirst, lack of cattle, and childlessness—
O Apāmārga, by means of you, we wipe all that away.
The death of thirst, the death of hunger, and furthermore, defeat at dice.
(4.17.7.c) O Apāmārga, with you we wipe away all that [evil]. 7 (4.17.8’) O Apāmārga, among all plants, you alone are the controller.
(4.17.8.c) With that [power] of yours, we wipe away what has settled upon you; now go forth free from disease. 8
The light is equal to the sun; night is equal to the day.
I make this true for my protection: let the sorceresses be powerless.
O gods, whoever, having fashioned a spell, should carry it off to the house of one who knows not—
Like a sucking calf to its mother, let it fall back upon him.
Having brought his evil upon himself, he who seeks to strike down another with it—
when that [evil] is burnt away, many stones will crackle loudly.

O thousandfold abode, with your shadow you [overwhelm] the spear-armed and the neckless; take back the spell (*kṛtyā*) that was fashioned against the one who has done you harm, O you who possess what is dear, take it back to him who is dear to you! By means of this herb, I have rendered all spells (*kṛtyā*) impotent.
(4.18.5.c) That [curse] which they have placed upon the field, that upon the cattle, or that upon your men;
(4.18.6’) He who has cast it was unable to undo it; he has shattered his foot and his toe. (4.18.6.c) He has brought us prosperity, but for himself, he has brought torment.
May the Apāmārga plant wipe away the *kṣetriya* disease and whatever curse there is; may it drive away the sorceresses and all the *arāyyas*.
Having wiped away the sorcerers and all the *arāyyas*, [may it protect us].
(4.18.8.c) O Apāmārga, with you we wipe away all that [evil].
(4.19.1’) You are the one who makes us friendless, and you are the one who makes us kinless;
(4.19.1.c) moreover, cut off the offspring of the sorcerers like a reed of the rainy season.
(4.19.2) You have been consecrated by the Brahmin Kaṇva Nārṣada.
Like an army, you go forth radiant; there is no fear where you arrive, O herb.
(4.19.3) You shall go at the head of the plants, illuminating them as if with light.
(4.19.3.c) Moreover, you are the savior of the simpleton, and also the slayer of the *rakṣas*.
(4.19.4’) When, O gods, you first drove out the *asuras* by means of you,
(4.19.4.c) from that time forth, O plant, you were born as the *apāmārga*.
Splitting with a hundred branches, your father is named Vibhindu. Split him apart who assails us from every side!
That which has become non-existent arose from the earth; it is that great expanse toward which he goes.
(4.19.6.c) Let that indeed, having been shaken off from there, strike back at the doer.
(4.19.7’) For you have come into being facing us; you are one whose fruit is directed toward us.
Ward off far away from me all curses and the deadly weapon. (4.19.7.c) Ward off far away from me all curses and the deadly weapon.
Protect me with a hundred; guard me with a thousand!
O Indra, Lord of plants, may you, the fierce one, bestow vigor upon me.
He looks toward, he looks back, he looks away—he sees.

(4.20.1.c) O Goddess, she beholds all of that: heaven, the intermediate space, and the earth. (4.20.2’) The three heavens, the three earths, and these six directions separately—O Goddess, Plant, through you may I behold all beings.
(4.20.3’) You are indeed the pupil of that divine Suparṇa.
(4.20.3.c) You have descended to the earth like a weary bride to her bridal litter.
(4.20.4’) The thousand-eyed god placed you in my right hand.
(4.20.4.c) By means of her, I see everything—both the Śūdra and the Ārya. (4.20.5’) Reveal your forms; do not conceal yourself.
(4.20.5.c) And so, O thousand-eyed one, look back upon the Kimīdins.
"Show me the male sorcerers, show me the female sorcerers;
show me all the *piśācas*—thus do I grasp you, O herb!
"You are the eye of Kaśyapa and the four-eyed bitch."
Do not let the *piśāca* pass you by, like one who glides past the sun in a cloudless sky.
(4.20.7.c) I have seized from its very haunt the *yātudhāna*, the *kimīdin*;
through him, I see all—both the *śūdra* and the *ārya*. (4.20.8.c)
(4.20.9) "He who flies through the intermediate space, and he who glides across the sky—he who considers the earth his refuge, show that *piśāca* to him!
(4.21.1) "The cows have come; they have brought auspiciousness. Let them sit in the cow-pen and take delight among us."
May there be here many prolific cows of various forms, yielding their milk for Indra through many dawns.
(1) Indra bestows wealth upon the sacrificer who praises him; he gives it freely and does not steal it back.
Increasing his riches more and more, he establishes the god-fearing man upon his unbroken field. (2)
They are not lost; no thief can harm them, nor does the distress of an enemy dare to assail them.
With those [cows] by which one worships the gods and gives gifts, the master of the herd dwells together with them for a long time.
No steed with dust upon its back overtakes them, nor do they ever go toward a place of slaughter.
(4.21.4.c) The cattle of that mortal sacrificer roam about following after that wide-striding, fearless one.

(4.21.5.a) Cattle are Bhaga; cattle are Indra; may they desire me. Cattle are the first draught of Soma. (4.21.5.c) O people, these which are the cattle—they are Indra. With my heart and with my mind, I desire Indra.
(4.21.6) You cows, you make even the emaciated fat; you make even the unlovely beautiful to behold.
(4.21.6c) You make the home auspicious, O you of auspicious speech; your great vitality is proclaimed in the assemblies.
(4.21.7) Abounding in offspring, grazing on excellent pasture, radiant, drinking pure waters at a good watering-place—
(4.21.7.c) Let neither the thief nor the malevolent man master you; may the missile of Rudra pass you by!

7 (4.22.1’) O Indra, cause this Kṣatriya of mine to prosper; make him the sole bull among the people. (4.22.1.c) Strike down all his enemies; I shall subject them to his power in the battles to come. 1
(4.22.2’) “Favor him with respect to villages, horses, and cattle; let him overcome whoever is his enemy.
(4.22.2.c) Let him be the pinnacle of lordships, O Indra among kings; subject every enemy to him.
(4.22.3’) “Let him be the master of wealth and treasures; let him be the king, the lord of the people.”
(4.22.3.c) O Indra, bestow great splendors upon this man; render his enemy devoid of luster.

(4.22.4’) O Heaven and Earth, yield for him abundant wealth, like two milch-cows yielding warm milk. May this king be dear to Indra, dear to the cows, dear to the plants, and dear to the cattle. (4.22.4)
(4.22.5’) I yoke you with Indra, the superior one, by whom men conquer and are not conquered;

(4.22.5.c) who shall make you the sole bull among the people and the highest of kings among men. 5. (4.22.6’) You are superior; your rivals are inferior—whosoever they may be, O King, those who are your adversaries.
(4.22.6.c) O sole bull, Indra’s friend, victorious one, bring hither the provisions of those who act as enemies!

(4.22.7’) With the face of a lion, devour all the tribes; with the face of a tiger, strike down the enemies! O sole bull, Indra’s friend, victorious one, extract the provisions of those who act as enemies!

I meditate upon Agni, the first, the wise one, whom the people of the five tribes kindle in many ways; him who has entered into every clan, we implore—may he deliver us from distress. Just as you carry the oblation, O Jātavedas, and just as you arrange the sacrifice with full knowledge, [so do so for us].
(4.23.2.c) Thus bring us favor from the gods; may he deliver us from distress.
(4.23.3’) Agni, who is most effective in every journey, who is employed in every rite, the sharer in every act—I praise him.
The slayer of demons, the increaser of sacrifice, invoked with clarified butter—may he deliver us from distress. (4.23.3.c) May he deliver us from distress.
We invoke Agni Vaiśvānara, the well-born Jātavedas, the all-pervading bearer of oblations; may he deliver us from distress.
By whom the seers kindled their strength as a companion, and by whom they overcame the magical powers of the Asuras.
May that fire by which Indra conquered the Paṇis deliver us from distress.

(4.23.5.c) By which the gods discovered immortality, by which they made the plants full of sweetness, by which the gods brought forth the light of heaven—may that [fire] deliver us from distress. (4.23.6)
In whose direction this shines, whatever has been born and whatever is yet to be born—exclusively his;
I praise Agni, I call upon him in my distress; may he deliver us from evil.
We meditate upon Indra, we ever meditate upon him; the hymns for the slayer of Vṛtra have come unto me.
(4.24.1.c) He who comes at the call of the donor who performs good deeds—may he release us from distress.
(4.24.2’) He who, with arms formidable among the formidable, advanced and shattered the strength of the Dānavas;
(4.24.2.c) by whom the rivers were won and by whom the cattle were recovered—may he release us from distress.
He who is the bull, the protector of the people, the finder of heaven, for whom the pressing-stones proclaim manly strength;
whose sacrifice, with its seven priests, is most exhilarating—may he deliver us from distress.
He for whom the barren cows, the bulls, and the oxen are prepared, for whom the sacrificial posts are set up as finders of heaven—may he deliver us from distress.
(4.24.4.c) For whom the bright Soma flows, purified by prayer—may they release us from distress.
(4.24.5’) Whose favor the Soma-pressers desire, whom they invoke as the wielder of the arrow in the quest for cattle;
in whom the hymn rests, in whom the vital power dwells—may they release us from distress.
He who was first born for the performance of action, whose power was first awakened;
by whom the raised thunderbolt was hurled against the serpent—may they release us from distress.
He who, as the master, leads battles to the clash, and who brings together the flourishing spoils of war.
(4.24.7.c) I praise Indra; seeking protection, I call upon him repeatedly: may he deliver us from distress.
(4.25.1’) We meditate upon the ordinances of Vāyu and Savitṛ—those two who enter into embodied beings and who protect them;
those two who have become the encompassers of the universe: may they deliver us from distress.
(4.25.2) Whose vastness is measured by the earthly realms, by whom the dust of the mid-air was fixed;
(4.25.2c) whose course no one at all has ever overtaken—may those two deliver us from distress.
(4.25.3) In thy ordinance the people settle down; when thou hast risen, O thou of wondrous luster, they stir forth.
(4.25.3.c) You two, Vāyu and Savitṛ, protect all beings; may you two release us from distress.
(4.25.4’) Away with evil-doing, O Vāyu and Savitṛ! Drive away the Rākṣasas and the Śimidās!
For you two provide nourishment and strength together; may you two release us from distress.
May Savitṛ and Vāyu bestow upon me wealth, nourishment, and well-disposed skill for my body. Grant us here great freedom from disease; may you two deliver us from distress.
O Savitṛ and Vāyu, you both gladden yourselves with the excellent, exhilarating, and mighty favor for our aid.
(4.25.6.c) Restrain [the flow] from the downward slope of your bounty; may those two deliver us from distress.
(4.25.7.a) May our most excellent blessings be established in the abode of the two gods;
(4.25.7.c) I praise the god Savitṛ and Vāyu; may those two deliver us from distress.
I honor you two, Heaven and Earth, the bountiful and harmonious ones, who have spread yourselves out across immeasurable leagues.

For you two have become the foundations of all treasures; as such, deliver us from distress. For you two have become the foundations of all treasures—O Goddesses, grown great, auspicious, and far-reaching.
(4.26.2.c) O Heaven and Earth, be gracious to me; may they release us from distress.
2 (4.26.3’) I invoke the two who are free from heat, who perform great penance, the wide and deep ones, who are honored by the sages.
O Heaven and Earth, be gracious to me; may they release us from distress. 3

(4.26.4’) You who sustain the nectar of immortality, you who sustain the oblations, you who sustain the rivers and you who sustain human beings—O Heaven and Earth, be gracious to me; may they release us from distress.
(4.26.5’) You who sustain the ruddy cows, you who sustain the lords of the forest, within whom all beings dwell—may they release us from distress.
(4.26.5.c) O Heaven and Earth, be gracious to me; may they release us from distress.
(5) (4.26.6’) You who satisfy with honey and you who satisfy with clarified butter—without whom nothing at all can be accomplished:
(4.26.6.c) O Heaven and Earth, be gracious to me; may they release us from distress. (6)
Whatever distress afflicts us here, or whatever has been done by human hands and not by fate—I praise Heaven and Earth; seeking protection, I call upon you both: deliver us from this affliction!
I think upon the Maruts; may they speak for me; may they favor this strength in the contest for booty.
Like swift steeds easy to control, I have called upon them for aid; may they deliver us from distress.
(1) They who always open the inexhaustible spring and pour their essence into the plants—those Maruts, whose mother is Pṛśni, I place before me; may they deliver us from distress. (2)
(4.27.3’) Milk of the cows, essence of the plants, the speed of the horses—O Seers, you who impel these;
(4.27.3.c) may the Maruts be gracious to us, may they be gentle, and may they release us from distress.
(4.27.4’) They carry the waters from the ocean up to heaven, and from heaven they pour them down upon the earth.
(4.27.4.c) Those Maruts who move about as lords over the waters—may they release us from distress.
(4.27.5.a) Those who satisfy [beings] with sour gruel, those with clarified butter, or those who mix them with the fat of birds;
(4.27.5.c) Those Maruts who, as lords over the waters, cause rain to fall—may they release us from distress.

O Maruts, if this [sin] has been committed by us through the Marut-host, or if, O gods, it has been done by us through the divine power in such a manner—O Vasus, you alone have the power to provide its remedy; may they deliver us from distress.
The sharp-edged host of the Maruts is renowned for its might; it is fierce in battles.
(4.27.7.c) I praise the Maruts; seeking protection, I call upon them repeatedly: may they release us from distress.

(4.28.1’) I meditate upon you two, Bhava and Śarva; take note of this [prayer] of mine, for whatever shines here within your domain—(4.28.1.c) you who rule over these bipeds and quadrupeds—release us from distress.
Those two who are superior even in the nearness, and who are known even in the distance as the most excellent among the wielders of arrows;
those two who have mastery over these bipeds and quadrupeds—may they release us from distress.
I invoke here the thousand-eyed slayers of Vṛtra; praising the two fierce ones, I come from afar across the pasture-lands.
(4.28.3.c) You two who have power over bipeds and quadrupeds—release us from distress!
(4.28.4.a) You two who were grasped together many times in the beginning, and who sent forth overwhelming power among the people;
(4.28.4.c) You two who have power over bipeds and quadrupeds—release us from distress!
Against whomsoever no one at all can prevail through weapons, whether among the gods or among men— those two who have mastery over his bipeds and quadrupeds, may they deliver us from distress.
O fierce ones, cast down your thunderbolt upon that sorcerer who performs witchcraft and digs up roots.

(4.28.6.c) Those two who have power over bipeds and those who have power over quadrupeds—may they both release us from distress. (4.28.7.a) Speak for us in battles, O fierce ones; strike with your thunderbolt against the *kimīdin*. (4.28.7.c) I praise Bhava and Śarva; seeking protection, I call upon you repeatedly.
