I think of you two, Mitra and Varuṇa, increasers of cosmic order, who are of one mind and who drive away the malicious. You protect the speaker of truth in battles; as such, deliver us from distress.
Of one mind, you two drive away the malicious; you protect the speaker of truth in battles.
(4.29.2.c) You two who, O observers of men, go toward the pressed juice with the brown one—release us from distress!
(4.29.3’) You two who protect Aṅgiras, Agasti, Jamadagni, and Atri, O Mitra and Varuṇa;
you two who protect Kaśyapa and Vasiṣṭha—release us from distress!
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who protected Śyāvāśva, Vadhryaśva, Purumīḍha, and Atri;
you who protected Vimada and Saptavadhri—deliver us from distress.
O Varuṇa and Mitra, you who protected Bharadvāja, Gaviṣṭhira, Viśvāmitra, and Kutsa.
O you two who protect Kakṣīvat and Kaṇva, deliver us from distress.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who protect Medhātithi and Triśoka, and you who [protect] Uśanas Kāvya;
O you two who protect Gotama and Mudgala, deliver us from distress.

Whose chariot, moving upon the path of truth with straight reins, pursues and strikes down him who walks crookedly—I praise Mitra and Varuṇa; seeking protection, I cry out to them: may they two deliver us from distress.
I move with the Rudras and the Vasus; I move with the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas.
(4.30.1.c) I sustain both Mitra and Varuṇa; I sustain Indra and Agni; I sustain both Aśvins.
(4.30.2’) I am the sovereign ruler, the gatherer of riches, the wise one, the first among those worthy of sacrifice.
(4.30.2.c) As such, the gods have distributed me in many places, making me dwell in many abodes.
I myself declare this, which is pleasing to both gods and humans:
whomsoever I desire, him I make fierce; him I make a Brahmin, him a seer, him a man of great wisdom.
Through me he eats food—he who sees, he who breathes, and he who hears what is spoken.
(4.30.4.c) Those who do not understand wait upon me; hear, O renowned one, for this which I speak to you is worthy of being heard.
4 (4.30.5.a) I bend the bow for Rudra, so that his arrow may slay the hater of sacred knowledge. 5 (4.30.5.c) I stir up conflict among the people; I have entered heaven and earth. 5
I bear Soma, the crusher; I bear Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, and Bhaga.
I bestow riches upon the one who offers oblations, providing excellent protection for the sacrificer who presses the juice.
I bring forth the Father upon the summit of this [world]; my womb is within the waters, in the ocean.
(4.30.7.c) Thenceforth I have spread out across all worlds; I touch even that sky with my summit.

(4.30.8.a) I alone blow forth like the wind, grasping all worlds; beyond the sky and beyond this earth, I have become so great in majesty. (4.30.8.c) I have come to be as vast as this through my own greatness.

(4.31.1’) O Manyu, with you as our charioteer, may they come forward—breaking through, exulting, and thrilled, accompanied by the Maruts; men with sharp arrows, whetting their weapons, having the form of Agni.
(4.31.2’) Like Agni, O Manyu, blaze forth; as our victorious army-leader, O conqueror, be summoned for us!
Having slain the enemies, distribute their wealth; measuring out your vigor, drive away the adversaries.
Overpower the enemy’s arrogance, O Manyu! Breaking, crushing, and utterly destroying, go forth against the foes!
Your fierce power has indeed been irresistible; as the sole-born subduer, you bring them under your control.
(4.31.4) You alone, O Manyu, are the one praised by the many; sharpen us for battle against every tribe.
With you as our ally, O you of unimpaired luster, we raise a brilliant shout for victory.
(4.31.5) A maker of victory, like Indra, and one who cannot be restrained—O Manyu, be our sovereign protector here.
(4.31.5.c) O Victorious One, we celebrate your beloved name; we know that source from which you have arisen.

(4.31.6’) O Vajra, O Arrow, by your innate power you are ever-present; you bear superior might for the sake of those who possess it. (4.31.6.c) O Manyu, through your wisdom, be with us in our prosperity; O Much-invoked One, be present in the clash for the great prize.
May Varuṇa and Manyu bestow upon us the combined wealth gathered from both sides.
Let the enemies, placing fear in their hearts, lie prostrate, utterly defeated.
O Manyu, wielder of the thunderbolt and arrow, he who honors you nourishes all power and strength in succession.
(4.32.1.c) With you as our ally—born of power, powerful through might—may we overcome both the Dāsa and the Ārya.
(4.32.2’) Manyu is Indra; Manyu indeed was the god; Manyu is the Hotṛ, Varuṇa, and Jātavedas.
The human tribes that exist worship Manyu; O Manyu, protect us, being in harmony with our fervor.
Come hither, O Manyu, you who are stronger than the strong; with fervor as your ally, strike down our enemies.

You are the slayer of foes, the slayer of Vṛtra, and the slayer of Dasyus; bring to us all treasures. For you, O Manyu, possess overwhelming power; you are self-existent, brilliant, and the subduer of adversaries.
(4.32.4.c) All-seeing, victorious, and more powerful [than the strongest], bestow vigor upon us in the battles!
(4.32.5’) Being without a share, I have gone away from you, O wise one, through the power of you, the mighty.
Therefore, O Manyu, I have provoked you in my lack of resolve; come to us in your own person as the giver of strength!
(4.32.6) Here I am for you; come toward us, O Conqueror, All-Bestower, facing us. O Manyu, Wielder of the Thunderbolt, turn toward us! Let us two slay the Dasyus, and be mindful of your kinship.
(4.32.7) Come forward and stand on our right; then let us two strike down many Vṛtras.
(4.32.7.c) I offer you the sustaining first portion of the honeyed [soma]; let us both drink it silently as the first.
7 (4.33.1’) May Agni burn away our evil; shine forth wealth upon us;
may he burn away our evil. 1
With a desire for good fields, for a good path, and for wealth, we sacrifice;
may he burn away our evil.
May he who is most excellent among these, and our own wise patrons, go forth.
May it burn away our evil.
(4.33.3.c) When, O Agni, the wise patrons [attain] through thee, may we too be born through thee;
may it burn away our evil. (4.33.4.c)
When the rays of the powerful Agni go forth in every direction,
may he burn away our evil with his light.
For you, O you whose face is turned everywhere, are the one who encompasses all from every side.
May he burn away our evil. 6 O you whose face is turned everywhere, carry us across [all] enemies as if with a boat;
may he burn away our evil. 7
May he carry us across for our well-being, as one crosses a river by boat;
may he burn away our evil.
The *brahman* is the head of this [sacrifice], the *bṛhat* is its back, and the *vāmadevya* is the belly of the rice-mess.
The meters are his wings, truth is his mouth; born from austerity, the sacrifice has spread abroad.
(1) Boneless, purified by the wind, cleansed and pure, they go to the world of purity. Fire does not burn their genitals; in the heavenly world, there is an abundance of women for them. (2)
Those who cook the spreading rice-mess—for them no misfortune ever comes.
Yama sits near him; he goes to the gods and rejoices with the Soma-loving Gandharvas.
Those who cook the spreading rice-mess—Yama does not steal away their seed.
(4.34.4.c) Having become a charioteer, he moves along on his chariot; having become a bird, he traverses beyond the sky.
(4.34.5’) He is the most excellent bearer among sacrifices, spread out wide; having cooked the spreading [oblation], he has entered heaven.
He extends the *āṇḍīka*, the *kumuda*, the lotus-fiber, the *śālūka*, the *śaphaka*, and the *mulālī*.
(4.34.5.e) May all these streams flow toward you, swelling with sweetness in the heavenly world; may lotus-pools stand around you on every side.
(4.34.6’) Pools of ghee, with honey for their banks, filled with fine liquor, milk, water, and curds.
(4.34.6.c) May all these streams flow toward you, swelling with sweetness in the heavenly world; may lotus-pools stand around you on every side.
(4.34.7’) I give four jars, divided into four parts, filled with milk, water, and curds.
(4.34.7.c) May all these streams come toward you, swelling with sweetness in the heavenly world; may lotus-pools stand around you on every side.
(4.34.8’) I place this rice-offering among the Brāhmaṇas—expansive, world-conquering, and leading to heaven.
May he not fail me, swelling with his own inherent power; may he be for me a cow of all forms, yielding my every desire.

That rice-meat which Prajāpati, the first-born of Cosmic Order, cooked for the Brahman through his ascetic fervor—that which is the sustainer of the worlds and their central navel—by means of that rice-meat may I overcome death.
By that [food] through which the creators of beings crossed beyond death—what they discovered through austerity and toil;
that ancient *brahman* which they cooked as *brahman* for the sake of *brahman*—by means of that food may I cross beyond death.
He who supported the earth, the sustainer of all, and who filled the mid-air with moisture.
He who propped up the sky erect by his greatness—with that food may I overcome death.
From whom the months were fashioned with thirty spokes, and from whom the year was fashioned with twelve spokes;
whom the days and nights, as they revolve, have not overtaken—with that food may I overcome death.
He who was the giver of life and became possessed of life, for whom the worlds flow with clarified butter—
for him whose all directions are full of light, may I cross over death by means of that food.
From which cooked [food] immortality was produced, and who became the sovereign lord of the Gāyatrī.
(4.35.6.c) In that [food] in which all forms of the Vedas are deposited—by means of that rice-offering may I overcome death.
(4.35.7’) May I strike down the hater, the scorner of the gods; let my rivals be defeated.
(4.35.7.c) I cook this Brahman-rice, the conqueror of all; may the gods hear me, who have faith.
May Agni Vaiśvānara, the bull of true might, burn them up— him who would harm us or seek to deceive us, and him who would act with hostility toward us.
May he burn him who seeks to deceive us though we seek not to deceive, and him who seeks to deceive those who do seek to deceive.

I place him within the two fangs of Vaiśvānara Agni. Those who seek him out in the house, at the cry of opposition, or on the new-moon night— all those flesh-eaters who wish to harm others, I overcome them all with my might.
I contend with the Piśācas; by force I bestow their wealth upon them. I slay all who seek to harm me; may my intention be fulfilled.
Those gods who laugh at that [enemy] and measure their speed against the sun—
(4.36.5.c) May I find them together with those cattle who are in the rivers and on the mountains. (4.36.6’) I am a burner of the Piśācas, like a tiger among cattle;
seeing me, they do not find a way to escape, just as dogs do not find a way out upon seeing a lion.
I am not able to coexist with piśācas, nor with thieves, nor with forest-dwellers;
therefore, the piśācas perish when I enter a village. This formidable power of mine enters whichever village it approaches.
(4.36.8.c) Therefore, the Piśācas perish; they do not understand their own evil.
(4.36.9’) Those who provoke my anger with their chatter, like gnats provoking an elephant—I consider them to be ill-disposed toward me, like small creatures in a great forest.
(4.36.9.c) I regard them as those who bring misfortune, like tiny animals in a vast wilderness.
May Destruction seize him as a horse is seized by its halter;
that malicious one who is angry with me shall not escape from the snares.
By you, O Herb, the Atharvans of old slew the Rākṣasas.
By you Kaśyapa was slain; by you Kaṇva and Agastya were slain. By you we drive away the Apsarases and the Gandharvas.
O goat-horned one, O goat, destroy all the Rākṣasas with your scent!
Let the Apsarases go to the river, to the crossing of the waters, to Avaśvasa;
let Gulgulū, Pīlā, Naladī, Aukṣagandhi, and Pramandanī go there.
Depart, O Apsarases; you have been awakened.

Where there are *aśvattha* and *nyagrodha* trees, great trees with crests—there you have awakened, O Apsarases who have departed. Where your green and white swings are, and where the *karkarya* cymbals sound together; there you have awakened, O Apsarases who have departed.
(4.37.5.c) Therefore, O Apsarases, depart; you have been awakened. (4.37.6’) This one has come, the potent one among plants and creepers:
let the goat-horned, the *arāṭakī*, the sharp-horned, drive [the demon] away.
I split the testicles even of the dancing Gandharva Śikhaṇḍin, the lord of Apsarases, and I go after his penis.
Terrible are the weapons of Indra; there are a hundred iron spears.
With them, let him pierce the Gandharvas who consume the oblation and who devour the *avaka* plants.
(8) Terrible are the weapons of Indra; a hundred are his golden spears.
With them, let him pierce the Gandharvas who consume the oblation and who devour the *avaka* plants. (9)
O Herb, burn up the *avakā* plants, the *abhiśoca* plants, and my own luminous ones within the waters; crush all the *piśācas* and overcome them!
Like a lone dog, like a lone monkey, [is] the boy with all-black hair.
Like one dear to behold, the Gandharva haunts women;
him we drive away from here with powerful sacred speech.
O Apsarases, you are indeed their wives; O Gandharvas, you are their husbands.
(4.37.12.c) Run away, O immortals; do not associate with mortals!
12 (4.38.1’) I summon here that Apsaras who breaks through, who conquers, who plays fairly, and who makes stakes into winnings. 1
I invoke here that Apsaras who gathers and scatters, who plays the game of dice skillfully, and who takes up the winnings in the stake. She who dances around while taking the winnings from the stake.
May she, seeking to win our deeds, attain the prize through her magic power;
may she come to us rich in milk; let them not conquer this wealth of ours.
(4.38.3) Those who take delight in the dice, bearing sorrow and anger—(4.38.4)
I summon here that Apsaras Ānandinī and Pramodinī. (4.38.4.c) Those who move along the rays of the sun, or those who follow after the beams of light;
she whose bull, like a prize-winning steed from afar, instantly traverses all the worlds while guarding them. (4.38.5)
(4.38.5.e) May he come to this oblation, enjoying it, together with the intermediate space, O possessor of vigor!

(4.38.6’) O possessor of vigor, together with the intermediate space, protect the young female calf here, O vigorous one! (4.38.6.c) These abundant drops are for you; come hither, O steed! Let this young female calf be yours here; let your mind be here.
O possessor of strength, together with the mid-air, protect the spotted calf here, O vigorous one!
This is the fodder, this is the stall; here we bind the calf. As we have power over you by name, Svāhā! 7.
On the earth they bowed down to Agni; he prospered.
Just as on the earth they bowed down to Agni, so may all bowings bow down to me.
1. The earth is the cow; Agni is her calf.
May she, with Agni as her calf, milk for me food, vigor, and desire—first long life, offspring, nourishment, and wealth; Svāhā!
They bowed down to Vāyu in the intermediate space; he prospered.
(4.39.3.c) Just as they have bowed down together to Vāyu in the intermediate space, so may they bow down in unison unto me.
(4.39.4’) The intermediate space is the cow; its calf is Vāyu. May she, with Vāyu as her calf, milk for me food, strength, and desire.

Heaven is the cow; the sun is her calf.
May she, with the sun as her calf, milk for me food, strength, and desire:
first, long life, offspring, prosperity, and wealth—svāhā!

In all directions they bowed down to the Moon; he prospered. Just as they bowed down to the Moon in all directions, so may all obeisances bow down to me! (4.39.8) The quarters are the milch-cows; of them, the Moon is the calf.
(4.39.8.c) May they, with the moon as their calf, milk for me food, vigor, desire, life-span first, offspring, nourishment, and wealth—svāhā!
(4.39.9’) Fire moves within fire, having entered it; the son of the seers, the protector against curses.
With a bow and with reverence, I offer to you; may I not falsely miss the portion of the gods.
Purified by the heart and by the mind, O Jātavedas, you who know all divine ordinances;
O Jātavedas, there are seven mouths of yours—to them I offer this oblation; may you graciously accept the offering.
Those who offer in the east, O Jātavedas, and those who would harm us from the eastern quarter—[may they be overcome].
(4.40.1.c) Having encountered Agni, let those who turn away be distressed; with this *pratisara* (protective amulet), I strike them back.

(4.40.7) O Jātavedas, those who offer oblations from above, who seek to harm us from the upward direction—
Having encountered the sun, let those who turn away be shaken; with this *pratisara* I strike them back.

(4.40.7.c) Those who offer oblations from the intermediate points of the quarters, O Jātavedas—those who seek to harm us from all directions—having encountered the sacred power (*brahman*), let those who turn away be shaken; with this *pratisara* I strike them back. (4.40.8.c)
(5.1.1’) He whose mantra has prospered, who has occupied his place, the immortal one increasing, of noble birth;
(5.1.1.c) he of unassailable life, shining like the sun—Trita, the sustainer, has upheld the three.
(5.1.2’) He who first established the cosmic laws, from him you create many forms.
(5.1.2.c) He who first entered the womb, he who perceived speech before it was uttered—he shall sustain [it].
(5.1.3’) He who for the sake of your sorrow surrendered his body—he let flow the gold, pure according to his own [laws].
(5.1.3.c) Herein they two establish the immortal names; may the clans bring forth garments for us.
When these [rays] go forth further toward the ancient seat, occupying every dwelling that is ageless— then, O Seer,
licking the two mothers of the dry [world], do you two set in motion the yoke-mate,
the lord of kinship. Therefore, O broad-striding one, I, the seer, offer this great homage to you with my poetic skill.
(5.1.5.c) When the two [wheels] move together toward the earth, there they grow great as the two banks of a river.
‖5‖ (5.1.6’) The seers have fashioned seven boundaries; the one who is in distress falls into only one of them.
(5.1.6.c) The pillar of Āyu stands in the nest of the highest, at the parting of the paths, upon the foundations. ‖6‖
(5.1.7’) And I go, possessing immortal life, performing the vow; O Asura, you are the self within my body, moving with joy.
(5.1.7.c) Or indeed, the powerful one bestows treasure, or he who gives the oblation attends to it with vigor.
(5.1.8’) Or the son praises the father’s sovereignty; the men have called upon the eldest boundary for their well-being.
Behold now those stations of yours, O Varuṇa; from your own sacred law, you manifest wondrous forms.
(5.1.9) With one half you fill [the world] with milk, and with the other half, O impetuous one, you increase your strength.
We have magnified the helpful friend Varuṇa, the vigorous son of Aditi.
(5.1.9.e) We have proclaimed to him these forms, which are praised by poets, O Heaven and Earth, you whose speech is truth.
(5.2.1’) That indeed was the eldest among all beings, from whom the fierce sacrifice of brilliant valor [proceeded].
(5.2.1.c) As soon as he was born, he overcomes his enemies, when all his helpers rejoice after him.

Increasing in power, possessing abundant strength, he, as an enemy, strikes fear into the Dāsa. Both the silent and the vocal [beings] are won by thee; they cry out together at thy offerings during the exhilarations. In thee they pour forth manifold wisdom, when these helpers become twofold or threefold.
(5.2.3.c) With the sweeter [Soma], mix that which is sweeter than sweet; with honey, fight against that honey.

(5.2.4’) If indeed the inspired singers rejoice after you as you win riches in every battle, (5.2.4.c) O mighty one, extend your strength more powerfully and firmly; let not the evil-minded Kaśoka-slayers deceive you.
(5.2.5’) Through you we prevail in battles, beholding many things worthy of combat.
(5.2.5.c) I urge on your weapons with my words; I sharpen your vital powers with my prayer. 5.
(5.2.6’) You bestow that [gift] in this lower and that higher dwelling wherein you have protected us with your aid.
(5.2.6.c) Settle the swift-moving Mother; then set in motion many heroic deeds.
(5.2.7’) Praise him upon the height, the one with many paths, the skillful, the most powerful, the Aptya among the Aptyas.
(5.2.7.c) He of abundant vigor shall display himself with might; he shall surpass the very measure of the earth.
(5.2.8’) May this Bṛhaddiva, the foremost winner of light, offer this hymn of praise as strength for Indra.
As a self-ruling king, he rules over the great stall of cattle; though swift and fervent, he encompasses all like the ocean.
(5.2.9’) Thus has the great Bṛhaddiva Atharvan spoken: his own body is indeed Indra.
(5.2.9.c) The two sisters dwelling in the mother, faultless, impel them and cause them to grow with power.
(5.3.1’) O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations; kindling you, may we nourish our bodies.
(5.3.1.c) May the four quarters bow down to me; with you as our overseer, may we conquer the hostile armies.
O Agni, repelling the wrath of our enemies, do you, as our protector, guard us on every side.
Let those who seek to do us harm go away, headlong down into the abyss; let the minds of these who wake against us be utterly destroyed.
May all the gods be present at my invocation—Indra, the Maruts, Viṣṇu, and Agni.
(5.3.3.c) May the mid-air be my wide world; may the wind blow for this desire of mine.
(5.3.4.a) May they sacrifice for me; may my intentions be fulfilled; may my mind’s purpose be true.
(5.3.4.c) May I not fall into any sin whatsoever; may all the gods protect me here.

(5.3.5’) May the gods bestow wealth upon me; may the prayer be with me, may the invocation of the gods be with me. (5.3.5.c) May the divine Hotṛ-priests grant this to us; may we be unharmed, possessing good heroes in our bodies.
5 (5.3.6’) O six divine expanses, make wide room for us! O all you gods, rejoice here!
(5.3.6.c) May no overpowering assault find us, nor any curse; may no treacherous hatred find us, O ye who are to be feared.
(5.3.7’) O three goddesses, grant us great protection for our offspring, for our bodies, and for our prosperity!
(5.3.7.c) May we not be abandoned by our offspring nor by our own persons; may we not fall into the power of the enemy, O King Soma.
(5.3.8’) May the wide-striding buffalo, invoked by many, grant us protection in this call for food.
(5.3.8.c) O Indra, Lord of the bay horses, be gracious to our progeny; do not harm us, nor abandon us.
(5.3.9’) Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, the Lord of the world, the divine Savitṛ, the overcomer of enemies—
(5.3.9.c) May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and both Aśvins—the gods—protect the sacrificer from destruction. (5.3.10’) May those who are our rivals fall away; with Indra and Agni we drive them off.
(5.3.10.c) The Ādityas and Rudras, reaching upward, have made for us a fierce guardian, a sovereign lord.

(5.3.11’) From over there we call Indra hitherward—he who wins cattle, wins wealth, and wins horses; (5.3.11.c) may he hear this sacrifice of ours at our invocation. O Lord of the Bay Steeds, you have become our gracious friend.
(5.4.1’) You who were born among the mountains, the most powerful of plants—

(5.4.1.c) O you who destroy fever with *kuṣṭha*, drive away the fever from here! (5.4.2’) Born on the mountain of fair wings, from the Himavat, they go toward it with riches, for they know it as the destroyer of fever.
(5.4.2.c) Having heard of it, they approach it with wealth; indeed, they know the destroyer of fever. 2.
The Aśvattha tree, the abode of the gods, is in the third heaven from here;
there the gods obtained Kuṣṭha, the manifestation of immortality. A golden ship with golden moorings moved in the sky.
(5.4.4.c) There the gods obtained Kuṣṭha, the flower of immortality. (5.4.5’) Golden were the paths; golden were the oars.
(5.4.5.c) The ships were golden, by which they carried away the Kuṣṭha.
(5.4.6’) O Kuṣṭha, bring this man here to me; drive him out! (5.4.6.c) Make him free from disease for me!
(5.4.7’) You were born from the gods; you are the well-disposed friend of Soma.
(5.4.7.c) Be gracious to this breath, to the diffused breath, and to my sight!
7 (5.4.8’) Born from the Himalayas in the north, you are led toward the people in the east;
there they have distributed the most excellent names of Kuṣṭha. 8
(5.4.9’) You are the highest of the *kuṣṭha* plants; your father is named the Highest.
(5.4.9.c) Destroy every consumption and make the fever sapless! (5.4.10’) Strike away the disease of the head, the affliction of the eyes, and the infirmity of the body.
(5.4.10.c) May Kuṣṭha drive all that away—the divine and even virile power.
10 (5.5.1’) Night is your mother, the mist is your father, and Aryaman is your grandfather.
(5.5.1.c) You are indeed named Silācī; you are the sister of the gods. 1
He who drinks you lives; you protect that man.
For you are the sustainer of all people and their guide. You climb from tree to tree like a maiden longing for a husband.
(5.5.3.c) You are Jayantī, you are Pratyatiṣṭhantī, you are indeed named Sparaṇī.
||3|| (5.5.4’) Whatever has been done with the staff, whatever with the arrow, or whatever harm has been wrought by the fire—of that you are the remedy; as such, provide a remedy for this man. ||4||
(5.5.5’) You arise from auspicious *plakṣa* trees, from *aśvattha*, *khadira*, and *dhava*;
(5.5.5.c) from auspicious *nyagrodha* and *parṇa* trees—come to us, O Arundhatī! (5.5.6’) O golden-hued one, blessed one, sun-colored one, most beautiful in form!
(5.5.6.c) Go to the sound, O Niṣkṛti; you are indeed named Niṣkṛti.
(5.5.7’) O golden-colored, fortunate one, full of vigor, with hairy flanks!
(5.5.7.c) You are the sister of the waters, O Lākṣā; Vāta has become your soul.
(5.5.8) Silācī by name, the maiden daughter of Ajababhru, was your father;
she was nourished by the flesh of the dark horse of Yama.
(5.5.9) Having fallen from the horse's mouth, she flowed down toward the trees.
(5.5.9.c) Having become a winged river, come to us, O Arundhatī!
(5.6.1’) Vena disclosed from the radiant horizon the Brahman first born in the east; he revealed its highest stations, both the foundation and the womb of being and non-being.
(5.6.1.c) He disclosed its highest stations, both the foundation and the womb of being and non-being. (1)
Those first [deeds] of yours which were performed by those who were unattainable—may they not deceive our heroes here; I place that very thing before you.
(5.6.2) In a thousand streams, those [soma-drops], honey-tongued and unfailing, have resounded together in the vault of heaven. (5.6.3)
(5.6.3.c) His watchful spies do not close their eyes; at every step there are snarers for the one who would cross.
(5.6.4’) Run forth well toward the winning of booty, you who overcome all obstacles.
(5.6.4.c) You shall go beyond those enemies upon the ocean; you are named Sanisrasas, the thirteenth month, the house of Indra.
(5.6.5’) “With this you have succeeded, O so-and-so! Svāhā!
(5.6.5.c) “O Soma and Rudra, armed with sharp weapons and sharp missiles, who are most gracious—be well-disposed toward us here! 5” (5.6.6’) “With this you have succeeded, O so-and-so! Svāhā!”
(5.6.6.c) O Soma and Rudra, wielders of sharp weapons and sharp missiles, who are most gracious—be merciful to us here!
6 (5.6.7’) May that one go far away; Svāhā!
(5.6.7.c) O Soma and Rudra, wielders of sharp weapons and sharp missiles, who are most gracious—be merciful to us here! 7
Release us from distress and from reproach; accept our sacrifice and bestow immortality upon us.
O weapon of the eye, O weapon of the mind, O weapon of the sacred word (*brahman*), and O weapon of ascetic heat (*tapas*)!
You are a missile, a slayer; let those who plot against us be without missiles.
Whoever, with evil intent, should assail us with his eye, with his mind, with thought, or with purpose—O Agni, do thou render them senseless by thy own senselessness; Svāhā!
(5.6.11) Thou art the house of Indra.
(5.6.11.c) I take refuge in you; I enter into you—with my whole movement, my whole person, my whole self, and my whole body—along with whatever belongs to me.
(5.6.12’) You are the protection of Indra.
(5.6.12.c) I take refuge in you; I enter into you—with all my movement, all my persons, all my self, and all my bodies—together with that which is mine.
(5.6.13’) You are the armor of Indra.
(5.6.13.c) I take refuge in you; I enter into you—with my whole movement, my whole person, my whole self, and my whole body—along with whatever belongs to me.
(5.6.14’) You are the protection of Indra.
(5.6.14.c) I take refuge in you; I enter into you—with my whole movement, my whole person, my whole self, and my whole body—along with whatever belongs to me.
14 (5.7.1’) Bring [the sacrificial fee] to us; do not withhold it, O Arāti! Do not harm our sacrificial fee as it is being led away.

(5.7.1.c) Homage to the one who seeks to destroy, to failure; homage be to the enemy! (5.7.2’) O Arāti, the man whom you set before you, the one who laments—homage we pay to him; do not disturb my gain. (5.7.2.c) Homage we pay to him; do not cause my prosperity to waver.
May the boon granted by the gods be fulfilled for us by day and by night.
We turn away from the stingy one; let there be homage to the stingy one.
Going forth, we invoke Sarasvatī, Anumati, and Bhaga.
(5.7.4.c) I have uttered acceptable and honey-sweet speech among the invocations of the gods.
(5.7.5’) May he whom I entreat with speech joined to the mind by Sarasvatī—may Śraddhā find him today, bestowed by the tawny Soma.
(5.7.5.c) May Śraddhā find him today, bestowed by the tawny Soma.
(5.7.6’) Do not destroy our gain, nor our speech! O Indra and Agni, bring us both riches!
(5.7.6.c) All of you, desiring to give to us today, take pleasure in [accepting] our offering! (5.7.7’) Go away, O unsuccessful one! We lead your missile far away from here.

(5.7.7.c) I know you, O Arāti, as you squint and thrust [at us]. (5.7.8’) Moreover, appearing naked and distorted, you accompany people with sleep; O Arāti, you seek to frustrate the thought and the intention of man. (5.7.8.c) You seek to frustrate the thought and the intention of man. (5.7.9’) She who is great, of immense measure, and has pervaded all the quarters—
(5.7.9.c) to that Nirṛti with golden hair, I have paid homage. (5.7.10’) Golden-colored, fortunate, with a golden seat, the great one—
(5.7.10.c) To that Hiraṇyadrāpī, the goddess of misfortune, I have paid homage.
(5.8.1’) With fuel of *vaikaṅkata* wood, carry the clarified butter to the gods;
O Agni, delight them here, and let all come to my invocation.
(5.8.2’) O Indra, come to my invocation; listen to this which I shall do. (5.8.2.c) May these *atisara* offerings dedicated to Indra bend my intention toward success.
(5.8.2.e) Through them, O Jātavedas, master of your own body, may we be able to perform heroic deeds. 2.
(5.8.3’) Whatever that godless one over there intends to do against us, O gods—let not Agni carry his oblation; O gods, do not favor him! Come to my very invocation!
(5.8.4’) Run past, overtake, and strike him down with Indra’s word!
(5.8.4.c) Like a wolf seizing a sheep, crush him! Let him not escape alive; bind away his very breath!
(5.8.5’) Him whom these men have set before them as a priest for their own destruction—O Indra, I cast that man beneath your foot, delivering him over to death!

(5.8.6’) Even if they have fled from the cities of the gods and have made the *brahman* their armor, (5.8.6c) fashioning it as a protection for their bodies and a safeguard while they chant— render all that sapless! (5.8.7’) Those which he has already overstepped and those which he shall yet make to overstep— render them all sapless!
(5.8.7.c) O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, turn them back again so that you may strike down that people.
(5.8.8’) Just as Indra, having obtained the cry of victory, cast them beneath his feet,
so do I cast those [enemies] down for all future years.
Right here, O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, pierce them in their vital organs with your fierce [weapon]. Right here, O Indra, trample them down; may I be dear to you.
We take hold of you, O Indra; may we abide in your favor. 9.9.9–e.
(5.9.1’) Svāhā to the sky! ‖1‖ (5.9.2’) Svāhā to the earth! ‖2‖ (5.9.3’) Svāhā to the intermediate space! ‖3‖
(5.9.4’) Svāhā to the intermediate space! (5.9.5’) Svāhā to heaven!
(5.9.6’) Svāhā to the earth!

(5.9.7’) The sun is my eye, the wind my breath, the intermediate space my self, and the earth my body. (5.9.7.c) Unassailable by name am I; here I am. This [Self] I deposit within myself for the protection of heaven and earth.
7 (5.9.8’) Upward [I raise] life, upward strength, upward power, upward the sorcery, upward the inspired thought, and upward sensory power!
(5.9.8.c) Bestower of life, consort of life, full of self-power, be my guardians; protect me!
(5.9.8.e) Be seated within my very self; do not harm me!
8 (5.10.1’) You are my stone armor, [to ward off] him who, being evil-minded, would attack me from the eastern quarter.
(5.10.1.c) May he meet with this [consequence].
(5.10.2’) You are my stone armor; may he who, being malevolent, would attack me from the southern direction, (5.10.2.c) may he meet with this [consequence].

(5.10.3’) You are my stone armor; whoever, being evil-minded, would attack me from the western quarter—may he meet with this [fate]. (5.10.4’) You are my stone armor; whoever, being evil-minded, would attack me from the northern quarter—may he meet with this [fate].
(5.10.4.c) May he meet with this [consequence].
(5.10.5’) You are my stone armor; may he who, being evil-minded, would attack me from the fixed quarter, (5.10.5.c) meet with this [consequence]. May he meet with this [consequence]. (5)
(5.10.6’) You are my stone armor; may he who, being malevolent, would attack me from the upward direction—may he meet with this [consequence].
(5.10.7’) You are my stone armor; may he who, being malevolent, would attack me from the intermediate directions of the quarters—may he meet with this [consequence].
(5.10.7.c) May he obtain this.
(5.10.8’) With the *bṛhat* [sāman], I invoke the mind through Mātariśvan;
from the sun, the out-breath and in-breath; from the intermediate space, the eye; from the earth, the body.
(5.10.8.e) We invoke the speech of Sarasvatī, whose mind is yoked [to us].

||8|| (5.11.1’) How did you speak here to the great Asura? How, O you of brilliant valor, to the father Hari? (5.11.1.c) Having given away Pṛśni as a sacrificial fee, O Varuṇa, you, O bounteous one, must consider again in your mind. ||1||
(5.11.2’) “I do not become Maghavan again out of desire; I have joined this spotted cow for the sake of vision.
(5.11.2.c) By what poetic wisdom, O Atharvan, and by what birth are you Jātavedas?
(5.11.3’) “Truly, I am profound through poetic wisdom; truly, by my birth I am Jātavedas.”
(5.11.3.c) Neither my servant nor my noblewoman has disregarded my vow by its greatness, since I shall uphold it.
(5.11.4’) O Varuṇa, self-sustained one, there is no other more wise than you, nor more skilled in intellect.
You know all these worlds; indeed, even that person who possesses magical power fears you.
For you indeed, O Varuṇa, self-dependent one, know all generations, O excellent leader. Is there anything else beyond this space? And is there anything below it, O immortal one?
5 Beyond this space there is one other thing; beyond that one, by another, even what is difficult to reach is brought near. 6
(5.11.6.c) This I declare to you, O Varuṇa, knowing it: let the Paṇis be those whose speech is downward-turned; let the Dāsas creep low into the earth.
(6) (5.11.7’) For indeed, O Varuṇa, you yourself proclaim many reproaches against those who turn back their gifts.
(5.11.7.c) Let there not be so many Paṇis; let not people call you one who bestows no wealth. (7)
(5.11.8’) Let not people call me one who bestows no gifts; O singer, I give Pṛśni back to you.
Come with all your powers to my entire hymn of praise, among all the human quarters.
(5.11.9’) Let your uplifted hymns of praise go forth among all the human quarters.
(5.11.9.c) Give now to me that which you have not yet given; you are my ally, my seven-step friend.
(5.11.10’) Our kinship is the same, O Varuṇa; our birth is the same. I know this, that our birth is indeed the same.
(5.11.10.c) I give to you that which I have not yet given; I am your ally, your seven-step friend.

The god, bestowing strength upon the god who praises him, the wise one upon the sage who lauds him—O Varuṇa, self-dependent, you have indeed begotten Atharvan, the father and kinsman of the gods. Bestow upon him a most highly praised gift; you are our friend and our supreme kin. Kindled today in the dwelling of man, O Jātavedas, you, a god, worship the gods. Bring them hither, O you of Mitra-like splendor; you are the wise messenger, the seer, and the perceptive one.
O Tanūnapāt, sweetening with honey the paths that lead along the way of Truth, make them savory, O fair-tongued one.
(5.12.2.c) Accomplishing our prayers with our thoughts and our sacrifice, bring our ritual to the gods.
(5.12.3’) Being invoked, worthy of praise, and to be celebrated, come, O Agni, in harmony with the Vasus!
You are the youthful Hotṛ-priest of the gods; as such, being impelled, perform the sacrifice for them as the most skilled sacrificer.
The sacred grass is strewn toward the east upon the earth’s surface at the beginning of days, for her to dwell upon.
It spreads out further and wider, a pleasant seat for the gods and for Aditi.
Let the spacious ones open wide, like wives adorning themselves for their husbands.
(5.12.5.c) O divine, wide, all-enlivening doors, be easy of access for the gods.
(5.12.6’) May the two worshipful ones, Dawn and Night, swelling with milk, sit down close together in their place;
the two celestial maidens, vast and gold-adorned, assuming a brilliant and radiant splendor.

(5.12.7) May the two divine Hotṛ-priests, the first, eloquent ones, measuring out the sacrifice for man to worship, (5.12.7c) the two poets who impel [the rites] in the assemblies, pointing toward the eastern light by their direction—
(5.12.8) may Bhāratī come swiftly to our sacrifice, and Iḷā, making it manifest here like Manu.
(5.12.8.c) Let the three goddesses— Sarasvatī and the others, skilled in their work— sit upon this pleasant sacrificial grass.
(5.12.9’) He who fashioned these two parents, Heaven and Earth, and adorned all beings with their forms—
O Hotṛ, being impelled today, do you, the more skilled sacrificer, worship that wise god Tvaṣṭṛ here.
(5.12.10’) Release [the oblations] by thyself, anointing them, according to the seasons, for the path of the gods.
(5.12.10.c) May Vanaspati, the immolator, and the god Agni, sweeten the oblation with honey and ghee.
‖10‖ (5.12.11’) As soon as he was born, Agni measured out the sacrifice; he became the leader of the gods.
(5.12.11.c) By the command of this Hotṛ, at the speech of the Cosmic Order, may the gods eat the oblation consecrated with Svāhā!
‖11‖ (5.13.1’) For Varuṇa, the seer of heaven, has given it to me; with my powerful words I dissolve your poison.
(5.13.1.c) Whether dug up, undug, or adhering, I have seized it; like a snake from the desert, your poison has perished. ‖1‖

(5.13.2’) That poison of yours which is waterless, that very one I have seized from you in these [plants]. (5.13.2.c) I seize your middle, your highest essence, and even your lowest; through fear, let it perish, and so too from you.
(5.13.3’) My roar is like a bull, like thunder with the clouds; with my fierce word I drive it away, and so too from you.
(5.13.3.c) With my men, I have seized that essence of his; may the sun rise up like light from darkness.
(3) (5.13.4’) With my eye I strike out your eye; with poison I strike out your poison.
(5.13.4.c) O serpent, die! Do not live! Let the poison come back upon you! (4)
O Kirātas, Pṛśnis, Upatṛṇyas, Babhrus, Āsitās, and Alīkas, listen to me!
Do not stand in the way of my friend; making yourselves heard, come down and take your pleasure in the underworld.
Of the Āsita, the Taimāta, the Babhru, and the Apodaka—
(5.13.6.c) From the son of Sattrāsāha, from Manyu, I unloose [the spell] as one unbinds the string from a bow, as one unharnesses chariots.
(5.13.7’) Āligī and Viligī, father and mother—we know you completely, O kinsmen; being powerless, what will you do? (5.13.7.c) We know you thoroughly, O relatives; being sapless, what will you do?
The daughter of Urugūlā was born as a slave-girl from the Asiknī river;
she rendered the poison of all those afflicted by *pratanka* devoid of its potency. Karṇā, the porcupine that descends from the mountain, declared this.
Whatever these dug-out [wells] may be, their poison is the most sapless of all.
9 Not a *tābuva* are you, not a *tābuva* indeed; you are certainly no *tābuva*. By means of the *tābuva*, [we render] the poison sapless. 10
(5.13.11’) Neither the stammerer nor the non-stammerer—verily, you are the stammerer.
(5.13.11.c) By means of the stammerer, [I destroy] the sapless poison.
‖11‖ (5.14.1’) The fair-winged bird found you; the boar dug you up with its snout.
(5.14.1.c) O plant that destroys the malicious, strike down the one who seeks to harm us; slay the practitioner of sorcery!
(5.14.2’) Strike down the sorcerers; strike down the practitioner of sorcery! Furthermore, O plant, slay him who seeks to harm us!
(5.14.2.c) And him who seeks to harm us, you must slay, O plant!

Having cut away the skin all around, as one strips the entrails from a deer, O gods, cast the *kṛtyā* back upon the maker of the *kṛtyā*, like a necklace. Having seized the *kṛtyā* by the hand, lead it back again to the maker of the *kṛtyā*.
Place it directly before us, so that it may strike down the one who fashioned the *kṛtyā*.
Let the *kṛtyās* be for the maker of the *kṛtyā*; let curses be for the one who utters curses.
Like a comfortable chariot, let the *kṛtyā* turn back again upon the maker of the *kṛtyā*.
Whether it was a woman or a man who fashioned this *kṛtyā* for his own evil,
we lead it back to him like a horse by means of its halter.
Whether you are made by the gods or made by men—
(5.14.7.c) We lead you back again, we who are united with Indra.
(5.14.8’) O Agni, conqueror of armies, overcome the hostile hosts! (5.14.8.c) We take back the magic spell from the spell-caster by means of a counter-spell.
O you who have pierced the wound, know him; strike down him who made it!
We do not sharpen our weapons for your slaughter, O you who did not create them. Go to him like a son to his father; like a snake that has been stepped upon, bite him ten times!

(5.14.10.c) Enter him as if into a snare; go back again to the performer of the *kṛtyā* who created the *kṛtyā*. (5.14.11’) Like a doe leaping up toward a wild elephant, let the *kṛtyā* seize the one who made it.
Let the straight-flying arrow fly toward heaven and earth;
let the *kṛtyā* seize that practitioner of the *kṛtyā* again, as a hunter seizes a deer. Let it go against him like fire, or like water flowing down with the current.
(5.14.13.c) May it turn back happily like a chariot; may the *kṛtyā* return to the one who fashioned the *kṛtyā*.
(5.15.1) One for me and ten for me, O plant, are the expellers.
Born of *ṛta*, O observer of *ṛta*, make honey for me, O honeyed one!
Twenty-two of you, O herb, are my purifiers;
born of *ṛta*, O observer of *ṛta*, make honey for me, O honeyed one.
Thirty-three of you, O herb, are my purifiers.
Born of Truth, O thou who art rich in Truth, do thou make honey for me, O honey-sweet one!
(3) And my four [removers] and my forty removers, O Plant—born of Truth, O thou who art rich in Truth, do thou make honey for me, O honey-sweet one! (4)
Five and fifty are my expellers, O herb;
born of *ṛta*, rich in *ṛta*, make honey for me, O honeyed one.
Six and sixty are my expellers, O herb.
Born of the *ṛta*, O you who possess the *ṛta*, make honey for me, O sweet one!
(5.15.6.c) Seven and seventy, O plant, are my expellers.
Born of the *ṛta*, O you who possess the *ṛta*, make honey for me, O sweet one! (5.15.7.c)
Eight and eighty are my healers, O herb;
born of Truth, O observer of Truth, make honey for me, O honeyed one.
Nine and ninety are my healers, O herb.
Born of Truth, O you who abide in Truth, make honey for me, O honey-sweet one! 9 Ten and a hundred, O herb, are my expellers.
Born of Truth, O you who abide in Truth, make honey for me, O honey-sweet one! 10
A hundred and a thousand are my speakers, O herb;
born of *Ṛta*, rich in *Ṛta*, make honey for me, O honey-sweet one!
If you are a single bull, release [the seed]; you are full of sap.
(5.16.2’) If you are a two-bull, release [the seed]; you are one who has no strength.
(5.16.3’) If you are a three-bull, release [the seed]; you are one who has no strength. (5.16.4’) If you are a four-bull, release [the seed]; you are one who has no strength.

(5.16.7) If you are a seven-bull, you are one who has shed his vigor.

(5.16.11’) “If you are the eleventh, you are the one who draws out the water.
(5.17.1’) Regarding the first sin against Brahman, they spoke: the boundless ocean, Mātariśvan, Vīḷuhara, Tapas, Ugra, Mayobhū, and the divine waters, the first-born of Cosmic Order (Ṛta).
King Soma first gave back the wife of the Brahman, free from anger.
Varuṇa and Mitra were the attendants; Agni, the Hotṛ, took her by the hand and led her away.
She must not be sent as a messenger; thus is the kingdom of the Kṣatriya protected.

(5.17.3.c) That which they call "the star," the one with disheveled hair, the ill omen descending upon the village—she is the wife of Brahmā; she consumes the kingdom wherever the hare-marked moon has fallen like a flaming torch. (5.17.4)
The student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) moves about, performing his various duties; he becomes a single limb of the gods.
Through him, Bṛhaspati recovered his wife who had been led away by Soma, just as the gods [recovered] the *juhū* ladle.
Indeed, the ancient gods spoke concerning this woman—the seven seers (*sapta-ṛṣayaḥ*) who sat down through their ascetic heat (*tapas*).

The terrifying wife of the Brahmin, when led away, brings about misfortune in the highest heaven. "Even if ten husbands, who were not Brahmins, preceded a woman,
if a Brahmin has taken her hand, he alone is her husband in every way.
Only a Brahmin is a husband, not a Kshatriya nor a Vaishya."
Sūrya goes forth proclaiming this to the five tribes of men.
(9) The gods have indeed given her back; men have given her back.
Taking hold of truth, the kings have given back the wife of the Brahmin. (10)
Having restored the wife of the Brahmin and been freed from sin by the gods,
they partake of the nourishment of the earth and worship the Wide-Striding One.
His wife, though a hundredfold fruitful and auspicious, does not lie upon his bed.

In whatever kingdom the wife of a Brahmin is detained through thoughtlessness, (5.17.12.c) in that house no one with deformed ears or a broad head is born, (5.17.13’) in whatever kingdom the wife of a Brahmin is detained through thoughtlessness. (5.17.13.c) 13.
In that kingdom where the wife of a Brahmin is detained through thoughtlessness, his charioteer— gold-necked— does not go at the head of the sacrificial animals;
nor does his white horse with black ears, yoked to the pole, receive honor.
In whatever kingdom the wife of a Brahmin is detained through thoughtlessness, (15) in that kingdom there shall be no lotus pond, nor shall the *aṇḍīka* lily or the lotus stalk grow;
in whatever kingdom the wife of a Brahmin is detained through thoughtlessness. (16)
They do not milk the speckled cow for him who waits upon her milking;
in whatever kingdom the wife of a Brahmin is detained through thoughtlessness,
there no auspicious cow exists, nor does the ox endure the yoke.

(5.17.18.c) Where the Brahmin dwells for a night in sin, he loses his discernment. (5.18.1) O King, the gods did not give this cow to you for eating; O Kṣatriya, do not desire to devour the cow of a Brahmin, which is not fit to be eaten.
A wicked kṣatriya, oppressed by dice and defeated by his own self,
might eat the cow of a brahmin today, thinking, "Let me live today, not tomorrow.
Like a female serpent covered with its skin, he is enveloped by the poison of his own sin.

O Kṣatriya, this cow of the Brāhmaṇa is harsh and unfit for consumption. (5.18.3.c) It surely leads away the ruling power and destroys splendor; like a fire that has been kindled, it consumes everything.
(5.18.4.c) He who regards a Brāhmaṇa as mere food drinks the very poison of the blind one. (5.18.4)

(5.18.5) He who strikes him, thinking him to be weak—a scorner of the gods, desiring wealth, and not from his heart—Indra kindles fire within that man’s very heart; he hates him as he moves through both worlds. (5.18.6) A Brahmin must not be harmed, any more than one would harm a beloved body.
For Soma is his heir, and Indra is his protector against curses.
(5.18.6.c) He swallows the hundred-jawed [serpent], yet he is unable to extract it;
so it is with the glutton who, though eating the food of the Brahmins, fancies, "I am eating something sweet. (5.18.7.c)
The tongue is the bowstring, the palate is the bow-tip, and the teeth are smeared with ascetic heat.
With these—bows whose strength is the heart and which are impelled by the gods—the Brahmin pierces those who revile the gods.
(5.18.9) The Brahmins are sharp-shafted archers possessing missiles; the arrow-flight they discharge is never in vain.
(5.18.9.c) Having pursued him with ascetic fervor and wrath, they shatter him from afar.
(5.18.10’) Those Vaitahavyas who formerly ruled over a thousand and ten hundred, having devoured the cow of a Brahmin, met their destruction. (5.18.10.c) They perished.

The cow herself, as she was being slaughtered, struck down those descendants of Vitahavya who had waited for the last-born calf of Kesara-prabandha. Those people numbered one hundred and one whom the earth shook off.
Having harmed a Brāhmaṇa woman and brought about her ruin, he perishes in a manner beyond recovery.
(5.18.12.c) The scorner of the gods wanders among mortals; having swallowed poison, he becomes a mere heap of bones.
He who harms a Brāhmaṇa, a kinsman of the gods, does not even reach the world of the ancestors. (5.18.13)
"Agni is indeed our guardian of the path; Soma is called our heir;
Indra is the slayer of the accuser—thus do the wise know it.
O Lord of Men, like a poisoned arrow; O Lord of Cattle, like a viper."
That terrible arrow of the Brahmin pierced those who were drinking.
(5.18.15.c) They grew beyond measure; they seemed to touch the very heavens.
Having harmed Bhṛgu, the Sṛñjayas and the Vaitahavyas met their destruction. (5.19.1)
Those people who have harmed the Brāhmaṇa Bṛhatsāman, the descendant of Aṅgiras—
may the ram that eats both kinds of food destroy their sheep and their offspring.
Those who have spat upon the Brāhmaṇa, or those who have sought to extort a fee from him.
(5.19.3.c) They sit in the middle of the stream, devouring your entrails and hair.
(5.19.4’) As long as the Brahman-cow is being cooked and it struggles against the fire, (5.19.4.c) so long does it destroy the splendor of the kingdom; no heroic son is born there.

Cruel is her devouring; she devours pungent flesh. That milk which is drunk from her is indeed a sin against the ancestors. (5.19.5) The fierce king who, thinking himself powerful, seeks to devour a Brahmin—(5.19.6) [he falls into ruin].
That kingdom is cast away where a Brahmin is defeated.
(5.19.7) Having become eight-footed, four-eyed, four-eared, four-jawed, two-faced, and double-tongued, she shakes down the kingdom of the oppressor of Brahmins. (5.19.7)
That kingdom indeed flows away like water from a broken boat;
for wherever they harm a Brahmin, misfortune destroys that kingdom.
The trees drive him away, saying, "Do not come into our shade."
(5.19.9.c) O Nārada, whoever covets the true wealth of a Brāhmaṇa—
(5.19.10’) King Varuṇa has declared this to be a poison ordained by the gods;
(5.19.10.c) having eaten the cow of a Brāhmaṇa, no one at all remains awake in the kingdom.
Those ninety-nine [Nivātakavaca hosts] whom the earth shook off—
having harmed the offspring of a Brāhmaṇī woman, they met with an impossible defeat.
They are those to which they bind a dead man, [like] a wall that crushes the footprints.
(5.19.12.c) O oppressor of the Brahmin, the gods have declared those tears to be your sacrificial underlayer. (5.19.13’) Those tears which rolled from the one who was grieving and being subdued—
(5.19.13.c) O oppressor of the Brahmin, the gods have ordained those as your portion of the waters.
That with which they bathe the dead, and with which one moistens the beard—
that portion of the waters, O oppressor of Brahmins, the gods have withheld from you.
Rain does not fall upon the oppressor of Brahmins, who belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa.

(5.19.15.c) No assembly is fit for him; he does not bring his friend under his control. (5.20.1) A loud-sounding drum, made of wood, gathered together with the products of the cow—making your voice heard, subduing rivals, roar against him like a lion about to conquer!
Bound to the wooden frame, he roared like a lion; like a bull bellowing toward a cow, you have stood firm.
You are the bull; your rivals are emasculated. Your vigor belongs to Indra; it overcomes all adversaries.
Like a bull in the herd, manifesting your power with force, roar as one seeking cattle, a winner of spoils.

(5.20.3.c) Pierce the hearts of our enemies with grief; let the foes depart, abandoned by their villages. (5.20.4’) Conquering the armies, extending our life upward, seizing and holding our households, look out in many directions! Hearing the drum’s voice speaking with effort, awakened by its sound and seeking protection, let the woman run toward her son, grasping him by the hand—she who was an enemy in battle, now terrified of death.
O drum, you have sounded your voice first; resplendent, speak upon the back of the earth!
Crushing the enemy host, O drum, speak with splendor and with truthful words.
(6) Let your roar resound between these two worlds; let your distinct sounds go forth swiftly.
Thirsting for battle, cry out and thunder, creating a hymn of praise for the triumph of our allies, O celestial-sounding one! (7)
Fashioned by inspired thoughts, let him utter his voice; rouse the weapons of the heroes!
O Indra-mediator, summon the warriors; with your allies, strike down the enemies.
(8) Roaring aloud, leading the way, with a bold host, making his presence known, he resounds through many villages. (9)
Seeking fortune and knowing the sacred ways, distribute fame among the many in this double kingdom.
O banner of excellence, winner of wealth, most powerful, victor in battle, you are sharpened by the sacred word (*brahman*).
Like a pressing-stone upon the filter for the stalks of soma, O drum, dance over the booty like a mountain seeking cattle.

Subduing enemies, overcoming those who attack, seeking cattle, victorious, and a breaker-through—like one skilled in speech reciting a mantra, bring forth your voice for victory in battle; utter here a cry for strength!
Shaking the unshakable, most frequent in the fray, conqueror of adversaries, the invincible leader in the van.
(5.20.12.c) Protected by Indra, observing the assemblies, illuminating the hearts of enemies, go swiftly!
(5.21.1’) O drum, utter heartlessness and dejection among the enemies!
We instill hatred, exhaustion, and fear among the enemies; strike them down, O drum!
Trembling in mind, eye, and heart,
let the enemies run away in fear when the clarified butter is offered with terror.
The wooden vessel has been prepared with the products of the cow, belonging to all lineages.

(5.21.3.c) Smeared with clarified butter, strike terror into the enemies! (5.21.4’) Just as wild forest animals are terrified by a man, even so, O drum, roar out against the enemies; terrify them and confound their minds! (5.21.5’) Just as goats and sheep run from a wolf, greatly terrified, (5.21.5.c) so, O drum, cry out against the enemies; terrify them and bewilder their minds. 5 (5.21.6’) Just as winged birds are startled at every dawn by a hawk, and just as [creatures are] by the roar of a lion—
(5.21.6.c) Thus, O drum, roar out against the enemies; terrify them and confound their minds!
(5.21.7’) By means of the drum and the skin of the spotted deer, all the gods who seek the battle were utterly terrified of the enemies.
(5.21.7.c) All the gods who strive for victory in combat were struck with great fear.
May those enemies of ours who advance in military ranks be terrified by the sound of the footsteps with which Indra sports along with his shadow.
May the twanging of bowstrings and the drums resound toward all directions.
The armies of the enemies, being defeated, flee in their ranks.
O Āditya, take back your eye; let your rays run after it.
Let them cling to the feet when the strength of the arms has departed.
(5.21.11’) You, O fierce Maruts, sons of Pṛśni, with Indra as your ally, crush the enemies! (5.21.11c) King Soma, King Varuṇa, Mahādeva, and even Death, and Indra—
(5.21.12’) these are the divine armies, having the sun as their banner, acting in unison.
(5.21.12.c) May they conquer our enemies; Svāhā!
‖12‖ (5.22.1’) May Agni drive away the fever from here; may Soma, the pressing-stone, and Varuṇa of purified skill [drive it away].
(5.22.1.c) May the altar, the sacrificial grass, and the brightly flaming fuel-brands drive away hostilities to that other place. ‖1‖

(5.22.2’) This one who makes all things yellowish-brown, burning and consuming like fire—therefore, O fever (*takman*), become sapless; then turn away or go downward! (5.22.3’) He who is knotty, knotted, like a crumbling ruin, and ruddy—
(5.22.3.c) Drive away the fever, O you of all-pervading power, downward and far away! (5.22.4.a) Having paid homage to the fever, I send it downward;
(5.22.4.c) let the slayer of Śakambhara’s fist return again to the great bulls. (5.22.4.d) 4. Let him return to the great bulls.
The Mūjavants are his home; the Mahāvṛṣas are his home.
As far as you have been born, O Takman, so great are you; you have settled among the Balhikas.
O Takman, you serpent, go away! O you who cause disease, you who cause lameness, drive far away!
Seek out the slave-girl Niṣṭakvarī; strike her down with the thunderbolt!
O Takman, go to the Mūjavants or to the Balhikas, or even further away!
Seek out the Śūdra woman Prapharvī; shake her off like a bird, O Takman!
Go away, O fever, and eat the great bulls of the Mūjavat mountains, our kinsmen;
we declare these other fields to you, or these lands belonging to others.
You do not take pleasure in another’s field; being self-controlled, show us mercy.
(5.22.9.c) The fever has indeed arisen; it shall go away to the Balhikas.
(5.22.10’) Whether you are cold or hot, or cause trembling along with coughing—terrible are your darts, O Fever; with them, avoid us!
(5.22.10.c) Terrible are your darts, O Fever; with them, avoid us!
"Do not make these your friends—the balāsa, the cough, and the fever.
Do not come back toward us again; O *takman*, that is what I tell you.
"O *takman*, together with your brother balāsa and your sister the cough..."
(5.22.12.c) May evil depart together with the rival to that stranger folk.

(5.22.13’) [Destroy] the fever that recurs every third day, the one that recurs every fourth day, the daily one, and the autumnal; destroy the *takman*—the cold, the *rūra*, the summer, and the rainy-season fever. (5.22.13.c) Destroy it!
From the Gandhāris, from the Mūjavats, from the Aṅgas, and from the Magadhas—like one departing who leaves behind a treasure, we entrust Takman to them.
Woven for me are Heaven and Earth; woven is the goddess Sarasvatī.

The worm that creeps around the eyes, that creeps around the nostrils, that goes into the teeth while they are chewing— that worm we crush. Two of like form, two of different forms, two black ones, two red ones.
Babhru, Babhrukarna, Grdhra, and Koka— these have been slain.
Those worms that have white flanks, those that are black with white forelegs,
and whatever others are of manifold forms— all these worms we crush to pieces.
The sun rises in the east, seen by all, the slayer of the unseen;
striking down those that are seen and those that are unseen, he crushes all worms.
The ye-vāṣas, the kaṣ-kaṣas, the ejatkas, and the śipavitnukas—[he destroys them].
Let the worm that is seen be slain, and let the one that is unseen be slain!
(5.23.8’) Slain is Yevāṣa among the worms, slain is Nadanimotā; I have ground them all to powder, like mustard seeds with a millstone.
(5.23.8.c) I have crushed them all together like mustard seeds with a millstone.
The three-headed, the triple-humped, the worm, the speckled,
the pale— its ribs I crush, and its head I hew away.
Like Atri, like Kaṇva, like Jamadagni, I slay you, O worms.
(5.23.10.c) With the sacred word of Agastya, I grind the worms to pieces.
(5.23.11’) Slain is the king of the worms, and their chief architect is slain;
slain is the worm whose mother is slain, whose brother is slain, and whose sister is slain. (5.23.11)
Slain are his household pests, slain are the surrounding pests;
and those that are like tiny insects—all of them are slain.
Of all the worms, and of all the species of worms—
(5.23.13.c) I split his head with a stone; I burn his mouth with fire.
(5.24.1’) Savitṛ is the overlord of all impelments;
may he protect me in this sacred formulation, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this foundation, in this [foundation].
(5.24.1.e) In this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!
(5.24.2’) Agni is the overlord of the trees; may he protect me in this sacred formulation (*brahman*), in this rite, in this priestly office (*purodhā*), in this foundation, in this [foundation].
(5.24.2.e) In this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods, Svāhā!
(5.24.3’) May He who is the overlord of givers, Heaven and Earth, protect me in this sacred word, in this rite,
in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this [foundation].
(5.24.3.e) In this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods—svāhā!
(5.24.4’) Varuṇa is the lord of the waters; may he protect me in this sacred formulation, in this rite, in this leadership, in this foundation, in this [foundation].
(5.24.4.e) In this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods, *svāhā*!
(5.24.5’) Mitra and Varuṇa are the lords of rain;
may they protect me in this sacred formulation (*brahman*), in this rite, in this priesthood, in this foundation, in this [foundation].
(5.24.5.e) In this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods— svāhā! (5.24.6’) O Maruts, lords of the mountains, may you protect me in this sacred formulation,
in this rite, in this priesthood, in this foundation, in this [foundation].
(5.24.6.e) In this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!
(5.24.7.a) Soma is the overlord of plants; may he protect me in this sacred formulation (*brahman*), in this rite, in this leadership, in this foundation, in this [foundation].
(5.24.7.e) In this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!
(5.24.8.a) Vāyu is the lord of the intermediate region; may he protect me in this sacred formulation (*brahman*), in this rite, in this leadership, in this foundation, in this [foundation].
(5.24.8.e) In this consciousness, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!
(5.24.9’) Sūrya is the overlord of eyes; may he protect me in this sacred formulation (*brahman*), in this rite, in this priesthood, in this foundation, in this [foundation].
(5.24.9.e) In this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!
(5.24.10’) The Moon is the lord of the constellations;
may he protect me in this sacred formulation (*brahman*), in this rite, in this priesthood, in this foundation, in this [state].
(5.24.10.e) In this consciousness, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!

(5.24.11’) Indra is the sovereign lord of heaven; may he protect me in this sacred formulation (*brahman*), in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this [foundation].
(5.24.11.e) In this consciousness, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods, *svāhā*!
(5.24.12’) May the father of the Maruts, the lord of cattle,
protect me in this sacred formulation (*brahman*), in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this [foundation].
(5.24.12.e) In this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods—svāhā!
(5.24.13’) Death is the overlord of creatures;
may he protect me in this sacred formulation, in this rite, in this priesthood, in this foundation, in this [foundation].
(5.24.13.e) In this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!
(5.24.14’) Yama is the sovereign lord of the ancestors; may he protect me in this sacred word (*brahman*), in this rite, in this priesthood, in this foundation, in this [state].
(5.24.14.e) In this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods— *svāhā*!
(5.24.15’) May the fathers who are beyond protect me in this sacred formulation (*brahman*), in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this [foundation].
(5.24.15.e) In this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods— *svāhā*!
(5.24.16’) May those who are lower than you favor me—
in this sacred formulation (*brahman*), in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this [foundation].
(5.24.16.e) In this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods, svāhā!
||16|| (5.24.17’) May those grandfathers protect me in this sacred formulation,
in this rite, in this priesthood, in this foundation, in this [foundation].
(5.24.17.e) In this consciousness, in this intention, in this blessing, in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!
||17|| (5.25.1) Gathered from the mountain, from the womb of heaven, from every limb; may the penis, the depositor of the seed of the embryo, place it like a feather upon an arrow. ||1||
(5.25.2’) Just as this great earth receives the embryo of living beings, (5.25.2.c) so do I place the embryo within you; for that purpose, I call upon you for aid.
(5.25.3’) O Sinīvālī, bestow the embryo; O Sarasvatī, bestow the embryo!
(5.25.3.c) May both the Aśvins, adorned with lotus-garlands, place the embryo within you.
(5.25.4’) May Mitra and Varuṇa grant you an embryo; may the god Bṛhaspati grant you an embryo;
may Indra and Agni grant you an embryo; may Dhātṛ bestow an embryo upon you. (5.25.4.c) May Dhātṛ bestow an embryo upon you.
May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms.
May Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you.
Whatever King Varuṇa knows, or whatever the goddess Sarasvatī [knows]...
(5.25.6.c) That which Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, knows—drink that which produces the embryo.

(5.25.7’) You are the embryo of the plants, the embryo of the trees; you are the embryo of every living being. O Agni, bestow the embryo here upon us. (5.25.7.c) O Agni, bestow the embryo here upon us.
(5.25.8’) Ascend, display your heroism; place the embryo in the womb!
(5.25.8.c) You are a bull, O possessor of virility; we lead you here for the sake of progeny.
(5.25.9’) Open wide, O Bārhatsāman; let the embryo lie within your womb.

(5.25.9.c) The gods have granted you a son, O Soma-drinker, who possesses both [natures]. (5.25.10’) O Dhātṛ, with the most excellent form, place a male child within the womb-tracts of this woman, so that he may be born in the tenth month. (5.25.10.c) Place a male child within the womb-tracts of this woman, so that he may be born in the tenth month.
With the most excellent form of Tvaṣṭṛ,
place a male child within the womb-channels of this woman, so that he may be born in the tenth month. With the most excellent form of Savitṛ, [place him] within the womb-channels of this woman.
Bestow upon her a male child so that he may be born in the tenth month.
O Prajāpati, with your most excellent form, place a male child within the womb-veins of this woman so that he may be born in the tenth month.
(5.26.1) May the Yajus-formulas, the sacrificial fuel-sticks, and Agni, the wise one, join you here with the cry of Svāhā!
(5.26.2) May the divine Savitṛ, the mighty one, knowing all, join [the elements] in this sacrifice with the cry of Svāhā!
(5.26.3) May Indra, the wise one, join the hymns and songs of praise in this sacrifice, well-yoked, with the cry of Svāhā!
(5.26.4) The *praisha* calls, the *nivids*, and the *svāhā*-utterances remain joined here with the wives for him who carries [the sacrifice].
(5.26.5) The meters, O Maruts, and the *svāhā*-utterances, like a mother carrying her son, carry him here when they are joined.
(5.26.6) Here has come Aditi with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and the sprinkling waters, as she extends the sacrifice—*svāhā*.
May Viṣṇu yoke manifold heats; may he yoke them well-yoked in this sacrifice—svāhā!
May Tvaṣṭṛ yoke manifold forms; may he yoke them well-yoked in this sacrifice—svāhā!
May Bhaga yoke blessings for him; may he, the wise one, yoke them well-yoked in this sacrifice—svāhā!
May Soma yoke many draughts of milk for this sacrifice, well-yoked; Svāhā!
(10) May Indra yoke many draughts of milk for this sacrifice, well-yoked; Svāhā!
(11) O Aśvins, come hither by means of the sacred word (*brahman*), increasing the sacrifice with the *vaṣaṭ*-call! (12)
(5.26.12.c) O Bṛhaspati, come hither with the sacred word; this is the sacrifice, this is the light for the sacrificer—*svāhā*!
(5.27.1’) His fuel-sticks rise upward, and the bright flames of Agni rise upward;
most radiant, fair of countenance, with his son, the Asura Tanūnapāt, who has many hands.
(5.27.2) The god among gods, the divine one, anoints the paths with honey and ghee.
(5.27.3) With honey he approaches the sacrifice, being impelled; Narāśaṃsa is Agni, the well-doing god, Savitṛ, the possessor of all boons.
(5.27.4) Toward this [sacrifice] he comes with power, the bearer of oblations, being praised with ghee and with homage.
(5.27.5) Agni, at the sacrifices where the ladles are extended, shall worship the majesty of this Agni.
5 (5.27.6) Three gracious ones stood forth at the extended offerings—the Vasus and the bestowers of wealth.
6 (5.27.7) The divine Doors, all of them, ever guard his ordinance. 7
(5.27.8) As they rule by the far-reaching domain of Agni, may the two holy ones, Dawn and Night, who swell with milk and dwell in close proximity, protect this sacrifice and our ritual service.
(5.27.9) O divine Hotṛ-priests, with the tongue of Agni, extol our upward-tending ritual; sing for us so that it may be well-sacrificed.

(5.27.9.c) May the three goddesses—*Iḍā*, *Sarasvatī*, and the great *Bhāratī*—sit upon this sacred grass (*barhis*), being praised. (5.27.10’) O God Tvaṣṭṛ, release for us that wonderful seed, rich in nourishment; open wide the navel of this abundance of wealth.
O Lord of the Forest, release [the victim], being gracious;
may Agni himself, the immolator, sweeten the oblation for the gods.
O Agni Jātavedas, perform the *svāhā* invocation!
(5.27.12.c) May all the gods enjoy this oblation, this *havis*, for Indra.
‖12‖ (5.28.1’) He measures out the nine vital breaths with nine [threads] for the sake of long life, for a hundred autumns.
(5.28.1.c) Three are in gold, three in silver, and three in iron; they are established through austerity. ‖1‖

Agni, Sūrya, Candramas, Earth, Waters, Heaven, the intermediate space, and the quarters and intermediate directions—may these, in harmony with the seasonal periods, carry me across by means of this threefold [sacrifice].
May the three nourishments rest upon the threefold [sacrifice]; may Pūṣan anoint [me] with milk and ghee.
(5.28.3.c) Abundance of food, abundance of men, abundance of cattle—may these resort to you here!
(5.28.4.a) O Ādityas, sprinkle this man with wealth; O Agni, being increased yourself, cause him to grow.
(5.28.4.c) O Indra, endow him with heroic vigor; may the threefold [sacrifice], which nourishes, take its place in him. (5.28.4)
May the Earth protect you with her green hue, the All-sustainer; may Agni, in harmony, fulfill [your needs] with his iron [strength].
May the White One, in accord with the plants, bestow upon you skill and a well-disposed mind.
This gold, born threefold from this birth, became one most beloved part of Agni; one part of Soma, when he was struck down, flew away.
