Those two swellings of yours that remain in the armpit, the testicles that have descended— I know the remedy for them: the *cīpudru* tree is the visible cure.
Whatever erysipelas is in the limbs, whatever is in the ears, or whatever is in the eyes—
We tear away the spreading sore, the abscess, and the disease of the heart.
We drive that unknown wasting sickness far away, downward, into the depths.
When the constellations made Śakadhūma their king—
(6.128.1.c) "They bestowed upon him an auspicious day, thinking, 'May he establish this kingdom.
(6.128.2’) "May there be an auspicious day for us at midday; may there be an auspicious day for us in the evening.
(6.128.2.c) "May there be an auspicious day for us at dawn among the days; may the night be an auspicious day for us."
O King Śakadhūma, grant us an auspicious day from the days and nights, from the lunar mansions, and from the sun and moon. You who have granted us an auspicious day in the evening,
at night, and likewise by day— [grant it to us now].

(6.128.4.c) To you, O King of Constellations, Śakadhūma, let there always be homage! (4) (6.129.1’) Through Bhaga, together with Śāṃśapa, and with Indra who is rich in healing power, I make myself fortunate; let my enemies flee away! (1)
By that fortune and splendor with which you overcame the trees, by that make me fortunate; let the enemies flee away!
That fortune which is blind, which returns again, and which is established in the trees—[by that make me fortunate].
By this, make me fortunate; let the enemies flee away.
This is the love-spell of the Apsarases, the Rathajitas and the Rāthajiteyīs. O gods, send forth the Love-god; let him burn with longing for me.
"May he remember me; may my beloved remember me!
O gods, send forth the god of love so that he may grieve for me. May he remember me, and may I never at any time remember another woman."
(6.130.3.c) O gods, send forth Smara; let him grieve after me!
(6.130.4.a) O Maruts, intoxicate me; O mid-air, intoxicate me!
(6.130.4.c) O Agni, do you intoxicate me; let him grieve after me!
I draw away from your head and from your feet that which has entered you.
O gods, send forth the *smara*; let him grieve after me.
O Anumati, give your consent to this; O Ākūti, accept this homage.
"O gods, send forth the god of love; let him grieve for me!
(2) Whether you run three *yojanas*, five *yojanas*, or even ten *yojanas*, you shall return from there once more and become the father of our sons. (3)

That passion which the gods poured into the waters, burning with intense heat, together with their meditation— that I inflame for you by the law of Varuṇa. That passion which all the gods poured into the waters, burning with intense heat, together with their meditation—
That [desire] of yours I heat by the law of Varuṇa.
That Smara whom Indrāṇī poured into the waters, burning with passion along with her thoughts—
that [desire] of yours I heat by the law of Varuṇa.

(6.132.4) That memory which Indra and Agni poured into the waters, burning with passion along with their intent— (6.132.4c) that I heat for you by the law of Varuṇa. (6.132.5) That memory which Mitra and Varuṇa poured into the waters, burning with passion along with their intent—
(6.132.5.c) That [bond] I heat for you by the law of Varuṇa. ||5|| (6.133.1’) The god who bound this girdle for me, who fastened it together, and who joined us;
(6.133.1.c) by whose divine command we move—may he seek the further shore, and may he release us. ||1||
Invoked and offered into, you are the weapon of the seers;
consuming the first portion of the vow, O girdle, be a slayer of heroes for me!
Since I am a student of sacred knowledge, I go forth from the living being to demand a man for Yama.
(6.133.3.c) With that [cord], through sacred knowledge, austerity, and exertion—with this very girdle, I bind him.
(6.133.4’) Born from faith and arisen from austerity, she became the sister of the seers who create all beings.
(6.133.4.c) O Girdle, bestow upon us intelligence and wisdom; furthermore, grant us austerity and sensory power.
(6.133.5) You whom the ancient world-creating seers girded around— as such, O girdle, embrace me for the sake of long life!
(6.134.1) May this thunderbolt satisfy [the one] of Truth; may it strike down his kingdom and take away his life.
May he break their necks; may he crush their napes, as the Lord of Might did Vṛtra’s.
1 Lower and lower than those above, hidden within the earth, let him not escape;
let him lie there struck down by the thunderbolt. 2
Seek out him who conquers; strike down him who conquers.
O Vajra, as you conquer, follow along the parting of the hair and strike down [the foe].
Whatever strength I consume, I shall exert; thus do I take up the Vajra.
(6.135.1.c) Shattering his vital aggregates, as Śacīpati [shatters] those of Vṛtra.
(6.135.2’) What I drink, I drink up; like the ocean, I drink it all up. Having drunk up the vital breaths of that one, we drink him up entirely.
(6.135.3) What I swallow, I swallow up completely, like the ocean, a great swallower;
having swallowed up the vital breaths of that man, we swallow him up.
(6.136.1) O herb, you are divine, born upon the divine earth.
We dig for you, O Nitatnī, from among the hair, for the sake of strengthening.
Strengthen those that are old, bring forth those yet unborn, and make those already born grow stronger.
Whatever hair of yours falls out, and whatever is cut away along with its root—
(6.136.3.c) With this herb, the universal remedy, I sprinkle you.
(6.137.1’) That which Jamadagni dug up for his daughter to grow her hair—
(6.137.1.c) that Vītahavya brought from the house of Asita.
They were to be measured by the rein, to be inferred by the fathom;
let your black hairs grow like reeds all around your head.
O herb, make firm the root, hold fast the tip, and extend through the middle!
(6.137.3.c) May your black hairs grow all around your head like reeds.
(6.138.1’) O herb, you are renowned as the most excellent of plants;
(6.138.1.c) make this man of mine today a eunuch, one who wears a topknot.
Make him impotent, wearing only a headband; furthermore, make him wear a turban.
Then may Indra split both his testicles with the pressing-stones.
O impotent one, I have made you impotent; O eunuch, I have made you a eunuch; I have made you sapless, utterly sapless.
(6.138.3.c) We place a turban upon his head and a jar beneath it.
(6.138.4’) Those two testicles of yours, fashioned by the gods, upon which virility rests—
I split those for you with a wooden pin, right above the scrotum of so-and-so.
Just as women split a reed with a stone for the sake of a cushion,
so do I split your penis upon his testicles.
You have grown as a Nyastikā plant, making me fortunate.
(6.139.1.c) A hundred are your spreading shoots, thirty-three are your descending roots.
(6.139.1.e) With that thousand-leaved plant, I dry up your heart.
1 (6.139.2’) May your heart dry up within me; moreover, may your mouth dry up.
(6.139.2.c) Now, wither me with desire; now, wander about with a parched mouth.
(6.139.3’) O unifying one, endowed with lotuses, tawny and beautiful, drive them together! Drive her and me together; make our hearts one. (6.139.3.c) Drive her and me together; make our hearts one.
Just as the mouth of one who has drunk water dries up, so do you wither away through desire for me; go forth, therefore, with a parched mouth.
Just as a mongoose, having torn apart a snake, joins it back together again...
(6.139.5.c) Thus, O powerful one, join together again what has been severed of my desire.
(6.140.1’) Those two tigers who have descended and wish to devour their father and mother— O Brahmanaspati, O Jātavedas, make them both harmless with your teeth.
"Eat rice, eat barley, and also beans and sesame—this portion is set apart for you both for the bestowal of treasures. O teeth, do not harm the father and the mother.
"Invited are the two joined, pleasant teeth, most auspicious."
(6.140.3.c) Let your terrible [nature] depart elsewhere from your bodies; do not harm the father and the mother with your fangs.
(6.141.1’) May Vāyu gather these together; may Tvaṣṭṛ sustain them for prosperity.
(6.141.1.c) May Indra speak in their favor; may Rudra provide for their abundance.
With a red-edged axe, fashion a mark upon the two ears;
let the Aśvins make it, and may that mark be multiplied through progeny.
Just as the gods and the Asuras did, and just as human beings have done.
(6.141.3.c) Thus, O Aśvins, bestow upon him the mark for a thousandfold prosperity.
(6.142.1’) Rise up, become abundant through your own greatness, O barley!
Crush all the vessels; let not the divine thunderbolt strike you down.
O god, listen to us as we address you here like barley;
rise up like the sky, and be inexhaustible like the ocean.
May your attendants be inexhaustible, and may your heaps be inexhaustible.

May those who give be inexhaustible; may those who eat be inexhaustible. Those who by means of inspired thought brought the forefront of speech, or those who with their mind spoke the sacred truths—having grown strong through the third prayer, they recognized the name of the Cow through the fourth.

He knows his father, he knows his mother; he becomes a son, he becomes one who bestows wealth again. He spread out the sky, the mid-air, and the heavens; he became this entire universe; he brought it hither.
Atharvan, the father, the kinsman of the gods, the embryo of the mother, the vital breath of the father, the youth.

(7.2.1.c) He who has perceived this sacrifice with his mind—proclaim him for us; speak of him here and now! (7.3.1’) By this manifestation, generating mighty deeds—for he is indeed the glowing one, the wide path for our choice—he rose up toward the support, the summit of the honey; by his own body he set his body in motion.
With one and with ten, O well-invoked one; with two and with twenty for the sacrifice;
with three and with thirty, you carry [the offerings], O Vāyu—unharness those teams here!
By means of sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; those were the first ordinances.
(7.5.1.c) Those great ones have attained the firmament where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide.
(7.5.2’) The sacrifice came into being; it has come into existence; it was born, and it has grown again.
(7.5.2.c) It became the overlord of the gods; may it bestow wealth upon us.

When the gods, with the oblation, sacrificed to the gods—the immortals—with a mortal mind—may we rejoice there in the highest heaven; may we behold that at the rising of the sun. When the gods performed the sacrifice with the Puruṣa as the oblation...
(7.5.4.c) Is there indeed anything more powerful than that with which they sacrificed by means of the *vihavya*?
(7.5.5’) The gods were bewildered; they sacrificed even with a dog, and they sacrificed in many ways with the limbs of a cow.
He who has perceived this sacrifice with his mind—proclaim him here, speak of him to us! 5.
Aditi is the sky, Aditi is the mid-air; Aditi is the mother, she is the father, she is the son.
All the gods are Aditi, the five peoples are Aditi; Aditi is what has been born, Aditi is what is yet to be born.
We invoke for our protection the great Mother of those who observe holy vows, the consort of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*).
(7.6.2.c) Aditi, who possesses mighty dominion, is undecaying, far-reaching, a good refuge, and an excellent guide.
(7.6.3’) We would ascend for our well-being the divine ship— well-oared, leakless, and flowing with safety— the Earth, the Heaven, the faultless Aditi, who is a good refuge and an excellent guide.
(7.6.4’) Now, at the impulse of strength, we celebrate with our speech the great Mother named Aditi;
she whose lap is the wide mid-air—may she grant us a triple-layered shelter.
(7.7.1’) I have performed the rite for the sons of Diti, for Aditi; I have honored the gods, the lofty ones who do not mock.
(7.7.1.c) For their abode is the oceanic realm; there is no one whatsoever beyond them who can reach them with homage.
(7.8.1’) From good, proceed toward what is better; let Bṛhaspati be your forerunner.
(7.8.1.c) Then, in this choice place upon the earth, make him free from enemies and possessed of all heroes.
Pūṣan was born upon the far path of paths, upon the far path of heaven, and upon the far path of earth.
He moves hither and thither, knowing his way, toward both most beloved dwelling places.
Pūṣan knows all these regions; may he lead us by the safest path free from fear.
(7.9.2.c) May he, the giver of well-being, the glowing one, the possessor of all heroes, go before us, never failing, knowing the way.
(7.9.3’) O Pūṣan, under your protection may we never come to harm;
(7.9.3.c) we here are your praisers.
May Pūṣan stretch forth his right hand from afar;
may he bring back to us what we have lost, and may we be reunited with that which was lost.
That breast of yours which is ever-present, which is a source of delight, which is gracious, easy to invoke, and bountiful—
(7.10.1.c) O Sarasvatī, that by which you nourish all desirable things— bring that here for us to suck. (7.11.1’) Your broad thunder, your lofty divine banner that pervades this entire world—
O God, do not strike down our grain with lightning, nor destroy it with the rays of the sun.

May the Assembly and the Council protect me, the two daughters of Prajāpati, acting in harmony. May he with whom I meet grant me his favor; may I speak pleasantly among my assembled kinsmen, O Fathers.
We know your name, O Assembly; your name is Nariṣṭā.
(7.12.2.c) May those who are the members of this assembly be of one voice with me.
(7.12.3.a) From these who are seated together, I take away splendor and discernment;
(7.12.3.c) O Indra, make me the fortunate one of this entire assembly.

(7.12.4) Whatever mind of yours has gone away, whether it be bound here or there, we cause that to return to you; let your mind delight in me. (7.13.1) Just as the sun, rising, takes up the splendors of the stars...

(7.13.1.c) Thus I take away the splendor of both women and men who are my enemies. (7.13.2’) As many as you see me, their rivals, as I approach— like the rising sun [takes the light] from those who sleep, so do I take away the splendor of my enemies.
I praise that god Savitar, who is within the two bowls, whose wisdom is that of a seer, the one of true impulsion and bestower of jewels; I praise him for his beloved thought.
He whose lofty splendor has shone forth in his impulse.
The golden-handed one of skillful wisdom has measured out the light from his creative impulse.
(2) O God Savitṛ, impel greatness for our first father, and grant him wide space;
then, O Savitṛ, day by day, impel for us many desirable things and abundant cattle. (3)

The domestic god Savitar, the most excellent, bestowing treasure and long life upon the fathers, let him drink the Soma; let him rejoice in this sacrifice. Even he who traverses all space moves according to his law.
O Savitar, I choose that most wonderful and well-disposed favor of yours, which is true in its impulse and possesses all desirable things.
(7.15.1.c) That swelling, thousand-streamed [milk] which Kaṇva milked for Bhaga, like a buffalo— (7.16.1’) O Bṛhaspati, O Savitṛ, cause him to grow; illumine him for great good fortune.
Sharpen him further, even though he is already sharpened; let all the gods rejoice after him. (7.16.1.c) 1.
May Dhātṛ, the lord and master of the world, bestow wealth upon us;
may he grant it to us in its fullness.
May Dhātṛ bestow upon the donor an eastern, undecaying life.
(7.17.2.c) May we receive the benevolence of the god who bestows all wealth.
2 (7.17.3’) May Dhātṛ bestow all desirable things upon the donor who desires offspring within his home.
(7.17.3.c) May all the gods, Aditi, and those who are in harmony with her, together bestow immortality upon him. 3
May Dhātṛ, Rāti, Savitṛ, Prajāpati, and Agni, the lord of treasures, accept this; may Tvaṣṭṛ and Viṣṇu, bestowing abundance through progeny, grant wealth to the sacrificer.
(7.18.1) Breathe forth, O Earth; cleave open this celestial firmament!
O Dhātṛ, you who rule over the celestial waters, unbind for us the leather bag of rain.
Neither the scorching heat has consumed it, nor has the frost destroyed it; may the earth, yielding life-sustaining gifts, burst open.
Even the waters flow for him like clarified butter; wherever Soma is, there is always prosperity.
Prajāpati generates these creatures; may Dhātṛ, being well-disposed, establish them.
Being of one mind, of one thought, and of one origin, may the Lord of Prosperity bestow prosperity upon me.
May Anumati today favor our sacrifice among the gods.
And may Agni, the bearer of oblations, be for you both and for me, the donor.
(1) O Anumati, you shall indeed grant us your approval; bestow welfare upon us.
Accept the offered oblation, O Goddess, and grant us progeny. (2)
May he, being well-disposed, grant us wealth accompanied by progeny that shall never fail.

May we not fall under his wrath; may we abide in his gracious favor and benevolence. O Anumati, you who are well-guided and bounteous, whatever name of yours is easy to invoke—may it be favorable to us.
(7.20.4.c) With that, O possessor of all boons, fulfill our sacrifice; bestow upon us, O fortunate one, wealth accompanied by heroic sons.
(7.20.5’) Anumati has come to this sacrifice for the sake of good fields and for the sake of heroic sons, well-born.
For her providence has become auspicious; may she, the guardian of the gods, protect this sacrifice. (7.20.5.c)
By Anumati all this was brought into being—whatever stands, whatever moves, and all that stirs.
O Goddess, may we abide in your favor; O Anumati, do you indeed grant us your consent. Gather together, all of you, with a single voice for the Lord of Heaven—the one, all-pervading guest of men.
He, the ancient one, dwells with the new; the path has turned toward him alone, though he is manifold.
May this thought of the seers, a light for the upholding of the world, be seen by us a thousandfold.
The ruddy sun has caused the converging dawns to come together.
(7.22.2.c) Spotless, of one mind, most full of spirit in their own dwelling, at the gathering of the cow.
(7.23.1’) Bad dreams, misfortune, the demon, the monster, and the stingy hags— (7.23.1.c) all those with evil names and evil voices, we cause them to perish from among us.
That which Indra dug out, that which Agni, the All-Gods, and the Maruts with their beautiful hymns [dug out]—
may Savitṛ, whose laws are true, Prajāpati, and Anumati bestow that upon us.
By the might of whom the regions were propped up, who by their heroic deeds are most manly and most powerful.
(7.25.1.c) To those two who rule unopposed with their powers—Viṣṇu and Varuṇa—the first invocation has gone.
(7.25.2’) That which shines here in his direction, and that which breathes forth and surveys all with its mighty deeds;
before the law of the god is established by his powers—Viṣṇu and Varuṇa, the first invocation has gone.
I shall now proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu, who measured out the earthly realms;
he who, striding out threefold with wide steps, propped up the highest dwelling place.
Viṣṇu is praised for those heroic deeds—he who, like a fearsome beast, wanders at will and dwells in the mountains.
May he come from the furthest distance. In whose three wide strides all worlds abide— O Viṣṇu, stride out widely; make wide space for our dwelling.
(7.26.3.e) Drink the clarified butter, O you whose source is clarified butter; further extend the life of the lord of the sacrifice.
(3) (7.26.4’) Viṣṇu strode across this [universe]; he established it in three steps; his gathered footprint is in the dust. (4)
Viṣṇu, the undeceivable guardian, strode forth his three steps,
maintaining from here the sacred laws. Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu, through which he has made his vows manifest.
The close ally and friend of Indra.
The wise ever behold that highest step of Viṣṇu,
Like an eye fixed in the heavens.
From heaven, O Viṣṇu, and from earth, O Viṣṇu, and from the great, wide mid-air—fill your hands with many riches; bestow them from the right and from the left.
May Iḍā herself clothe us according to her sacred law, she at whose station those seeking the gods purify themselves.
(7.27.1.c) The *śakvarī* verse, whose feet are dripping with ghee and whose back is sprinkled with soma, has approached the sacrifice as one belonging to the All-Gods (*vaiśvadevī*).
(7.28.1’) The Veda is well-being; the wooden mace is well-being; the axe is well-being; the sacrificial altar is well-being; the axe is our well-being.

May those gods—makers of oblations, worthy of sacrifice, and desiring the sacrifice—enjoy this sacrifice. (7.28.1.c) May those gods—makers of oblations, worthy of sacrifice, and desiring the sacrifice—enjoy this sacrifice.
O Agni and Viṣṇu, great is that majesty of yours; you guard the secret name of the hidden ghee.
Bestowing the seven treasures in every house, may your tongue move toward the ghee.
O Agni and Viṣṇu, you enjoy the great and beloved abode of yours; you take pleasure in the secret [offerings] of the ghee.

(7.29.2.c) Waxing strong with fair praise in every house, may your tongue rise up toward the clarified butter. (7.30.1’) May Heaven and Earth make me well-anointed; may this Mitra make me well-anointed;
(7.30.1.c) may Brahmaṇaspati make me well-anointed; may Savitṛ make me well-anointed.
O Indra, with your many and most excellent aids today, O Maghavan, O Hero, quicken us!
May he who hates us fall low; may our breath forsake him whom we hate.
[Approach] the beloved, the one worthy of praise, the youthful one who increases through oblations.
(7.32.1.c) We have come bearing homage; may he grant me long life.
1 (7.33.1’) May the Maruts sprinkle me, may Pūṣan sprinkle me, may Bṛhaspati sprinkle me;
(7.33.1.c) may this Agni sprinkle me with offspring and with wealth; may he grant me long life. 1
O Agni, drive away my born rivals; O Jātavedas, push back those yet unborn.
Place beneath your feet those who attack us; may we, being sinless, belong to Aditi.
With power, overcome other rivals; O Jātavedas, push back those yet unborn.
Prosper this kingdom for the sake of good fortune; may all the gods rejoice after him.
These hundred veins of yours and the thousand arteries—of them all, I have sealed the openings with a stone.
I place what is beyond your womb further away; let neither offspring nor mother harm you.
I make you childless and without offspring; I make a stone your covering.
Our two eyes are like honey; our face is anointing itself.
(7.36.1.c) Make me dwell within your heart; let our minds be united.
(7.37.1’) With a garment born of my own mind, I clothe you, so that you may belong to me alone, and never even mention the names of other women.
I dig this healing herb: it makes me look upon my husband with joy;
it is a turning back for one who has departed, a welcoming greeting for one who approaches.
By means of it, the Asura woman brought Indra down from among the gods.
With that, I turn you toward me, so that I may be very dear to you.
You face the Soma; you face the Sun;
you face all the gods—to you we speak aloud.
"I speak, not you; speak in the assembly, not I.
You belong to me alone; do not mention the names of other women.
Whether you be beyond the people or across the rivers."
(7.38.5.c) This herb has indeed brought you here to me, as if having bound you with a cord.
||5|| (7.39.1’) The divine, well-winged, milk-yielding, great one; the embryo of the waters, the bull of the plants;
(7.39.1.c) him who satisfies [all] from every side with rain—may he establish us in our cow-pen as the abode of wealth. ||1||
Whose law all cattle follow, in whose law the waters abide, and in whose law the Lord of Prosperity is established—
to that Sarasvant we call for protection. [1] Toward the returning Sarasvant, the giver to the donor, the lord of prosperity, who dwells in wealth— we call.
Clothed in the increase of wealth and the desire for renown, they have taken their seat here, the abode of riches.
The falcon, the observer of men, whose gaze is directed toward his dwelling, has pierced through the desert wastes and across the waters.
Crossing all the lower regions, may he come hither as a friend with Indra, bringing auspiciousness.

The falcon, the celestial bird with the gaze of a man, thousand-footed, hundred-sprung, bestower of vigor—may he bestow upon us that wealth which has been carried away; may it be ours among our ancestors, accompanied by the *svadhā* offering.
O Soma and Rudra, draw out in all directions the disease that has entered our home.
Drive Nirṛti far away into the distance; release us from whatever sin has been committed.
O Soma and Rudra, place all these remedies within our bodies.
Untie and release from us whatever sin has been committed and bound to our persons.
Some of them are auspicious for you, some are inauspicious; you bear them all with a well-disposed mind.
Three voices are deposited within him; of these, one has flown away following the sound.
You both have conquered; you are not defeated. Neither of these two has been defeated.
O Indra and Viṣṇu, when you two contended, you distributed that thousandfold [booty] in three portions.
Brought hither from the man who belongs to all people, from the river—far indeed I think you have been extracted; the remedy for jealousy is your name.
Like this fire burning, like a forest fire consuming separately,
quench this jealousy of his as one would extinguish a blazing fire.
O Sinīvālī of the broad tresses, you who are the sister of the gods!
Enjoy the oblation offered; O Goddess, grant us progeny.
She who has beautiful arms, lovely fingers, who is prolific and bears many children—to that Sinīvālī, the mistress of the people, offer the oblation.

(7.46.3) O Goddess who art the mistress of the people, facing toward Indra, coming with a thousand locks—O wife of Viṣṇu, for you the oblations have been offered; O Goddess, impel your husband toward prosperity!
(7.47.1) I repeatedly invoke at this sacrifice Kuhū, the goddess of good deeds, whose works are known, she who is easy to call upon.
May she bestow upon us wealth containing all boons; may she grant us a praiseworthy hero-son who bestows hundreds.
(1) Kuhū, the immortal consort of the gods, may she accept our invocation at this oblation.
May she, longing for us, hear our sacrifice today; may she, the wise one, grant us the increase of riches. (2)
I invoke Rākā with fair praise, she who is easy to call; may the auspicious one hear us and take notice of us herself.
May she sew together our works with a needle that never breaks, and grant us a heroic son, worthy of hymns and a giver of a hundredfold wealth.
O Rākā, those gracious thoughts of yours which are well-adorned, by which you bestow riches upon the donor—(with those, come to us).
With those [waters], come to us today with a gracious mind, O blessed one, bestowing upon us thousandfold prosperity.
May the longing wives of the gods protect us; may they aid us in our striving for strength and the winning of booty.
Those who belong to the earth and those who abide in the domain of the waters—may those goddesses, who are easily invoked, grant us refuge.
And let the divine ladies, the wives of the gods, partake: Indrāṇī, Agnāyī, Aśvinī, and Rāṭ;
let Rodasī and Varuṇānī hear us; let the goddesses partake, they who are the season of women.
Just as the lightning bolt strikes a tree every day irresistibly, so [let it strike] him.
(7.50.1.c) Thus may I today bind the gamblers with dice, leaving none unbound.
(7.50.2’) May fortune come from every side to me—from the swift and the slow, from the clans that do not yield—may the winnings gathered in my hand be mine.
(7.50.2.c) May fortune come from every side; let the winnings be within my hand.
I praise Agni, the possessor of good wealth, with prostrations; may he, being well-disposed here, distribute our reward for us.
Like chariots seeking prize, I bring forth [the hymn]; may I accomplish the laud of the Maruts in the right direction.
May we conquer the opposing host with you as our ally; protect our share in every battle.
O Indra, grant us wide space and a path easy to traverse; O Maghavan, shatter the manly strength of our enemies!
I have conquered you who were drawn up in line, and I have conquered you who were hemmed in.
Just as a wolf seizes a sheep, so do I seize your winnings!
Moreover, like a gambler who wins the stake and gathers his winnings at the right time, he who desires the gods does not withhold his wealth; Indra pours riches upon him with his own powers.
O Much-invoked One, may we overcome this evil-minded poverty with cattle, and all-starved hunger with barley.

(7.50.7.c) May we, unharmed, be the first among kings to win riches through our military forces. 7 (7.50.8’) Victory is in my right hand; victory is placed in my left. (7.50.8.c) May I be a winner of cattle, a winner of horses, a winner of wealth, and a winner of gold. 8
O Dice, give me a throw fruitful like a cow that yields milk!
Bind me with a stream of winnings as one fastens a bow with a sinew.
May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind, and from above, and from below, against the evildoer.

May Indra from the front and from the middle grant us, his friends, ample space for our friendship. (7.51.1) May there be concord between us and our own people, and concord with those who are strangers. O Aśvins, bestow upon us here that concord. (7.52.1)
Let us be of one mind and of one intent; let us not be separated by the divine mind.
Let no cries of distress arise when the vast slaughter has been wrought; let the arrow fall when the day of Indra has arrived.
O Bṛhaspati, from the state of being in the beyond, you have released [us] from the curse of Yama.
The Aśvins, the physicians of the gods, O Agni, have driven death away from us by their powers. (1) Come together; do not abandon the body. Let out-breath and in-breath remain here, joined as one.
Live for a hundred autumns, growing strong; Agni shall be your protector and Vasiṣṭha your supreme lord. (2)
(7.53.3) That life of yours which has been cast away, let the out-breath and the in-breath bring it back again.
(7.53.3c) Agni shall fetch it from the lap of Nirṛti; I cause it to enter back into you once more.
(7.53.4) Let not this breath abandon me, nor let the out-breath depart, leaving me behind.
I entrust him to the Seven Seers; may they carry him safely to old age.
(4) Enter, O out-breath and in-breath, like two oxen into their pen!
May this man, a treasure-house of old age, grow here unharmed. (5)
We breathe forth your breath; I drive away your consumption.
May this Agni, the most excellent, bestow life upon us from every side.
Rising up from the darkness, we ascend to the highest firmament.
We have gone to the god Sūrya among the gods, the supreme light.
We worship the *ṛc* and the *sāman*, by which they perform the sacred rites;
these two rule in the assembly and present the sacrifice to the gods.
The *ṛc*, the *sāman*, the oblation, vigor, the *yajus*, and strength— may this Veda,
when questioned, not harm me, O Lord of Might.
Those paths of yours from heaven, by which you have set forth the universe...
With those, O Vasu, grant us well-being.
The poison that was gathered from the black *tiryañcirāji* viper and from the *pṛdāku* snake— that poison of the *kaṅka* joint this plant has destroyed.
This plant is born of honey, dripping with honey, honey-sweet, and honey itself.
It is the remedy for what is crushed, and it is the destroyer of the mosquito.
From wherever you have been bitten, from wherever you have been stung, from that very place we call you away.
The poison of the tiny gnat, which bites so sharply, is sapless.
(3) O Brahmanaspati, this one who is crooked, with mangled joints and deformed limbs—you make his faces crooked and twisted; bend them all together like a blade of reed. (4)
Of this sapless, screeching one who creeps along downward—its poison has indeed been expelled; thus have I struck it down. There is no strength in your arms, nor in your head, nor in your middle.
(7.56.6.c) "Then why do you, O evil woman, carry that small child upon your back?
(7.56.7.a) "The ants devour you; the peahens tear you apart. (7.56.7.c) "All of you, speak clearly: the poison of the *śārkoṭa* is sapless."
(7.56.8) You who strike with both [your] tail and your mouth—there is no poison in your mouth; how much less could there be in your tail?
(7.57.1) That which was agitated in me while speaking with hope, or while wandering among the people making my request—
Whatever is torn in my body, Sarasvatī shall fill that with clarified butter.
Seven [streams] flow for the child accompanied by the Maruts; the sons have turned the *ṛta*s toward their father.
Both indeed belong to him, both are his; both strive, and both prosper for him.

O Indra and Varuṇa, drinkers of the pressed juice, drink this pressed Soma, the intoxicating draught, you who uphold the sacred law. Let your chariot come toward the sacrifice for the feast of the gods, to the place of libation, for your drinking.
O Indra and Varuṇa, you two bulls, drink of the most honey-sweet, potent Soma.
(7.58.2.c) This juice has been poured out for you both; having sat down upon this sacred grass (*barhis*), may you rejoice.
(7.59.1’) He who would curse us when we do not curse, and he who would curse us when we do curse—like a tree struck by lightning, let him wither away to the very root.
(7.59.1.c) Like a tree struck by lightning, let him wither away to the very root.
Bearing strength, a winner of wealth, and wise, with a non-terrible, friendly eye, I come to the house with a well-disposed mind, offering praise: "Rejoice; do not fear me.
These houses are sources of bliss, full of vigor and rich in milk.
May those who stand full on the left know us as we approach.
(2) Those from whom one departs when traveling abroad, and in whom there is much goodwill—those homes we invoke; may they know us as we approach. (3)
Summoned here are our friends, possessing abundant wealth and delighting in sweet pleasures; may you be free from hunger and thirst. O house, do not be afraid of us!
Summoned here are the cows; summoned here are the goats and sheep.
And so, may the sweet essence of food be invited into our homes.
(5) May our houses be full of pleasant speech, fortunate, rich in nourishment, filled with laughter and joy; may they be free from thirst and hunger. Do not be afraid of us! (6)
"Stay right here; do not go away. Nurture all forms. I shall return with auspiciousness; may you become more numerous through me.
"O Agni, whatever austerity we perform through our ascetic heat..."
May we be dear to sacred learning, long-lived, and wise.
O Agni, we perform austerity; we practice fervent heat. Hearing what we have heard, may we be long-lived and wise.

This Agni, the lord of the virtuous, the ancient bull, like a charioteer, has conquered the foot-soldiers as our domestic priest. Established at the navel of the earth, he flashes forth; may he cast beneath his feet those who seek to attack us.
We invoke with hymns Agni, the conqueror of armies and the subduer, from his highest dwelling place.
May he carry us across all difficulties; may the divine Agni, the patient one, carry us beyond all misfortunes.
(7.63.1) That which the black bird, as it flew forth, dropped—may the waters protect me from all that evil, from that distress. (7.64.1)
(7.64.2) This which the black bird has pecked with your mouth, O Nirṛti—
may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that sin.
(7.65.1) For you, O Apāmārga, have grown with your fruit turned backward.
Drive all curses far away from me; keep them at a distance from here.
Whatever evil deed, whatever stain, or whatever we have done with a sinful mind—O Apāmārga, you who face every direction, we wipe all that away with you.
Whatever we have done while sitting together with one who has black teeth, one with deformed nails, or a cripple— O Apāmārga, by means of you, we wipe all that away.
Whether it was in the atmosphere, or if it was in the wind, or if it was in the trees, or if it was in the shrubs.
(7.66.1.c) That which we heard being raised up, O Brahmin, may that return to us again.
(7.67.1’) May sensory power return to me, may my self, wealth, and sacred knowledge return;
(7.67.1.c) May the sacrificial fires belonging to the *dhiṣṇya* hearths be established here once more, each in its proper place.
O Goddess Sarasvatī, among your divine ordinances and celestial abodes, accept the oblation offered; O Goddess, grant us progeny.
This ghee-filled oblation is for you, O Sarasvatī; this is the sacrificial offering that is the mouth of the ancestors.
These most auspicious words have been spoken to you; through them may we be rich in sweetness.
(2) Be gracious to us, O Sarasvatī, most auspicious and most merciful;
may we not be severed from your sight. (1)
May the wind blow auspiciously for us; may the sun shine auspiciously for us.
May the days be auspicious for us; may the night be established as auspicious for us. May the dawn shine upon us with auspiciousness. 1.69.1.1–e.

Whatever he offers with his mind, whatever with his speech, with sacrifices, with oblations, and with Yajus formulas— may Nirṛti, in agreement with Mṛtyu, strike down that offering of his before it reaches the Truth. May the sorcerers, Nirṛti, and the Rākṣasas slay his truth with falsehood.
(7.70.2.c) May the gods, impelled by Indra, churn his sacrificial butter; may that which he offers not reach its intended goal.
(7.70.3’) Like two swift, supreme hawks swooping down together, let them strike the ghee of the one who attacks us, and whoever seeks to harm us.
(7.70.3.c) Let them slay the one who assails us, and whoever intends us injury.
I bind both your arms behind you; I bind your mouth. By the wrath of the divine Agni, by that [wrath], I have struck down your oblation.
I bind your arms; I bind your mouth.

(7.70.5.c) By the wrath of that terrible Agni, I have destroyed the oblation. (5) (7.71.1’) O Agni, victorious one, we place you around us as a fortress—you, the inspired sage, of bold appearance, day by day the slayer of the treacherous. (1)
Arise now and behold Indra’s seasonal portion!
If it is cooked, offer it; if it is uncooked, wait.
The oblation is cooked; come hither, O Indra! The sun has reached the midpoint of its journey.
(7.72.2.c) Friends sit around you with their treasures, like householders surrounding the lord of a caravan as he travels.
(7.72.3’) I consider it cooked on the udder, cooked on the fire; I consider this newest rite well-prepared.
O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, performer of many deeds, drink of the curd of the midday libation, being well-pleased.
Kindled is Agni, O Bulls; the charioteer of heaven has appeared. The heated *gharma* is milked for you both, for the sake of nourishment and sweetness.
For we, the singers, many in number, invoke you, O Aśvins, at the shared feasts.
O Aśvins, Agni is kindled and the *gharma* is heated for you; come hither!
Surely the milch-cows are milked here by the bull; O wonder-workers, the wise ones rejoice.

(2) The pure sacrifice, accompanied by the cry of *svāhā*, which is the cup for the gods and the drinking-vessel of the Aśvins—having taken it from the mouth of the Gandharva, all the immortals, taking delight in it, lick it. (3)
The ghee and milk offered in the cows—that is your portion, O Aśvins; come hither!
O lovers of sweetness, sustainers of the assembly, lords of the virtuous, drink the heated *gharma* from heaven!
4 May the heated *gharma* reach you, with the *svahotṛ* priest; let the Adhvaryu move forward for you, bearing milk. 5
O Aśvins, enjoy this pressed honey for the sake of our progeny; drink of the milk of the ruddy cow.
(5) Run hither with the milk, O milker of cows, and quickly pour the milk of the ruddy cow into the heated vessel.
Savitṛ, the most excellent, has looked upon the firmament; he shines forth following the departure of Uṣas. (6)
I invoke this well-milking cow; may the skillful milker milk her.
May Savitṛ impel for us the most excellent stimulation; the Gharma is heated—proclaim that clearly!
Bellowing, the mistress of treasures, seeking her calf with her mind, has come down.
May this inviolable cow yield milk for the Aśvins; may she increase for our great good fortune.

Welcome as the friend of the house and the guest in the dwelling, O wise Agni, come to this sacrifice of ours. Having struck down all assailants, bring hither the possessions of those who act as enemies.
O Agni, be strong for great good fortune; may your splendors be most excellent.
Bestow upon us a well-governed household, and trample down the powers of those who act as enemies.
May you indeed be blessed with abundant pasture, and may we likewise be blessed.
(7.73.11.c) Eat grass, O inviolable one, at all times; drink pure water as you move along.
(7.74.1’) We have heard that the mother of the red *apacits* is black;
by means of the root of the divine sage, I pierce them all.
I pierce their first; I pierce their middle one as well. Here I cut off their last one, like a lock of wool.
With the word of Tvaṣṭṛ, I have made your jealousy flow away.
And furthermore, O Lord, whatever wrath is yours, that we pacify for you.
O Lord of Vows, united with the vow, shine here forever with a gracious mind.
May we all, possessing offspring, sit near you, O Jātavedas, once you have been kindled.
May you be prolific, grazing on lush pastures, radiant, and drinking pure waters at a fine watering-place.
Let not the thief nor the malevolent man master you; may the missile of Rudra avoid you.
You are knowers of the tracks, playful, united, and named after all things.
(7.75.2.c) Come to me, O Goddesses, with the Gods! (7.75.2.e) Sprinkle us with ghee in this cow-pen, in this dwelling-place!
2 (7.76.1’) From those who have slipped away, may there be those who have slipped away even further; from the non-existent ones, may there be those who are more non-existent.
(7.76.1.c) They are more sapless than a stalk, more easily dissolved than a call.
(7.76.2’) Those swellings on the neck, and those on the armpits;
the swellings on the joints that fall away of their own accord—(7.76.2.c) [may they all go forth].
He who crushes the ribs and settles in the hollow of the breast—drive him out entirely, the *jāyānya*, whoever has taken refuge upon the hump.
Winged, the *jāyānya* flies; he enters into the man.
That is the medicine for both the undecaying and the one with a wound.
We indeed know your origin, O Jāyānya, from whence you are born, O Jāyānya. How then can you strike us down, we who offer the oblation in your house?
Drink boldly the Soma from the jar, O Indra, Vṛtra-slayer, hero in the battle for riches!
At the midday libation, pour yourself full; as the dweller in wealth, bestow wealth upon us!
O Sāṃtapanas, Maruts, enjoy this oblation!

(7.77.1.c) [We call upon] you, O destroyers of enemies, who go beyond this world. (7.77.2’) O Maruts, O Vasus, if some mortal of malicious intent seeks to strike down our thoughts, may he be caught in the snares of deceit; may you slay him with your most scorching heat.
(7.77.2.c) May he be bound by the snares of malice; may you strike him down with your fiercest flame.

The Maruts, who return every year, the well-praised ones with wide dwellings, the troop-led companions of men—may they release us from the snares of sin; may the Sāṃtapana gods, exhilarating and gladdening, grant us joy.
I loosen your cord, I loosen your yoke, I loosen your fastening.
Right here, O Agni, abide for evermore!
O Agni, I yoke you with divine prayer so that you may uphold sovereign powers for this man.
Shine forth for us wealth that is auspicious here; speak this word among the gods on behalf of the one who offers the oblation.

Whatever portion the gods, dwelling together in greatness, have prepared for you at the new moon, with that, O possessor of all boons, fulfill our sacrifice; bestow upon us wealth, O fortunate one, along with heroic sons.
I alone am the new moon; in me dwell the doers of good deeds; these [gods] abide within me.
(7.79.2.c) In me all the gods, both the Sādhyas and those with Indra as their chief, have come together.
(7.79.3’) Night has arrived, the gatherer of treasures, bringing in strength, nourishment, and wealth. To the New Moon we offer our oblation; milking out strength, she has come to us with her milk.
On the new moon day, none other than you has brought forth all these forms, encompassing them.
Whatever desire we have as we offer this oblation to you, may that be ours; may we be masters of riches.
4 The full moon has triumphed.
Dwelling there with the gods in majesty, may we rejoice upon the back of the firmament with abundant food.
We sacrifice to the full moon, the vigorous bull;
may he grant us imperishable wealth that never fails.
O Prajāpati, none other than you has generated all these forms as their encompasser.
Whatever desire we have when we offer oblations to you, let that be ours; may we be masters of riches.
The full moon was the first among the days to be worthy of sacrifice, even amidst the deep darkness of the nights.
(7.80.4c) But those who honor you with sacrifices, O worthy of sacrifice, they, the doers of good deeds, have entered that firmament.
(7.81.1’) These two move one after the other by means of *māyā*; like two playful children, they go around the ocean.
One beholds all beings; the other, ordaining the seasons, is born anew.
Becoming ever new as you are born, you go forth as the banner of the days at the head of the dawns.
Arriving, you distribute the portion to the gods; O Moon, you extend a long life.
O Soma-stalk, Lord of Battles, you are indeed named "The Unfailing."
(7.81.3.c) Make me not deficient in offspring and in wealth.
(7.81.4’) You are the New Moon; you are beautiful to behold; you are complete; you are all-encompassing.
May I become complete and all-encompassing through cattle, horses, offspring, livestock, houses, and wealth.
(7.81.5) "He who hates us and whom we hate—of him do thou swell with thy vital breath!
(7.81.5c) May we swell with cattle, horses, progeny, livestock, houses, and wealth!
(7.81.6) "The stalk which the gods cause to swell, which the imperishable ones consume as the imperishable..."
(7.81.6.c) By that means may Indra, Varuṇa, and Bṛhaspati, the guardians of the world, cause us to swell with abundance.
(7.82.1’) Sing forth a beautiful hymn; [win] the prize of cattle. Bestow auspicious riches upon us!
Lead this sacrifice of ours to the gods; let the streams of clarified butter flow pure and honey-sweet.
In me I first take up the fire, together with dominion, splendor, and strength.
In me I place progeny, in me I place long life—*svāhā*!—in me the fire.
(2) Right here, O Agni, maintain wealth for us; let not the destroyers who perceive [us] beforehand lay thee low. (3)
(7.82.3.c) O Agni, may [the people] be well-governed by your sovereign power; may he who sits near you increase, never being struck down.
3 (7.82.4’) Agni Jātavedas, the first, has looked along the forefront of the dawns, along the days;
he has entered after the sun, after the dawns, after the rays, and after heaven and earth. 4
Agni has looked out toward the forefront of the dawns; Jātavedas, the first, has looked out toward the days.
He has looked out toward the many rays of the sun; he has stretched across heaven and earth.
O Agni, ghee is yours in the celestial dwelling; with ghee Manu kindles you today.
(7.82.6.c) May the divine daughters bring clarified butter for you; may the cows yield clarified butter for you, O Agni.
(7.83.1’) O King Varuṇa, your golden dwelling is within the waters.
From there, may the King, firm in his vows, release me from all bonds.
O King Varuṇa, from every bond, from every fetter, release us here.
Whatever we have uttered, O Varuṇa—"O Waters, O Invincible Ones," "O Varuṇa"—from that, O Varuṇa, release us.
Loosen the highest bond from us, O Varuṇa, loosen the lowest, and untie the middle one.
(7.83.3.c) Thus, O Āditya, may we be blameless under your law and before Aditi.
3 (7.83.4.a) Release from us all those snares, O Varuṇa—those that are highest and those that are lowest, which belong to Varuṇa.
4 (7.83.4.c) Drive away from us bad dreams and misfortune; then may we go to the world of the righteous. 4
Invincible, Jātavedas, immortal, the sovereign Agni, sustainer of dominion, shine here!
Dispelling all maladies, protect our household today with your auspicious human-like [flames].
O Indra, you were born for the sake of lovely dominion and power, O bull among the peoples.
You drove away the unfriendly folk and made wide space for the gods.
Like a fearsome beast, roaming and dwelling in the mountains, may he come hither from the farthest distance.
O Indra, whetting your sharp bolt and keen blade, strike down the enemies and drive away the plunderers.

(7.85.1) That very vigorous one, impelled by the gods, the mighty conqueror, the overcomer of chariots, with unbroken fellies, the swift victor in battle— that Tārkṣya we invoke here for our well-being.
(7.86.1) Indra the protector, Indra the helper, the hero who is easily invoked at every call— we invoke him.
I now invoke Śakra, Indra, who is invoked by many; may the bountiful Indra grant us well-being.
Rudra who is in the fire, he who is within the waters, he who has entered the plants and the herbs—he who has fashioned all these worlds: let there be homage to that Rudra, to Agni.
Depart! You are an enemy, or you are indeed an enemy. You have mixed poison with poison; indeed, you have mixed poison with poison. Go toward the serpent itself; slay him!
I have invoked the celestial waters; we have been united with their essence.
(7.89.1.c) Rich in milk, O Agni, have I come; unite me with splendor! (7.89.2’) O Agni, unite me with splendor, unite me with progeny, and unite me with long life!
May the gods take note of this of mine; may Indra take note together with the seers!
O Waters, carry away this: whatever is blameworthy and whatever is impurity;
whatever treachery and falsehood I have committed, and whatever curse I have uttered against one who was not my enemy.
You are fuel; may I prosper. You are kindling; may I prosper completely.
(7.89.4.c) You are brilliance; bestow brilliance upon me.
(4) (7.90.1’) Tear it away as of old, like the tangled tangle of a creeping plant;
(7.90.1.c) Strike down the vital power of the Dāsa. (1)
(7.90.2) Let us, together with Indra, divide that accumulated wealth of his.
(7.90.2c) By the ordinance of Varuṇa, I cause your vigor to fade away. (7.90.3) So that the penis may fall away, and he may be without virility among women.
Of Avastha, of Knadīvat, of Śāṅkura, and of Nitodin—whatever is stretched out, let that be slackened; whatever is drawn tight, let that be loosened.
May Indra, the good protector, the possessor of wealth, be gracious with his aids, he who is all-knowing.
May he drive away hatred; may he grant us safety. May we be masters of heroic vigor.
May that Indra, the good protector and the self-strong, drive our enemies far away from us.
May we abide in the favor of that worshipful one, and in his auspicious goodwill.
With Indra and with fury, may we overcome those who attack us,
slaying the Vṛtras without opposition.
With stable oblation, we lead Soma to what is stable.
(7.94.1.c) So that Indra may make our subjects entirely his own and of one mind.
(7.95.1’) Upward have his two dark, trembling, vulture-like [eyes] flown toward heaven; they are the burning and the glowing, the two burners of his heart.
(7.95.1.c) They are the burning and the glowing, the two burners of his heart.
I have raised these two up, like two oxen exhausted from labor;
like two barking dogs, like two springing wolves.
They are strikers, piercers, and indeed thorough tormentors.
(7.95.3.c) I bind his penis, whoever—whether woman or man—has carried off from here.
(7.96.1’) The cows have settled in their place; the birds have flown to their dwelling.
The mountains stand firm in their stations; I have fixed the two kidneys in their place.
Since we have chosen you here today, O wise Hotṛ, as this sacrifice proceeds—
O most powerful one, steadfast and firm, come to the Soma, knowing well the sacrifice!
O Indra, Lord of the Bay Steeds, unite us with our minds, with cattle, with patrons, and with well-being.
Bring together with the sacred prayer (*brahman*) that which is ordained by the gods; bring [us] into the goodwill of the gods who are worthy of sacrifice.
O Agni, send forth those longing gods whom you have brought hither, to their own dwelling place.
Having eaten and drunk the sweet draughts, O Vasus, bestow riches upon this man.

(7.97.4) O gods, we have made easy paths for you to your seats; may you who have come to my libation be pleased. Carrying and bringing your own treasures, ascend after [the sun] to the sky, to the wealthy *gharma*.
(7.97.5) O sacrifice, go to the sacrifice; go to the lord of the sacrifice.

Hail to those who have been offered; hail to those who have not been offered!
O gods who know the way, having found the way, go upon the way!
O Lord of the Mind, place this sacrifice of ours among the gods in heaven.
Svāhā! In heaven, svāhā! On earth, svāhā! In the intermediate space, svāhā! I place [this] in the wind, svāhā!
The sacrificial grass is anointed with the oblation of clarified butter; may it be united with Indra, the Vasu, and the Maruts;
may it be united with the gods, the Viśvedevas. May the oblation go to Indra, svāhā!
Strew around, enclose the altar; do not steal the kinswoman lying there.
This golden, tawny seat for the Hotṛ-priest—these are the gold neck-ornaments in the world of the sacrificer.
I turn away from evil dreams, from bad dreams, and from misfortune.
I, as Brahman, create a separation; may the sorrows that have sleep for their face be driven far away.
(7.100.1.c) Whatever food I eat in a dream is not found in the morning; may all that be auspicious for me, for it is not seen by day. (7.101.1)

Having paid homage to Heaven and Earth, to the Intermediate Space, and to Death, I stand upright and stir [the water]; may the lords not harm me. Which Kṣatriya, seeking what is better for us, will lead us out from this blameless malice?
Who desires sacrifice? And who desires meritorious works? Who among the gods seeks long life?

(7.103.1.c) Who, delighting in friendship with Bṛhaspati, shall fashion his bodies at will—[he who seeks] the speckled cow given by Varuṇa to Atharvan, the well-milking one that has its calf ever-present? (7.104.1)
Departing from what belongs to men and choosing the divine word,
turn back toward our guidance together with all your friends.
O Agni Jātavedas, whatever we have done through forgetfulness or whatever we have failed in our conduct, [forgive us].
(7.106.1.c) Therefore, O wise one, protect us for our welfare; let there be immortality for us and our friends.
(7.107.1’) The seven rays of the sun descend from heaven, bringing down the waters of the ocean in streams; may they cause the arrowhead to fall away.
(7.107.1.c) The waters of the sea, in their flowing currents, have caused that shaft to drop off.

O Agni, whoever would steal from us or seek to harm us, whether by secret means or openly, whether he be a stranger or one of our own kin—let him go back, toothless and powerless. O Agni, let there be neither a dwelling place nor offspring for them.
O Jātavedas, whoever would attack us while we are sleeping or awake, standing or moving about—[let him go back].
(7.108.2.c) O Jātavedas, in alliance with Vaiśvānara and in harmony with him, burn those [enemies] back.
(7.109.1’) Homage to this fierce, tawny one who has mastery over his own body through the dice.
With clarified butter I honor Kali; may he be gracious to us in such a state.
O Agni, carry ghee for the Apsarases; carry dust for the dice, sand, and water.
May the gods, enjoying the offering of the oblation according to their respective portions, rejoice in both kinds of offerings.
The Apsarases revel in communal joy between the oblation-holder and the sun.

(7.109.3.c) May they join my two hands with clarified butter; may they deliver my rival, the gambler, into my power. (7.109.5) He who has made this wealth for us to win, he who [determined] the casting and the remainder of the dice—may that god, enjoying this oblation, rejoice with the Gandharvas in our common revelry.
(7.109.6) "O you who dwell together," such is your name; for the dice are fierce-looking sustainers of the kingdom.
To them, O Indus, let us pay worship with our oblation; may we become masters of riches.

(7.109.6) Since I have called upon the gods in my need, since we have lived the life of sacred studentship (*brahmacarya*), and since I have grasped the brown dice—may they be gracious to us in such a state. (7.109.7)
O Agni and Indra, for the donor, you two have slain the Vṛtras without opposition;
for you both are the greatest slayers of Vṛtra. By you two they conquered the light of heaven in the beginning, you two who took your stand over all the worlds.
I invoke Agni and Indra, the bulls of the people, whose arms wield the thunderbolt, the slayers of Vṛtra.
The god Bṛhaspati has approached you with the cup;
O Indra, enter among us with our songs for the sake of the sacrificer who presses the soma.
(7.111.1’) You are the belly of Indra, the receptacle of Soma, the self of the gods and of men.

(7.111.1.c) Procreate here those offspring of yours which are in these [women], and let those of yours which are elsewhere rejoice here. (7.112.1’) Beautifying Heaven and Earth, who are near with their goodwill and possess great ordinances—
The seven divine waters have flowed forth; may they release us from distress.
May they release me from the curse, and also from that which pertains to Varuṇa, and from the fetter of Yama, and from every offense against the gods.

O *tṛṣṭika*, O *tṛṣṭavandana*, cut down that one, O *tṛṣṭika*, so that those who hate the deed shall be like [the enemies] of this man who possesses the male organ. You are *tṛṣṭa*, you are *tṛṣṭikā*; you are poison, you are the poison-destroyer.
(7.113.2.c) Just as the discarded wife [seeks] the bull, like a cow longing for her calf.
(7.114.1’) From your flanks I take [it], from your heart I take it;
(7.114.1.c) from the appearance of your mouth, I take all your splendor.
(7.114.2) May diseases depart, may anxieties depart, and may curses depart! May Agni slay the demoniac women; may Soma slay those who seek to do harm.
(7.115.1) Fly away from here, O evil Fortune! Perish from here! Fly away to the far distance!

(7.115.1.c) With an iron hook we bind you fast to your enemy. (7.115.2’) That ill-omened, unlovely mark which has fallen upon me and clung to me like a creeper to a tree—O Savitṛ, place that elsewhere than on us; O golden-handed one, bestowing wealth upon us! One hundred and one fortunes have arisen together with the body from birth for the mortal man.
Of these, we cast forth the most evil ones; O Jātavedas, bestow the auspicious ones upon us.
I have separated these [fortunes] like cows standing scattered in a wasteland.
(7.115.4.c) May the meritorious fortunes remain; those that are evil, I have destroyed.
(7.116.1’) Homage to Rūra, to Cyavana, to Nodana, to Dhṛṣṇu;
homage to Śīta, who fulfills former desires.
(7.116.2) He who comes upon this frog on one day or on two days—
let that lawless one come upon him!
(7.117.1) Come, O Indra, with your joyful bay horses whose hair is like peacock feathers!
(7.117.1.c) Let no one hold you back as fowlers hold a bird; pass them by like a desert.
‖1‖ (7.118.1’) I cover your vital organs with armor; may King Soma clothe you with immortality.
(7.118.1.c) May Varuṇa grant you a space wider than the wide; may the gods rejoice after you as you conquer. ‖1‖
(8.1.1’) Homage to Antaka, to Death! May your out-breath and in-breath delight here.
(8.1.1.c) May this man remain here together with his vital breaths, in the portion of the Sun, in the world of immortality.
(8.1.2’) Bhaga has lifted him up; Soma, rich in stalks, has lifted him up.
(8.1.2.c) May the Maruts, the gods, and Indra and Agni lift him up for his well-being. 2 (8.1.3’) Here is your life-force, O Asura; here is your breath, here is your vitality, here is your mind.
(8.1.3.c) We rescue you from the snares of Destruction with divine speech. 3
(8.1.4’) Step forth from here, O man; do not fall away, casting off the fetter of death.
(8.1.4.c) Do not be cut off from this world, from the sight of Agni and Sūrya.
4 (8.1.5’) For you let Vāta Mātariśvan blow; for you let the immortal waters rain down.

(8.1.5.c) May the sun shine auspiciously upon your body; may Death have compassion for you—do not perish! (8.1.6’) O man, I make for you an ascent, not a descent; I provide for you life and skillful strength.
(8.1.6.c) For mount this immortal, comfortable chariot, and then, long-lived, you shall proclaim your wisdom in the assembly.
(8.1.7’) Let not your mind go there, nor let it vanish; do not abandon the living, nor follow the fathers.
(8.1.7.c) May all the gods protect you here!
(8.1.8’) Do not set your heart on those who have departed, who lead one away to the far distance.
(8.1.8.c) Ascend from darkness to light; come, we take hold of your hands.
(8.1.9’) Śyāma and Śabala, the two dogs sent by Yama who guard the path—come hither, do not look back, do not stand there with your mind turned away.
Do not follow this path; it is fearsome. I tell you this: do not go where you have not gone before. O man, do not fall into this darkness; there is danger beyond, but safety here below.
May the fires that dwell within the waters protect you; may the fire that men kindle protect you.
(8.1.11.c) May Vaiśvānara Jātavedas protect you; let not the lightning strike you down from heaven.
||11|| (8.1.12’) Let not the flesh-eater harm you; move away from the treacherous pit. May the sky protect you; may the earth protect you. (8.1.12.c) And may the sun and the moon protect you.
(8.1.12.e) May the atmosphere protect you from the weapon of the gods.
||12|| (8.1.13’) May Bodha and Pratibodha protect you; may Asvapna and Anavadrāṇa protect you;
(8.1.13.c) may Gopāyan and Jāgṛvi protect you. ||13||
(8.1.14’) May they protect you; may they guard you. To them, homage! To them, svāhā!
‖14‖ (8.1.15’) May Vāyu, Indra, Dhātṛ, and the protecting Savitṛ place you among the living in the gathering-place.
(8.1.15.c) Let not breath nor strength abandon you; we summon your life-force back to you. ‖15‖
(8.1.16’) May the jaw with its teeth not seize thee; may darkness not find thee; may the tongue not perish upon the sacrificial grass. How mightest thou be?
(8.1.16.c) May the Ādityas and the Vasus lift thee up; may Indra and Agni [lift thee up] for well-being.
(8.1.17’) May Heaven lift thee up, may Earth lift thee up, may Prajāpati have grasped thee.
(8.1.17.c) May the plants, whose king is Soma, deliver you up from death.
||17|| (8.1.18’) O gods, let this man remain right here; let him not go from here to the world beyond.
(8.1.18.c) By means of a thousandfold power, we rescue him from death. ||18||
I have raised you up from death; may those who bestow vigor breathe life into you.
Let not women with disheveled hair, nor those weeping with tearful faces, bewail you. I have brought you back; I have found you. You have returned, renewed once more.
(8.1.20.c) O you with all your limbs! I have found for you your entire sight and your entire life-span.
(8.1.21’) Light has emerged for you; darkness has departed from you.
(8.1.21.c) We cast away from you death, destruction, and consumption. {2}

(8.2.1’) Take hold of this attainment of immortality; may your lifespan be unbroken and reach old age. (8.2.1.c) I bring back to you the breath and life-force; do not go to the dust or the darkness, do not perish. (8.2.2’) Come hither toward the light of the living; I bring you back for a hundred autumns.
(8.2.2.c) Casting off the snares of death and all ill-fortune, I bestow upon you a longer and more extended life.

(8.2.3’) From the wind I have found your breath, and from the sun, your sight. (8.2.3.c) Whatever mind is yours, I place that within you; be conscious with your limbs, speak with your tongue, and utter speech.
(8.2.4’) With breath I blow upon you, as one does upon fire when born, you who belong to the two-footed and the four-footed.
(8.2.4.c) Homage to your eye, O Death; homage to your breath have I paid.
(8.2.5’) Let this man live; let him not die! We cause him to rise up again.
(8.2.5.c) I prepare a remedy for him; O Death, do not slay this man!
(8.2.6’) The life-giving, non-harming, living herb— (8.2.6.c) the protecting, conquering, and victorious one—I invoke here for his safety.

(8.2.7’) Speak for him; do not seize him! Let him go, remaining yours but with his full span of life; let him remain here. (8.2.7.c) O Bhava and Śarva, be gracious, grant us protection, ward off misfortune, and bestow long life!
(8.2.8’) O Death, speak for him; have mercy on him! Let him depart from here.
(8.2.8.c) Unharmed in every limb, with beautiful hair, may he, reaching a hundred years through old age, enjoy prosperity by his own self.
8 (8.2.9’) May the weapon of the gods avoid you; I carry you across the region, and I have delivered you from death.
(8.2.9.c) Far away I drive off the flesh-eating fire; I set up a boundary for you so that you may live. 9
(8.2.10’) That path of yours, O Death, which leads through the realm and is unassailable— protecting this man from it, we, as the Brahman, fashion for him a coat of mail.
(8.2.11’) I bestow upon you out-breath and in-breath, old age, death, long life, and well-being.
(8.2.11.c) I ward off all the messengers of Yama sent by Vaivasvata as they roam about.
(8.2.12’) Far away I drive off hostility, Destruction, the Seizer, the flesh-eating Piśācas, (8.2.12.c) and every demon and evil being; we strike them down like darkness. (12)

O Agni, from the immortal life of Jātavedas, I win for you the breath of one who possesses long life. So that you may not be harmed, O immortal one, I make it so that you may be in harmony; may this be accomplished for you.
May Heaven and Earth be auspicious to you, free from distress, and full of splendor.
(8.2.14.c) May the sun shine auspiciously upon you; may the wind blow pleasantly for your heart.
(8.2.14.e) May the divine waters, rich in milk, flow auspiciously over you.
(8.2.15’) May the plants be auspicious to you; I have raised you up from the lower earth toward the higher earth.
(8.2.15.c) There, may both Ādityas, Sūrya and Candramas, protect you.
||15|| (8.2.16’) That garment which is your outer robe, and that girdle which you fasten— (8.2.16.c) we make that auspicious for your body; let it be soft to the touch for you. ||16||
When you, O barber, shave the hair and beard with a sharp-edged razor that possesses keen luster, may you make my face beautiful; do not steal away my life-span.
May rice and barley be auspicious for you—free from disease and free from decay.
(8.2.18.c) These two drive away consumption; these two release one from distress.
(18) (8.2.19’) Whatever you eat, whatever you drink—the grain, the milk of the plow, (8.2.19.c) whatever is edible and whatever is inedible—I make all your food free from poison. (19)
(8.2.20’) We entrust you to both day and night;
(8.2.20.c) from the *arāyas* who desire to devour, protect this one for me!
(20) {4} (8.2.21’) A hundred, ten thousand, and a million years—we grant you two, three, and four ages.

(8.2.21.c) May Indra and Agni, and all the gods, grant their approval to you without resentment. ‖21‖ (8.2.22’) We entrust you to Autumn, to Winter, to Spring, and to Summer. (8.2.22.c) To you belong the pleasant rains, in which the plants flourish. ‖22‖
Death rules over bipeds; death rules over quadrupeds.
Therefore, I rescue you from Death, the Lord. Do not be afraid. (8.2.24) You are unharmed; you shall not die; you shall not die. Do not be afraid.
(8.2.24.c) Indeed, they do not die there, nor do they go to the lowest darkness.
(8.2.25’) Everyone indeed lives there—the cow, the horse, the man, and the beast—where this *brahman* is performed as a protective enclosure for the sake of life. (8.2.25.c) 25.
May he protect you from rivals, from malevolent spells, and from kinsmen.
Be unharmed, immortal, and long-lived; let not your vital breaths abandon your body.
(8.2.27) Those hundred and one deaths, and the destructive powers that must be overcome—
(8.2.27.c) May the gods release you from that [danger] of Agni Vaiśvānara.

‖27‖ (8.2.28’) You are the body of Agni, the deliverer; you are the slayer of demons, the slayer of rivals. (8.2.28.c) Furthermore, you are the dispeller of disease, the medicinal plant named Pūtudru. ‖28‖ {5}
I sprinkle the demon-slaying, vigorous one; I approach the Friend for his most extensive protection.
May Agni, sharpened by our rites and kindled, protect us from harm by day and by night.
O Jātavedas, kindled with your flame, touch the sorcerers with your iron teeth!

(8.3.2.c) Seize the foolish gods with your tongue; having seen them, place the flesh-eaters upon your seat! (8.3.3’) O you who know both, set down both your fangs, you who are destructive, sharpening the lower and the upper. And traverse the mid-air, O Agni; with your jaws, seize and crush the sorcerers!
