(8.3.3.c) And traverse the mid-air, O Agni; with your jaws, seize and crush the sorcerers! (8.3.3.c) And traverse the mid-air, O Agni; with your jaws, seize and crush the sorcerers! (8.3.3.c) And traverse the mid-air, O Agni; with your jaws, seize and crush the sorcerers! (8.3.3.c) And traverse the mid-air
O Agni, split open the skin of the sorcerer; let the destructive thunderbolt strike him down with its heat!
O Jātavedas, crush his joints asunder; let the flesh-eating, flesh-craving [fire] tear him apart!
O Agni Jātavedas, wherever you now see him—whether he stands still or moves about—[destroy him].
(8.3.5.c) And the sorcerer flying through the mid-air—pierce him with your arrow, O archer, sharpening your shaft!
(8.3.6’) Bending your arrows with sacrifices, O Agni, and smearing the points with your whips and thunderbolts;
(8.3.6.c) with those pierce the sorcerers in the heart; break their arms as they face you!
(8.3.7’) And, O Jātavedas, strike down those who have already begun their attack, and with your spears, strike down the Yātudhānas as they are attacking!
(8.3.7c) O Agni, blazing forth, strike them down first; let the ravenous, spotted vultures devour them!
7 (8.3.8’) Speak out here, O Agni, which one it is—the Yātudhāna who does this!
(8.3.8.c) Grasp him with kindled fuel, O Most Youthful One; deliver him over to the eye of the one who beholds men.
(8.3.9’) With your sharp eye, O Agni, protect the sacrifice; lead it forward toward the Vasus, O wise one.
Let not the sorcerers deceive you as you blaze against the injurious demons, O Beholder of Men.
(8.3.10’) Beholding men, look around among the people for the *rakṣas*; crush its three foreparts.
(8.3.10.c) O Agni, crush its ribs with your heat; cut the root of the sorcerer in three ways.
10 {6} (8.3.11’) Let the sorcerer go three times into your snare, O Agni, he who strikes the *ṛta* with falsehood.
(8.3.11.c) O Jātavedas, flashing with your flame, bind him down right before the eyes of this singer.
(8.3.12’) Whatever curse a pair utters today, O Agni, or whatever harshness of speech the revilers produce;
(8.3.12.c) whatever arrow is born from anger and the mind—with that, pierce the sorcerers in their hearts.
Crush the sorcerers with your heat; O Agni, crush the *rakṣas* with your flame.
Crush the fools who worship false gods with your radiance; crush those who feast on life-breath as they burn away.
May the gods today crush the wicked; may the released curses turn back against him.
(8.3.14.c) Let arrows strike the thief of speech in his vital parts; let the sorcerer fall into the snare of everyone.

14 (8.3.15’) The sorcerer who smears himself with human flesh, who [smears himself] with the flesh of horses or cattle, (8.3.15.c) or who steals the milk of the cow—O Agni, shatter their heads with your fiery heat! 15
Let the sorcerers bring poison upon the cattle; let the evil-doers be cut down for Aditi.
May the god Savitar cast them away; may they lose their share of the plants.
(16) The milk of the cow belongs to the year; let not the sorcerer, O watcher of men, consume it. (17)
(8.3.17.c) O Agni, whichever one should desire to satisfy himself with thy nectar, pierce him in his vital organ with thy flame as he faces thee.
(8.3.18’) From of old, O Agni, thou hast crushed the sorcerers; the *rakṣas* have never conquered thee in battles.
(8.3.18.c) Burn up the flesh-eaters together with their roots; let them not escape from thy divine missile.
O Agni, protect us from below and from above; protect us from behind and from the front.
May those ageless and most fierce flames of yours burn up the one who speaks evil against us.
O Agni, as a seer with your wisdom, protect us from behind, from the front, from below, and from above.

(8.3.20.c) O Agni, you who are ageless, a friend to your friend, an immortal among mortals—be such for us. (8.3.21’) O Agni, bestow that eye upon the singer, with which you may see the hoof-smiting sorcerers; like Atharvan, with your divine light, burn away the truth-despising, mindless one.
O Agni, O victorious one, we set thee around us as a fortress— thou who art wise, bold in hue day by day, the slayer of the treacherous.
With poison, strike down the Rakṣasas and those who act with treachery.
(8.3.23.c) O Agni, with your sharp flame and with your cresting rays of light!
||23|| (8.3.24’) Agni shines forth with his lofty radiance; he makes all things manifest by his greatness.
(8.3.24.c) He overcomes the godless, malevolent illusions; he sharpens his two horns to gore the Rākṣasas. ||24||
O Jātavedas, those two horns of yours which are ageless, possessing sharp weapons and sharpened by prayer—
with those two, O Jātavedas, pierce with your flame the Kimīdin who attacks us with an evil heart and faces us head-on. 25.
Agni, the immortal with bright radiance, drives away the demons;
he is pure, purifying, and worthy of praise.
O Indra and Soma, burn up the demons, crush them, and cast down those who thrive in darkness, O bulls!
(8.4.1.c) Crush those who lack devotion, burn them down, strike them dead, drive them away, and pierce the devourers!
(8.4.2’) O Indra and Soma, let the evil-doer be scorched by his own wickedness, like a cooking-pot placed upon the fire.
(8.4.2.c) Against the hater of sacred prayer, the flesh-eater with the terrible eye, the *kimīdin*—bestow upon him relentless hatred!

O Indra and Soma, cast the evildoers into the pit, into the bottomless darkness from which not even one of them shall ever rise again; let that be your wrathful might for the sake of victory. O Indra and Soma, hurl down from heaven and from earth your weapon, the crusher of the one who speaks evil.

(8.4.4.c) Fashion forth from the mountains a thunderbolt that resounds through heaven, with which you two may consume the waxing *rakṣas*. (8.4.5’) O Indra and Soma, hurl down from heaven those stone-hurling bolts heated by fire;
with those unaging, flame-smiting weapons, pierce the devourers into the abyss so that they go forth voiceless.
O Indra and Soma, may this prayer encompass you from every side, as a girth-girth encircles two prize-winning horses.
O Lords of Men, quicken with wisdom this oblation which I present to you, and these sacred hymns, as if you were two kings.
Take heed of us with your impetuous deeds; strike down the treacherous, crooked Rākṣasas who seek to harm us.
(8.4.7.c) O Indra and Soma, let there be no easy path for the evildoer who at any time seeks to harm me with malice.
(8.4.8’) He who, with false words, accuses me while I walk with a sincere mind—may he, the speaker of untruth, O Indra, be like water held in the hollow of one’s hand; may he be of the non-existent!
(8.4.9) Those who, by their ways, scatter him who speaks the truth, or those who by their own wills corrupt what is auspicious—

may Soma deliver them over to the serpent, or place them in the lap of Destruction. (8.4.10) O Agni, whoever seeks to harm our essence— the nourishment of our food, our horses, our cattle, or our bodies— [may he be destroyed].
(8.4.10.c) Let the enemy, the thief, the doer of theft, go to destruction; let him be deprived of both his body and his progeny.
{9} (8.4.11’) May he be far removed from both his body and his progeny; may he lie beneath all the three earths.
(8.4.11.c) O gods, may the glory of him wither away who seeks to harm me by day and who seeks to harm me by night. {11}
(8.4.12’) Truth and untruth, two words, contend with one another for the sake of the discerning person.
Of these two, that which is truth, whichever is more upright—that alone Soma protects; he strikes down the untruth.
(8.4.13’) Indeed, Soma does not further the crooked man, nor the warrior who maintains himself through falsehood.
(8.4.13.c) It slays the demon, it slays the one who speaks falsely; both lie ensnared by Indra.

||13|| (8.4.14’) Whether I am one whose god is falsehood, or whether I have spoken to the gods in vain, O Agni; (8.4.14.c) why, O Jātavedas, are you angry with us? May those of deceitful speech fall into destruction! ||14||
(8.4.15’) May I die this very day if I am a sorcerer, or if I have consumed the vital breath of a man.
(8.4.15.c) Then may he be deprived of his ten sons who falsely calls me a sorcerer.
(8.4.16’) He who calls me a sorcerer when I am not a sorcerer, or the demon who says "I am pure"—[may they both perish].
(8.4.16.c) May Indra strike him down with his great weapon; may he fall as the lowest of all living beings!

16 (8.4.17’) She who comes forth at night like an owl, hiding her body from the malicious one—(8.4.17.c) may she fall into the endless pit! May the pressing-stones strike down the *rakṣas* with their clanging sounds! 17

Spread out, O Maruts, search among the people; seize the Rākṣasas and grind them to pieces—those who fly about at night having become birds, or those who have placed their hostility toward the divine sacrifice.
O Indra, Maghavan, hurl down the stone from heaven sharpened by Soma; whet it thoroughly!
(8.4.19.c) From the east, from the west, from below, and from above, strike down the *rakṣas* with the mountain!
(8.4.20’) These here, those dog-demons (*śvayātu*), fly about; seeking to harm, they seek to harm Indra, the one who cannot be deceived.
(8.4.20.c) Śakra sharpens his weapon for the malevolent; now let him hurl the thunderbolt at the sorcerers. {10}
Indra has become the destroyer of the sorcerers who steal the oblations as they seek to attack.
Let the mighty Śakra come against the Rākṣasas, shattering them like an axe through a forest, or like a vessel being broken.
Slay the owl-sorcerer, the screech-owl sorcerer, the dog-sorcerer, and the cuckoo-sorcerer!
(8.4.22.c) Crush the demon with beautiful wings and the demon with vulture wings like a grinding stone, O Indra!
(8.4.23’) Let not the demon, the follower of sorcery, overcome us; let those Kimīdin demons who come in pairs be driven away.
(8.4.23.c) May the Earth protect us from earthly distress, and may the Atmosphere protect us from celestial distress.
O Indra, slay the male sorcerer and also the woman who exults in her magic power.
Let the foolish gods with crooked necks perish; let them not behold the sun as it rises.
Look back, look around! O Indra and Soma, remain awake.
(8.4.25.c) Cast down your weapon upon the Rākṣasas; hurl the thunderbolt at the sorcerers! {11} (8.5.1’) This protective amulet, a hero, is bound for the hero.
(8.5.1.c) It is powerful, a slayer of rivals, a brave warrior, a guardian, and most auspicious.
(8.5.2’) This amulet is the slayer of rivals, rich in heroes, powerful, victorious, and fierce; (8.5.2.c) as a hero it goes forth, destroying and turning back the sorcery.
(8.5.3’) By means of this amulet Indra slew Vṛtra; by means of this the wise one brought the Asuras to defeat.
(8.5.3.c) By this he conquered both these, heaven and earth; by this he conquered the four quarters.
(8.5.4’) This amulet of Srāktya is a turner-back, a protector; powerful, subduing the adversaries, and self-controlled, may it guard us on every side. (8.5.4.c) 4.

(8.5.5’) This Agni has said, and Soma has said it; Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ, and Indra have said it. (8.5.5.c) These gods, my domestic priests, shall drive away the sorceries with their counter-spells. (8.5.6’) I have placed between myself and [the enemy] heaven and earth, as well as day and the sun.

(8.5.6.c) May those gods, my priests, drive back the sorceries with their counter-spells. With the *srāktya* amulet, like a wise seer, I have conquered all hostile armies; I strike down the demons. Whatever sorceries belong to the Aṅgirases, whatever sorceries belong to the Asuras—[I overcome them].
(8.5.9.c) The spells (*kṛtyā*) that have been wrought by oneself, and those brought by others—
(8.5.9.e) let both of these go away to the far distances, beyond the ninety navigable rivers.
(8.5.10’) May the gods— Indra, Viṣṇu, Savitṛ, Rudra, and Agni— bind this amulet as armor for him.
Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, Virāj, Vaiśvānara, and all the seers.
You are the highest among plants, like the ox among moving creatures, like the tiger among beasts of prey. We have found him whom we sought—the one who watches over us from nearby.
He indeed becomes a tiger, and also a lion, and also a bull;
he is the crusher of rivals who wears this amulet.
Neither the Apsarases, nor the Gandharvas, nor mortals slay him.
(8.5.13.c) He who wears this amulet shines forth across all the quarters.
(8.5.14’) Kaśyapa created you; Kaśyapa brought you into being. (8.5.14.c) Indra wore you among men; wearing you, he conquered his adversaries.

(8.5.14.e) The gods made the jewel of a thousand powers their armor. ‖14‖ (8.5.15’) Whoever seeks to strike you down with sorcery, with consecrations, or with sacrifices—(8.5.15.c) O Indra, strike him back with your hundred-jointed thunderbolt! ‖15‖
This indeed is the *pratīvarta* amulet, powerful and victorious;
may it protect our offspring and wealth, being a secure defense and most auspicious.
May we be without rivals from below, and without rivals from above.

(8.5.17.c) O Hero, Indra, place us behind that which has no rival; place the light before us. The thick, formidable armor belonging to Indra and Agni— which none of all the gods can pierce— may that great [armor] protect my body on every side, so that I may be long-lived and reach old age.
The divine amulet has ascended upon me for great safety from harm.

(8.5.21’) May Indra bestow manly strength upon it; O gods, enter into this post, so that he may be long-lived for a hundred autumns, reaching old age with full vitality. Bestower of well-being, Lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, dispeller of the scornful, the Controller— may Indra, the victorious and unconquered, drinker of Soma, the bull who grants fearlessness, bind this amulet for you.
(8.6.1’) Those two who, as soon as you were born, your mother cleansed for you— the finders of a husband— let not the ill-named one there covet them, nor the *aliṃśa*, nor the *vatsapa*.
(8.6.2’) [Drive away] the *palālānupalāla*, the *śarku*, the *koka*, the *malimluca*, and the *palījaka*.
(8.6.2.c) Āśreṣa, you who wear a covering, with a bear’s neck, you who close your eyes!
(8.6.3.a) Do not wrap yourself up; do not creep toward me; do not creep between my thighs.
(8.6.3.c) I prepare for her a remedy, a *baja*-plant that drives away evil names.
The ill-named and the well-named, both desire what is enclosed.
We drive away the *arāyas*; let the well-named one seek out the woman.
(8.6.5) That black, hairy demon, whether he be born from a pillar or be a snout-like creature—
(8.6.5.c) From her testicles and from her pubic region, we strike away the *arāya* demons.
(8.6.6’) The one who sniffs after, the one who feels about, the flesh-eater, and the one who licks repeatedly— The brown *baja* has destroyed the *arāya* and the *śvakiṣkin*. 6.
(8.6.7) But he who lies with you in sleep, appearing as a brother or even as a father—
let the *baja* strike him down from here, those who have the form of eunuchs and are *tirītinas*.
(8.6.8) He who stalks you while you sleep, he who seeks to harm you while you are awake.
(8.6.8.c) As the sun moves around them, he has caused those who were fainting to vanish like a shadow.
(8.6.9.a) O herb, destroy that man who makes this woman bring forth a stillborn child or one that dies at birth; make him as blind as a lotus without eyes.
(8.6.9.c) O herb, you must cause him to perish. 9.

Those who dance around the houses at evening, braying like donkeys; those who are *kusūla*, *kukṣila*, *kakubha*, *karuma*, and *srima*— O Herb, destroy them by your fragrance, scattering them in all directions.
Those who are pot-bellied, those with deformed ears, who wear skins and coarse garments;
like eunuchs dancing about, those who make a noise in the forest—we cause them to perish from here.
Those who cannot endure the sun as it burns yonder from the sky—[we cause them to perish].
(8.6.12.c) We destroy the *arāyas* who dwell in goatskins, the foul-smelling ones with red mouths, and the *makakas*. (8.6.13’) Those who, having placed themselves excessively upon their shoulders,
carry [burdens], and who prick the hips of women— O Indra, destroy those *rakṣasas*.
Those who go forward like bridegrooms, bearing horns in their hands,
who stand at the oven, who laugh aloud, and who produce light in the thicket— those we cause to perish from here.
Those whose forefeet are behind and whose heels are in front, whose faces are turned backward...
(8.6.15.c) Those born from threshing floors, those born from dung-smoke, the *uruṇḍas* and the *maṭmaṭas*, those with testicles like jars and those who are impotent—
(8.6.15.e) O Brahmaṇaspati, destroy them all by means of this awakening spell!
(8.6.16’) May they have rolling eyes, may they be unable to walk, may they be without women, and may they be eunuchs!

(8.6.16.c) Bestow your healing medicine, O Bheṣaja, upon him who seeks to separate this woman from her husband, she who has no husband though she has a husband. (8.6.17’) [Subdue] the Uddharṣin, the Munikeśa, the Jambhayan, and the Marīmṛśa; [subdue] the Upeṣan, the Udumbara, the Tuṇḍela, and the Śāluḍa.
(8.6.17.e) Strike him down with your foot and your heel, like a cow kicking a water-jar as she moves.
(8.6.18’) May he who touches your embryo, or kills your newborn child— may Piṅga, the wielder of the fierce bow, pierce his heart.
May he drive away the Piṅga Gandharvas, who kill those born from the womb and lie in wait for women giving birth, as the wind drives away the clouds.
May he maintain what has been gathered and preserved; may that which is beneficial not fall away.
(8.6.20.c) May those two fierce healers, Nīvibhārya, protect your embryo.
(20) (8.6.21’) From Pavīnasa, from Taṅgalva, from Śāyaka, and even from Nagnaka—may Piṅga protect you, for the sake of offspring and for your husband, from the Kimīdin demons. (21)
From the two-faced, four-eyed, five-footed, fingerless one;
from the stalk that creeps forward, protect us from the one who rolls about.
(22) Those who eat raw flesh, and those who eat the bloody flesh of man—protect us from them. (23)
(8.6.23.c) Those hair-crested ones devour the embryos; we drive them away from here.
(8.6.24’) Those who slink away from the sun, like a daughter-in-law from her father-in-law—let Bāja and Piṅga pierce their hearts.
(8.6.24.c) Let Bāja and Piṅga pierce their hearts. 24.
O tawny one, protect the newborn; let them not make [the child] a male or a female.
Let the egg-eaters not harm the embryos; drive away these Kimīdin demons from here! Childlessness, the death of offspring, weeping, misfortune, and sin—[drive these away].
(8.6.26.c) Having fashioned it like a garland from a tree, place that upon the one who is unloved.
{16} (8.7.1’) Those plants which are brown, those which are bright, the red ones, and the speckled; the dark ones and the black ones—all the plants we summon hither. {1}
(8.7.2’) May they protect this person from consumption sent by the gods— (8.7.2.c) those plants of which heaven is the father, earth the mother, and the ocean has become the root.
(8.7.3’) The waters are the first; they are the divine herbs.
(8.7.3.c) These have driven away from your limb by limb the wasting disease born of sin.
(8.7.4’) Spreading out, branching, and growing with single shoots, I invoke the plants that extend themselves;
(8.7.4.c) those that are fibrous and thorny, those with many branches—I call upon these herbs belonging to all the gods, formidable, and the sustainers of men.
Whatever conquering power you possess, O subduers, and whatever strength is yours—by that, O plants, release this man from this consumption; furthermore, I prepare a remedy.
I [take] the life-giving plant, the one that harms no one, the living herb.
(8.7.6.c) I invoke here Arundhatī, Unnayantī, Puṣpā, and Madhumatī, for this man’s safety. (8.7.7’) May the wise ones, who possess the earth, come hither to my words,
so that we may carry this man across from distress.
(8.7.8) Food of Agni, embryo of the waters, those plants that grow ever renewed—may they, steadfast, possessing a thousand names, be brought hither as healing remedies.
(8.7.9) The plants have the water as their essence; they are the inner womb of the *avakā* plant.
(8.7.9.c) May those with sharp horns scatter away misfortune.

(8.7.10’) Those that release [the bonds], those that free from Varuṇa, the fierce ones, those that corrupt poison, and those that destroy the seat of power and corrupt the *kṛtyā*—may those plants come here! (8.7.10) {17}
May the most powerful plants, which have been purchased and praised, protect the cow, the horse, the man, and the livestock in this village.
Sweet is their root, sweet is their tip; the middle of these plants has become sweet.

(8.7.12.c) May these [cows], whose leaf is honey-sweet and whose flower is honey-sweet, who partake of honey and enjoy the nectar of immortality, yield for us clarified butter as food, with the bull as their leader.
(8.7.13’) As many and of whatever kind these plants are that exist upon the earth—
(8.7.13.c) May those thousand-leaved plants deliver me from death and from distress.
||13|| (8.7.14’) The tiger-skin amulet, the protector among plants, guarding against imprecations; (8.7.14.c) may it drive away all diseases and demons far from us. ||14||
They tremble before her as before the roar of a lion; they flee from her when she is brought forth as if before a fire.
May the consumption of cattle and men, driven away by the plants, pass into the navigable rivers.
(8.7.16) The plants have released themselves from Agni Vaiśvānara.

(8.7.16.c) Spread over the earth are those plants of which the Lord of the Forest is king. (8.7.17’) Those that grow as descendants of Aṅgiras upon the mountains and upon the level plains—may those plants be full of milk, auspicious for us, and a blessing to our hearts. Those plants which I know and those which I see with my eyes—
those unknown and those we recognize, and those in which we know nourishment is gathered—
may all these herbs together heed my words.
(8.7.19.c) So that we may carry this man across from misfortune. (8.7.20’) The holy fig tree, the *darbha* grass, and Soma, the king, are the immortal oblation;
rice and barley are the two medicines, the two immortal sons of Heaven. (20) {18}

(8.7.21) Rise up! You are thundering; you are roaring, O plants, when Parjanya, O you whose mother is Pṛśni, favors you with his seed. (8.7.22) With that nectar, we cause this man to drink this strength.
(8.7.22.c) Moreover, I prepare this remedy so that he may live to a hundred years.
(22) (8.7.23’) The boar knows the plant; the mongoose knows the healing herb.
(8.7.23.c) Those which the serpents and the Gandharvas know—those I invoke for his protection. (23)
As many herbs as cows, the inviolable ones, eat, and as many as goats and sheep [eat],
so many herbs brought hither shall grant you protection. (25) As many herbs as physicians know to be medicine for human beings...
I bring as many of these all-healing plants toward you.
(26) Those that are flowering, those that are in fruit, those that bear fruit, and those that are fruitless—may they yield for him, like mothers, for his safety. (27)
I have lifted you up from the five-fold fetter and from the ten-fold one;
likewise, from the foot-fetter of Yama and from every sin against the gods.
May Indra churn [the enemy], the churning one, the powerful Śakra, the hero, the breaker of forts.

(8.8.1.c) So that we may slay the armies of our enemies by the thousands. (8.8.2’) May this stinking rope, when blown upon, make that army stink; (8.8.2.c) seeing the smoke and the fire from afar, let fear take hold in the hearts of our enemies.
(8.8.3’) O Aśvattha tree, crush those men; O Khadira tree, devour them! Let them break like a sudden fracture; let the executioner slay them with his weapons.
(8.8.4’) Let the Paruṣāhva plant make those rough ones rough; let the executioner slay them with his weapons.
(8.8.4.c) May they quickly be broken like arrows, bound together by a great net!
(8.8.5’) The atmosphere was the net; the vast quarters of space were the poles of the net.
(8.8.5.c) Having ensnared the Dasyus with it, Śakra scattered their army.
For great is the net of the mighty Śakra, who possesses the prize-winning steeds;
with it, press down upon all the enemies so that not even one among them may escape.
Great, O heroic Indra, is your net—you who are worth a thousand and possess a hundredfold prowess.

(8.8.7.c) With his army, Śakra struck down a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, and a hundred million *dasyus* after challenging them. (8.8.8’) This great world was the net of the mighty Śakra; by means of that Indra-net, I shroud all those [enemies] in darkness. (8.8.9) Exhaustion, fierce failure, and incurable affliction;
fatigue, sloth, and delusion—with these I bind them all. (8.8.10) I deliver them over to Death; they are bound by the nooses of Death.

(8.8.10.c) Those who are the malevolent messengers of Death—to them I lead these men away, bound. {20} (8.8.11’) Let the messengers of Death, the messengers of Yama, lead them away; let them block the waters. (8.8.11.c) Let more than a thousand be slain; let the blade of grass of Bhava be their death. {11}
The Sādhyas go forth with might, raising one net-pole;
the Rudras one, the Vasus one, and one is raised by the Ādityas.
May the Viśvedevas go above, bending [the pole] with might.
(8.8.13.c) Let the Aṅgirases go forth, striking down the great army with their center.
(8.8.14’) The lords of the forest, the products of the forest, the herbs, and the creepers;
the bipeds and the quadrupeds—I impel them so that they may slay that army. (8.8.14.c) 14.

I command the Gandharvas, Apsarases, serpents, gods, holy beings, and ancestors—whether seen or unseen—that they shall slay this army. These death-nooses have been sown; having stepped upon them, you shall not be released.
(8.8.16.c) Let this missile strike that army by the thousands! (16) (8.8.17’) This sacrificial vessel is kindled by fire; this is a thousandfold oblation.
(8.8.17.c) O Bhava and Pṛśnibāhu, and Śarva, destroy that army! (17)
Let them fall into the mouth of Death—into hunger, exhaustion, slaughter, and fear!
O Indra and Śarva, with your nets of eyes, strike down that army!
Vanquished and driven away, let the enemies tremble; pursued by the sacred spell (*brahman*), run away!
(8.8.19.c) Among these whom Bṛhaspati has driven away, let not any one escape.
(8.8.20’) Let their weapons fall down; let them not be able to fix an arrow to the string.
(8.8.20.c) Then, while they are greatly terrified, let their arrows strike their vital organs.
(8.8.21) May Heaven and Earth cry out against them, as may the Mid-region together with the gods!
Let them find neither a kinsman nor a firm support; striking one another down, let them go unto death.
(8.8.22) The four quarters are the mares of the divine chariot; the sacrificial cakes are its hooves, and the mid-region is its fender.

(8.8.22.c) Heaven and Earth are the two sides; the seasons are the reins; the intermediate directions are the attendants; speech is the chariot-rail. ||22|| (8.8.23’) The year is the chariot; the recurring year is the seat of the chariot; the Virāj is the pole; Agni is the front of the chariot. (8.8.23.c) Indra is the driver on the left; the moon is the charioteer. ||23||

(8.8.24’) From here, conquer! Conquer further! Completely conquer! Conquer, svāhā! (8.8.24.c) May these conquer! May those yonder be conquered! Svāhā to these; may there be ill-fortune for those yonder!
(8.8.24.e) With the blue-and-red [weapon], I strike them down. ‖24‖ {21}
(8.9.1’) From where were those two born? Which is that half [of the body]? From which world, from which earth [did they come]?
(8.9.1.c) The two calves rose up from the ocean of Virāj; I ask you, by which of these two were they milked?
(8.9.2’) He who, having made the ocean his womb, lay down upon the threefold seat and caused it to roar with his greatness—
(8.9.2.c) The calf, the wish-fulfilling cow of Virāj, has made its bodies hidden in the far distance.
(8.9.3’) Those three which are great, of which the fourth releases speech—
(8.9.3.c) Let the wise one know this as Brahman through austerity, in which the one is joined, in which the one is joined.
From the *bṛhat* [meter], the *sāmans* were fashioned; from the sixth, the five [vocalic meters] were fashioned. The *bṛhat* was fashioned from the *bṛhatī*; from what was the *bṛhatī* measured?
The *bṛhatī* was fashioned from the measure of the mother; from the measure of the mother it was fashioned.
(8.9.5.c) From Māyā indeed was Māyā born; from Māyā was Mātali born.
||5|| (8.9.6’) The image of Vaiśvānara is above the sky, as far as Agni has spread across the two worlds.
(8.9.6.c) From there, from that sixth [day], the hymns proceed; from here they proceed toward the sixth day of the ritual cycle. ||6||

(8.9.7’) We six seers, O Kaśyapa, ask you this, for you indeed join together what is joined and what is fit to be joined. They call Virāj the father of Brahman; bestow her upon us, your friends, in her many forms. (8.9.8’) She, following whom the sacrifices fall away when she falls away, and who they attend when she is attended.
(8.9.8.c) She whose ordinance and impulse the Yakṣa moves—she is Virāj; the seers [are] in the highest heaven.
(8.9.9.a) Breathless, she goes by means of the breath of those who breathe; Virāj follows after Svarāj.
(8.9.9.c) Some behold her, the all-touching, well-formed Virāj; others do not behold her.
Who knows the pairing of Virāj? Who [knows] her seasons, and who her ritual order?
Who [knows] her steps, how many times they have been milked? Who [knows] her abode and how many dawns she has?
This is she who first shone forth; she moves, having entered into these other [dawns].
(8.9.11.c) Within her are great majesties; the bride, the mother of nine sons, has prevailed.
||11|| (8.9.12’) Adorned with their own splendor, Dawn and Night, winged with meters, move together toward their common womb.
||12|| Wives of the Sun, they move together, discerning, radiant, unaging, and rich in seed. ||12||
Three have followed the path of *ṛta*; three heats have followed the seed.
One quickens progeny, one [quickens] vigor, and one protects the kingdom of those who seek the gods.
The seers, fashioning the two wings of the sacrifice, established Agni and Soma as that which was the fourth.
(8.9.14.c) The Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, the Anuṣṭubh, and the Bṛhadarkī—bringing the light of heaven to the sacrificer.
(8.9.15’) Five dawns follow the five milkings; the cow with five names follows the five seasons.
The five directions are fashioned by the fifteenfold [stoma]; they have a single head toward a single world.
Six beings were born, the first-born of Cosmic Order; six indeed carry the *sāman* chants throughout the six-day rite.
Six yokes there are for the plough, following each *sāman*; they speak of six heavens and earths, six wide expanses.
They speak of six months that are cold and six that are hot; tell us which season among them is the extra one.
(8.9.17.c) Seven Suparṇas, the seers, have sat down; seven meters follow, and seven consecrations.
(8.9.18’) Seven oblations, seven kindling-sticks, seven honeys, and seven seasons indeed.
(8.9.18.c) Seven clarified butters have encompassed existence; we have heard that they are called the seven vultures. (18)
(8.9.19’) The seven meters, each increasing by four syllables, are superposed one upon another.
(8.9.19.c) How do the *stomas* find their support in them? How are they established within those *stomas*?
(8.9.20’) How does the *gāyatrī* pervade the *trivṛt*, and how is the *triṣṭubh* fashioned by the *pañcadaśa*?

(8.9.20.c) How is the *jagatī* [connected] with the thirty-three? How the *anuṣṭubh*? How the twenty-onefold? ‖20‖ (8.9.21’) Eight are the born beings, the first-born of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*); eight are the divine priests of Indra.
(8.9.21.c) Aditi has eight wombs and eight sons; toward her on this eighth night, the oblation goes. ‖21‖
(8.9.22’) Thinking thus what is most beneficial, I have come to this tradition; I am your friend, your auspicious one.
(8.9.22.c) Your *kratu* is of common origin and is propitious; knowing all, he moves among you all.
22 (8.9.23’) Eight belong to Indra, six to Yama, and seven to the *ṛṣis*, distributed sevenfold.
(8.9.23.c) The waters followed after those five [elements] for the sake of men and plants.
||23|| (8.9.24’) For the young cow, yielding her first milk, yielded the *vaśa* and the *pīyūṣa* exclusively for Indra;
(8.9.24.c) and then she satisfied the fourfold groups: the gods, humans, the *asuras*, and the seers. ||24||

(8.9.25’) Who indeed is the cow? Who is the sole seer? What is the abode? And what are the blessings? (8.9.25.c) That which is the singular increaser of the sacrifice upon earth, the one-seasoned—what indeed is it? ‖25‖ (8.9.26’) The cow is one; the sole seer is one; the abode is one; the blessings are of one kind.

(8.9.26.c) On earth, the Yakṣa is the sole increaser; the single season does not exceed it. {24} (8.10.26’) In the beginning, this universe was indeed Virāj. When she was born, everything was afraid of her, thinking, "She alone will become all this.
{1} She stepped forth; she stepped down into the Gārhapatya fire.
(8.10.2.c) He who knows this becomes a householder, a master of the home.
(8.10.3’) She stepped forth; she stepped down into the Āhavanīya fire.
(8.10.3.c) The gods go to his invocation of the gods; he becomes dear to the gods, he who knows this. (8.10.3) 3.
She stepped forth; she stepped down into the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire-altar.
He who knows this becomes one who is intent on sacrifice, worthy of sacrificial gifts, and a guest in a dwelling.
She stepped forth; she stepped down into the assembly hall.
(8.10.5.c) He who knows this goes to his assembly; he becomes one worthy of the assembly.
||5|| (8.10.6’) She stepped forth; she stepped into the assembly.
(8.10.6.c) He who knows this goes to his assembly; he becomes one worthy of the assembly. ||6||
He stepped forth; he stepped down into the place of address.
He who knows thus goes to the address of this [earth] and becomes one worthy of being addressed. 7. He stepped forth; he stood having stepped out fourfold into the intermediate space. 8.
The gods and humans said to her: "She alone knows that upon which both of us may subsist; let us summon her. They summoned her, saying:
"O Urjā, come! O Svadhā, come! O Sūnṛtā, come! O Irāvatī, come!"
Indra was her calf; the Gāyatrī was the rope for tying her; the cloud was her udder.
The Bṛhat and the Rathantara were two of her teats; the Yajñāyajñiya and the Vāmadevya were the other two.
By means of the Rathantara, the gods milked the plants; by the Bṛhat, they milked wide space.

(8.10.15’) He milks the waters with the Vāmadevya [Sāman], and the sacrifice with the Yajñāyajñiya. ‖14‖ (8.10.16’) Verily, for him the Rathantara milks the plants, and the Bṛhat milks wide space. ‖16‖ (8.10.17’) He who knows the Vāmadevya as the waters, and the Yajñāyajñiya as the sacrifice. ‖17‖ {26}
She stepped forth; she came to the trees. The trees struck her down, and she became whole again after a year.
Therefore, what is cut from the trees grows back again after a year. His hostile rival is cut down who knows thus.
She stepped forth; she came to the Fathers. The Fathers struck her down, and she became whole again after a month.
Therefore, they offer the monthly and half-monthly [oblations] to the ancestors; he who knows this knows the path leading to the fathers.
She moved away; she went to the gods. The gods slew her; she became the half-month.
Therefore, they utter the *vaṣaṭ* call to the gods at the half-month. He who knows this knows the path leading to the gods.
She stepped forth; she came to the humans. The humans slaughtered her, and she immediately became whole.
Therefore, they offer [the sacrificial food] to humans on both days; they bring it to the house of him who knows thus.
She stepped forth; she came to the Asuras. The Asuras called out to her, "O Illusion, come!"
(8.10.21.c) Virocana, the son of Prahrādi, was her calf; an iron vessel was her milking bowl.
(8.10.21.e) Dvimūrdhan, the son of Ṛtviya, milked her; he milked her as mere illusion.
(8.10.23’) She moved away; she went to the Pitṛs. The Pitṛs called out to her: "O Svadhā, come!"
(8.10.23.c) King Yama was her calf, and the vessel was a silver bowl. (8.10.23.e) Antaka Mārtyava milked her; he milked her as the very *svadhā* offering.
(8.10.24’) She moved away; she came to human beings. Human beings invoked her, saying, "O possessor of food, come!"
(8.10.24.c) Manu Vaivasvata was her calf, and the earth was the vessel.
(8.10.24.e) Pṛthī Vainya milked her; he milked from her both agriculture and grain.
(8.10.25’) She stepped forth and came to the Seven Seers. The Seven Seers called out to her: "O thou rich in sacred knowledge (*brahman*), come hither!"
King Soma was her calf, and the *chandas* were her vessel.
Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa milked her; he milked from her both sacred knowledge (*brahman*) and ascetic heat (*tapas*).
She stepped forth; she went to the gods. The gods called out to her: "O Strength (*ūrj*), come hither!"
Indra was her calf, and the *camasa* cup was her vessel.

The divine Savitṛ milked her; he milked her as strength itself. She moved away; she went to the Gandharvas and Apsarases. The Gandharvas and Apsarases called out to her: "O you of holy fragrance, come!"
Citraratha was the calf of that [cow] Sauryavarcas, and a lotus leaf was her vessel.
Vasuruci milked that Sauryavarcas; he milked out nothing but a holy fragrance.
It rose up and came toward the common folk; the common folk called out to it, "Hide yourself! Come hither!"
(8.10.28.c) Of her, Vaiśravaṇa Kubera was the calf, and an unbaked clay vessel was the milking vessel.
(8.10.28.e) Rajatanābhi Kaberaka milked her; he milked her while she was still hidden.
(8.10.29’) She stepped forth; she came toward the serpents. The serpents called out to her, "O Poisonous One, come!"
Takṣaka Vaiśaleya was her calf; an alābu gourd was her vessel.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra Airāvata milked her, and he milked out nothing but poison. Therefore, if one were to consecrate someone who knows this with an alābu gourd, it would strike back at him.
One should not strike back even in thought; however, one may strike back [with the words], "I strike you back.
When one strikes back, it is poison indeed that one strikes back.
Poison indeed is poured after his hateful rival by him who knows thus.
From heaven, from earth, from the intermediate space, from the ocean, from fire, and from the winds, the Madhukasha was indeed born.
Having honored her who is clothed in immortality, all creatures rejoice toward her with their hearts.
Great is her milk, possessing every form; they say that the seed of the ocean is hers.
(9.1.2.c) Whence she comes, bestowing the *madhukā* plant—therein is breath, therein is the immortal deposited.
(9.1.3’) Men on this earth, investigating in many ways, behold her movement;
for from Agni and Vāta was born the *madhukā*, the fierce granddaughter of the Maruts. (9.1.3.c) 3.

The mother of the Ādityas, the daughter of the Vasus, the breath of living beings, the navel of immortality—golden-hued, honey-tongued, dripping with clarity, the great splendor moves among mortals. (9.1.4) The gods generated the honeyed tongue; its embryo became the one of all forms. (9.1.5)
(9.1.5.c) The mother nourishes him when he is born and young; once born, he gazes upon all beings.

(9.1.6’) Who knows him? Who has perceived him—he who is the inexhaustible jar of Soma within her heart? May the wise Brahman rejoice in him. (9.1.6.c) May that one of excellent intelligence revel in this.
He knows them both, and he perceives those two inexhaustible breasts of hers that yield a thousand streams;
they pour forth nourishment without faltering.
Making the sound *hiṅ*, the great one, bestowing vital strength, she approaches with a loud voice, fulfilling her sacred vow.
(9.1.8.c) Lowing toward the three heats, she utters her cry; she flows with milks.

(9.1.9’) The waters sit beside her as she swells, as do the Śākvara bulls who are self-ruling. They rain down; they cause [her] to rain; for one who knows that, the waters fulfill desire and provide nourishment.
(9.1.10’) Your voice, O Prajāpati, is the thunder; as a bull, you cast forth your vigor upon the earth.
(9.1.10.c) For from Agni and the winds was born the honey-whip, the fierce granddaughter of the Maruts.
(9.1.11’) Just as Soma is dear to the Aśvins at the morning pressing...
(9.1.11.c) Even so, O Aśvins, may splendor be established within my self.
||11|| (9.1.12’) Just as Soma is dear to Indra and Agni at the second pressing, (9.1.12.c) even so, O Indra and Agni, may splendor be established within my self. ||12||
Just as Soma is dear to the Ṛbhus at the third pressing, even so, O Ṛbhus, may splendor be established within my self.
May I produce sweetness; may I win sweetness.
(9.1.14.c) Rich in milk, O Agni, have I come; unite me with splendor. (9.1.15’) O Agni, unite me with splendor, unite me with progeny, and unite me with long life.
(9.1.15.c) May the gods take note of this of mine; may Indra, together with the seers, take note.
Just as honey-makers gather honey in the springtime,
so may splendor be established within my self by the Aśvins.
Just as bees smear this honey upon the springtime [flower], so may splendor be established within my self by the Aśvins.
(9.1.17.c) Thus, O Aśvins, may splendor, brilliance, strength, and vital power be established within me.
(17) (9.1.18’) Whatever honey is in the mountains, in the hills, in cows, and in horses; whatever honey is in the flowing surā—may that honey be in me. (18)
(9.1.19’) O Aśvins, lords of splendor, anoint me with the honey of the bee, so that I may utter speech full of luster among the people.
(9.1.20’) O Prajāpati, your voice is the thunder; as a bull, you cast forth vigor upon the earth and in heaven.
(9.1.20.c) All creatures live upon that; by it he bestows the remainder as nourishment.
(9.1.21’) The earth is the staff, the intermediate space is the womb, the sky is the whip, lightning is the lash-tip, and the golden drop is the flash.
(9.1.22’) Verily, he who knows the seven honey-sweet things of the whip becomes rich in sweetness.
(9.1.22.c) A Brahmin, a king, a cow, a bull, rice, barley, and honey as the seventh. (9.1.23’) He becomes full of sweetness; his food becomes sweet;
he conquers the worlds that are full of sweetness—he who knows thus. (9.1.23.c) 23.
When it thunders in a cloudless sky, Prajāpati himself manifests for his creatures.
Therefore, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, one should stand and say: "O Prajāpati, awaken me!
For him who knows this, both his offspring and Prajāpati awaken after him. 24. {2}
(9.2.1’) With ghee and with the oblation of clarified butter, I honor the bull, the slayer of rivals, according to my desire.
(9.2.1.c) Being praised, crush my rivals down with your great heroic power!
(9.2.2’) That which is not dear to my mind, that which my eye consumes [sees] but does not welcome—
(9.2.2.c) That evil dream I cast upon my rival; having praised Kāma, may I now break him apart.
(9.2.3’) O Kāma, [cast] the evil dream and misfortune, childlessness, lack of cattle, and destitution; O fierce Lord, cast them back upon him who would plot harm against us.
(9.2.3.c) O fierce Lord, cast them back upon him who would plot harm against us.
(9.2.4’) Drive them away, O Kāma; drive them far away, O Kāma! Let those who are my rivals go to ruin.
When they have been driven down into the lowest darkness, O Agni, do you utterly burn up their dwellings.
(9.2.5’) This daughter of yours, O Kāma, is called the milch-cow, whom the seers call Speech, the Virāj.

(9.2.5.c) With that [power], exclude my rivals; let breath, cattle, and life turn away from them. (9.2.6’) By the power of Kāma, Indra, King Varuṇa, and Viṣṇu, by the might of Savitṛ, and by the office of Agni the Hotṛ, I drive away my rivals, as a skillful steersman drives a boat upon the waters.
(9.2.7’) May my fierce and powerful steed, the overseer, make me truly free from rivals.
(9.2.7.c) May all the gods be my protectors; may all the gods come to this my invocation.
(9.2.8’) Rejoicing in this clarified butter mixed with ghee, you who have Kāma as your chief, take your delight here.
(9.2.8.c) Making [the world] free from rivals for me alone.
||8|| (9.2.9’) O Indra and Agni, having indeed mounted the same chariot at my desire, cause my rivals to fall low;
(9.2.9.c) when they have fallen, O Agni, burn down the dwellings of those lowest of men into the deepest darkness. ||9||
(9.2.10’) “Slay, O Kāma, those who are my rivals; cast them down into blind darkness!

(9.2.10.c) Let them all be deprived of their senses and tasteless; let none of them live for even a single day! (9.2.11’) “Kāma has slain those who were my rivals; he has made for me a wide world to prosper.”
(9.2.11.c) May the four quarters bow down to me; may the six wide expanses bring me ghee.
(9.2.12’) Let them float downward, like a severed boat from its mooring; for those driven away by the arrow, there is no returning again.
(9.2.12.c) For those driven away by the arrow, there is no returning again.
Agni is barley, Indra is barley, Soma is barley.
May the gods, the warders-off of barley, ward him off.
(9.2.14) Let him wander about, deprived of all his heroes, driven away, hated by his friends, and cast out by his own kin.
(9.2.14.c) And when the lightnings descend upon the earth, may your fierce god crush our rivals.
14 (9.2.15’) This *bṛhatī* lightning, both fallen and unfallen, sustains all peals of thunder.
(9.2.15.c) Rising with wealth and splendor, may the powerful Āditya thrust down my rivals. 15

O Kāma, that triple-layered protection of yours which has arisen, that impenetrable *brahman*-armor fashioned for you—by that, exclude my rivals; let breath, cattle, and life itself avoid them. By that [power] with which the gods repelled the Asuras, and by which Indra drove the Dasyus into the deepest darkness.
(9.2.17.c) Therefore, O Kāma, drive my rivals far away from this world.
(17) (9.2.18’) Just as the gods drove out the Asuras, and just as Indra forced the Dasyus into the lowest darkness;
(9.2.18.c) so you, O Kāma, drive my rivals far away from this world. (18)
(9.2.19’) Desire was born first; neither gods, nor ancestors, nor mortals have attained him.
(9.2.19.c) Therefore you are superior and ever great; to you, O Desire, I pay homage.
‖19‖ (9.2.20’) As vast as heaven and earth are in their breadth, as far as the waters flow, as far as fire [reaches]—
(9.2.20.c) Therefore you are greater and ever more mighty; to you, O Kāma, I offer homage.
(9.2.21’) As many as are the quarters, the intermediate directions, and the divergent regions visible from heaven;
(9.2.21.c) therefore you are greater and ever more mighty; to you, O Kāma, I offer homage.
As many as there are bees, bats, and *kurūrava* insects, as many as there are *vaghā* birds and snakes dwelling in trees—from all these you are greater, forever great; to you, O Kāma, I pay homage.
O Kāma, O Manyu, you are greater than that which blinks, you are greater than that which stands still, and you are greater than the ocean.
(9.2.23.c) Therefore you are more excellent and ever-great; to you, O Kāma, I pay homage. (9.2.24’) Indeed, neither the wind attains your desire, nor fire, nor the sun, nor even the moon.
(9.2.24.c) Therefore you are more excellent and ever-great; to you, O Kāma, I pay homage.

(9.2.25’) O Kāma, those auspicious and blessed forms of yours, by which that which you choose becomes true— with those, do you enter into us; drive away evil thoughts elsewhere. ‖25‖ {5} (9.3.1’) That which is measured out, that which is counter-measured, and also that which is fully measured—
(9.3.1.c) We unloosen the bindings of the hall that possesses all boons.

||1|| (9.3.2’) Whatever has been bound upon you, O possessor of all boons—the fetter and the knot that have been made—(9.3.2.c) even as Bṛhaspati, I loosen that with my voice by means of my strength. ||2||
(9.3.3’) He stretched it out, he tore it apart, he made its knots firm;
(9.3.3.c) as one who knows the joints [unties them], so with Indra we loosen [the bonds].
(9.3.4’) Of the bamboo poles, of the bindings, of the girth-rope, and of the straw—
(9.3.4.c) O Viśvavārā, we unfasten the bindings upon your wings.
(9.3.5’) Of the tongs, the straw-mats, and the embrace,
(9.3.5.c) and of this binding of the wife of Māna— we unfasten them all.
(9.3.6’) Those internal loops which they have fastened for the sake of play—those we loosen for you. O Lady of the Mind, be auspicious and well-disposed toward our bodies!
(9.3.7’) The oblation-holder, the fire-hall, the seat of the wives, and the assembly hall.
(9.3.7.c) O divine hall, you are the seat of the gods.
(7) (9.3.8.a) The net, the crest-ornament, spread out with a thousand eyes at the center— (9.3.8.c) that which is bound and fastened, we loosen it by means of sacred prayer. (8)
O House, may he who receives you and he by whom you were measured—
may both of them, O Mistress of the Measuring Line, live to reach old age.
Go to him there, you who are firm, bound, and adorned.
(9.3.10.c) O house, loosen that which is bound of thee, limb by limb, joint by joint. {6} (9.3.11’) He who built thee, O house, has gathered together the lords of the forest;
for the sake of progeny, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati made thee, O house. (9.3.11.c) 11.
Homage to him! We offer homage to the Giver and to the Lord of the House;
homage to Agni who moves forward, and homage to you, O Person!
Homage to the cows and to the horses, and to whatever is born within the house.
(9.3.13.c) O thou who art prolific, o thou who art rich in offspring, we loosen thy snares.
13 (9.3.14’) Thou concealest Agni within, together with men and cattle; (9.3.14.c) O thou who art prolific, o thou who art rich in offspring, we loosen thy snares. 14

With that expanse which lies between heaven and earth, with that I accept this house for you. That which is the intermediate space, the measure of the region, that I make into a belly for my treasures;
with that I accept the house for him. 15.15.15c-e.
(9.3.16) Rich in vigor, rich in milk, measured and built upon the earth—
O house, bearing all kinds of food, do not harm those who receive you! (9.3.17) Covered with grass, clad in straw, like the night, the house is the dwelling place for the world.
(9.3.17.c) Measured, you stand upon the earth like a female elephant with feet.
(9.3.18’) Uncovering it, I loosen for you what was bound fast.
(9.3.18.c) What was pressed down by Varuṇa, may Mitra unbind it in the morning.
The hall built by Brahmā, built and measured out by the seers—
may Indra and Agni protect that hall, the immortal, Soma-like seat.
Nest upon nest, treasury within treasury, it is gathered together.
(9.3.20.c) Therein the mortal is born, from whom all things are produced.
{7} (9.3.21’) That which is built with two sides, four sides, or six sides;
(9.3.21.c) that hall with eight sides or ten sides, the consort of the measuring-cord—Agni lies within it like an embryo. {21}
(9.3.22’) Facing west, O house, I approach you from the west, you who are non-injurious;
for within you are fire and waters—the first gate of Cosmic Order (ṛta).
(9.3.23’) I bring these waters forward, free from disease and destroyers of disease.
(9.3.23.c) I settle down in the houses together with Agni, the immortal.
(9.3.24’) Do not cast a noose upon us; let the heavy burden become light.
O house, we carry you wherever we desire, as one carries a bride.

(9.3.25) From the eastern direction of the hall: homage to the Greatness! Svāhā to the gods to whom svāhā is due! (9.3.26) From the southern direction of the hall: homage to the Greatness! Svāhā to the gods to whom svāhā is due!
(9.3.27) From the western direction of the hall: homage to the Greatness! Svāhā to the gods to whom svāhā is due!

(9.3.28) To the northern direction of the hall, homage to its greatness! Svāhā to the gods, svāhā to those worthy of svāhā! (9.3.29) To the fixed (downward) direction of the hall, homage to its greatness! Svāhā to the gods, svāhā to those worthy of svāhā! (9.3.30) To the upward direction of the hall, homage to its greatness! Svāhā to the gods, svāhā to those worthy of svāhā!
To every direction of the hall, homage to its majesty! Svāhā to the gods who are to be invoked with *svāhā*!

This thousandfold, brilliant bull, rich in milk, bearing all forms within his flanks—bestowing prosperity upon the donor and the sacrificer, the son of Bṛhaspati, the ruddy one, has stretched out the thread of the sacrifice.
(9.4.2’) He who has become the counterpart of the waters, O Agni, the master over all like the goddess Earth;
(9.4.2.c) the father of calves, the lord of the cows—may he grant us increase by the thousands.
(9.4.3’) A man, full within, firm, rich in milk—the bull bears the vessel of wealth.

(9.4.3.c) May Agni Jātavedas carry him, who has been offered, to Indra by the paths traveled by the gods. ||3|| (9.4.4’) He is the father of calves, the lord of the cows; he is also the father of the great *gargara* vessels. (9.4.4.c) The calf, the afterbirth, the fresh milk, the colostrum, the curd-mixture, and the clarified butter—these indeed are his seed. ||4||
This is the portion of the gods, this is the grudge, the essence of the waters, of the plants, and of the clarified butter.
Śakra chose the draught of Soma; his body became the great pressing-stone.
(5) You carry the jar filled with Soma; you are Tvaṣṭṛ, the fashioner of forms and the progenitor of cattle. (6)
(9.4.6.c) May these female creatures here be auspicious to you; O Svadhiti, bestow upon us those which are these, and those which are yonder.
(9.4.7.a) He bears the goat; his seed is ghee; they call him thousandfold nourishment and that sacrifice.
(9.4.7.c) The bull, wearing the form of Indra—may he, the auspicious one, come to us, O gods, as a gift.
The vigor of Indra, the two arms of Varuṇa, the shoulders of the Aśvins, and this hump belong to the Maruts.
Those who are wise, the seers, and the learned say that he has been brought together as Bṛhaspati.
You, rich in milk, extend yourself as the divine clans; they call you Indra, they call you Sarasvant.
(9.4.9.c) He who, as a Brahmin, offers up a bull as a sacrifice, bestows a thousand [cows] with a single mouth.
(9.4.10’) Bṛhaspati and Savitṛ have bestowed vital strength upon you; from Tvaṣṭṛ and Vāyu your very self has been brought hither.
(9.4.10.c) With my mind I offer you into the intermediate space; may both Heaven and Earth be your sacrificial grass.
(9.4.11’) May the Brahman priest extol with auspicious praise the limbs of that bull who, like Indra among the gods, goes about bellowing loudly for the sake of cattle.
(9.4.12’) Let there be two sides belonging to Anumati; let there be two flanks belonging to Bhaga.
(9.4.12.c) Mitra said of the two knee-bones: "These belong to me alone.
(9.4.13’) The buttocks belonged to the Ādityas; the two hips belonged to Bṛhaspati.
(9.4.13.c) The tail belongs to the god Vāta; with it he shakes the plants.
The intestines were those of Sinīvālī; they said the skin belonged to Sūryā.
They said the foot of the one who rises was that of the bull when they fashioned [the sacrifice].
The breast was that of the one who reviles his kin; the vessel for Soma was held firm.
(9.4.15.c) When all the gods had come together, they fashioned [the bull] into a sacrificial victim. (9.4.16’) They gave the dewclaws to Saramā and the hooves to the tortoises;
(9.4.16.c) they assigned his undigested food to the insects and the worms to the dogs.
With his two horns he strikes down the Rakṣas; with his eye he destroys misfortune.
With his two ears he hears what is auspicious—he who is the inviolable lord of cows.
He performs a hundredfold sacrifice; the fires do not consume him.
(9.4.18.c) All the gods favor him who offers a bull to a Brahmin.
(9.4.19’) Having given a bull to the Brahmins, he makes his mind more expansive; (9.4.19.c) he beholds the prosperity of his cows within his own pen.
May there be cattle, may there be progeny, and may there be bodily strength;
may the gods grant all that to the giver of the bull.
May this Indra, having drunk, bestow upon us conscious wealth.

(9.4.21.c) This one, beyond the sky, milks the well-yielding cow that has her calf ever-present—the cow that grants all desires and is possessed of wisdom. (9.4.22’) Tawny-hued, bestowing vigor from the atmosphere, the all-formed impetus of Indra has come to us. Granting us long life and progeny, may he attend to us with the increase of wealth.
Mix us here with nourishment in this cow-pen;
mix us with the seed of the bull, O Indra, which is your own virility.
We place this youth among you; sporting with him, move about according to your will.

(9.4.24.c) Do not abandon us, O you who are blessed by birth; attend to us with the increase of wealth! 24 {10} (9.5.1’) Lead him here; take hold of him! May he go to the world of the righteous, knowing the way.
(9.5.1.c) Having crossed through the many great darknesses, may the goat ascend to the third heaven. 1

(9.5.2’) “I lead you around as a portion for Indra, for the patron at this sacrifice, as a wise seer. (9.5.2.c) Those who hate us—seize them! May the heroes of the sacrificer be free from sin. (9.5.3’) “Wash away the tracks, [erasing] whatever evil deed has been committed; treading with clean hooves, may he come forward, knowing the way.”
(9.5.3.c) Having crossed over the darknesses and seeing clearly in many ways, may the Unborn One ascend to the third heaven.
(9.5.4’) O dissector, having peeled off this dark skin, cut it joint by joint with the knife; do not disregard it.
Do not harm it; fashion it limb by limb and place it upon the third heaven.
(9.5.5’) With a verse I place the pot upon the fire; pour in the water, set it down.
(9.5.5.c) Let the immolators surround it with fire; let it go forth as a libation to where the world of the righteous is.
(9.5.6’) If one has not heated it thoroughly while heating it, let him heat it over the third cauldron until it reaches the firmament.
(9.5.6.c) From fire you have arisen as fire; conquer this world that is full of light!

(9.5.7’) They say that Agni is unborn, that light is unborn, and they say that what belongs to the living Brahman is unborn. (9.5.7.c) The unborn [goat] drives away the darkness far away when it is given in this world by one who has faith. (7)
May the fivefold rice-offering, about to stride forth, step out in five ways toward the three lights.
Go to the midst of those who have sacrificed and performed good deeds; take your station upon the third firmament.
O goat, ascend to where the world of the righteous is; like a *śarabha*, he shall pass unharmed over all difficulties.
(9.5.9.c) The five-rice-offering, when given to a Brahmin, satisfies the giver with satisfaction.
(9.5.10’) The goat places the donor upon the three-fold vault, the triple heaven, the triple-backed ridge of the firmament.
(9.5.10.c) The five-rice-offering, when given to a Brahmin, is one cow of all forms that milks every desire. {11}
(9.5.11’) This is your third light, O Fathers; he gives to the Brahman a goat with five portions of rice.
(9.5.11.c) The goat, when given in this world by one who has faith, drives away the darkness far away.
(9.5.12’) Desiring the world of those who have sacrificed and performed good deeds, he gives to the Brahman a goat with five portions of rice.
(9.5.12.c) May he, pervading the world, conquer this; may he be auspicious to us when accepted.
‖12‖ (9.5.13’) For the Unborn was born from the heat of Agni, the sage from the sage, the wise one from strength.
(9.5.13.c) May the gods, according to the seasons, ordain that which is sacrificed, fulfilled, fully accomplished, and consecrated with *vaṣaṭ*. ‖13‖
One should give unsoiled clothing and gold as a sacrificial fee;
thus one attains those worlds, both celestial and terrestrial.
May these divine, Soma-like streams flow toward us—streams with ghee on their backs, dripping with honey.

(9.5.15.c) You have propped up the earth and the sky upon the back of the firmament, on the seven-rayed [vault]. (9.5.16’) You are the Unborn; you are the heavenly world of the Unborn.
