O Agni, with that [power] by which you carry a thousand, and with which you carry all wealth, with that,
carry this sacrifice of ours to the light so that it may go among the gods.
The cooked goat, consisting of five portions of rice, establishes [the sacrificer] in the heavenly world, driving away destruction.
(9.5.18.c) By that may we conquer the worlds possessed of the sun.

||18|| (9.5.19’) That which was placed in the Brahmin and that which was placed among the people, those drops of the cooked rice of the Unborn—(9.5.19.c) may Agni know all that of us in the world of good deeds, at the meeting-place of our paths. ||19||
(9.5.20’) O Agni, the Unborn indeed strode forth across this [world]. Of him, this earth became the chest, and the sky the back.
The intermediate region was the middle, the quarters were the sides, and the two oceans were the belly.
(9.5.21’) Truth and Order were his two eyes; the All is truth, faith is the breath, and the Virāj is the head.

(9.5.21.c) This, indeed, is the immeasurable sacrifice, namely the goat with five portions of rice. (9.5.22’) He who gives a goat with five portions of rice as a sacrificial fee attains the immeasurable sacrifice and wins the immeasurable world.
(9.5.22.c) He who gives a goat with five portions of rice, illuminated by the sacrificial fee.
One should not break his bones, nor should one extract the marrow.
Taking him whole, one should cause him to enter this and that.
This and that indeed becomes his form; by means of that, one unites him with it.
(9.5.24.c) For him who gives a goat with five portions of rice, radiant with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the earth milks forth nourishment, greatness, and vigor.
(9.5.25’) For him who gives a goat with five portions of rice, radiant with sacrificial fees, there are five gold ornaments, five new garments, and five cows that yield all desires.
Five golden ornaments become light for him; garments become armor for his body.
He who gives a goat with five portions of cooked rice, whose light is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), attains the heavenly world.
She who, having first found a husband, then finds another man later—
(9.5.27.c) And those two who give a goat together with fivefold cooked rice shall not be separated.
(9.5.28’) He becomes a sharer of the same world with her who is born again as his wife—(9.5.28.c) he who gives a goat with fivefold cooked rice, which has the sacrificial fee as its light. (28)
Having given a cow whose calf is of the same age, a draft-ox, a pillow, a garment, and gold, they go to the highest heaven. [They lead] themselves,
their father, their son, their grandson, and their grandfather.
I invoke those who are dear: the wife, the progenitor, and the mother.
(30) O Naidāgha, he who knows the season named Naidāgha—this goat with five portions of rice is indeed the season named Naidāgha. (31)
(9.5.31.e) He utterly burns away the prosperity of his unpleasant rival and prospers by himself.
(9.5.32’) Verily, he who knows the season named "Acting" takes away, as it were, the ever-acting prosperity of his unpleasant rival.
(9.5.32.e) This season is indeed named "Acting," which is the goat with five portions of rice.
(9.5.33’) He who knows the season named "Conjoining" seizes, again and again, the fortune of his hostile rival as he is being conjoined.
(9.5.33.e) This indeed is the season named Saṃyat, which is the goat with five portions of cooked rice.
(9.5.34’) Verily, he who knows the season named Pinvant makes swell after swelling the fortune of his hateful rival.
(9.5.34.e) This season, indeed, is named Pinvan, which is the goat with five portions of cooked rice. (9.5.35’) He who knows the season named Udyant [the Rising]—
verily, at every rising, he takes away the fortune of his hateful rival.
(9.5.35.e) This season, indeed, is named "Rising," which is the goat with five portions of rice.
(9.5.36’) He who knows the season named "Overpowering" overpowers the prosperity of his hateful rival again and again.
(9.5.36.e) This season, indeed, is named Abhibhū, which is the goat with five portions of cooked rice.
(9.5.37’) Cook the goat and the five portions of cooked rice.
(9.5.37.c) May all the quarters, being of one mind and united, together with the intermediate regions, accept this from you. ||37||
(9.5.38’) May they protect you; for you, for your sake, I offer this oblation of clarified butter to them.
‖38‖ (9.6.1’) He who knows Brahman as directly perceived—he whose joints are the ritual requisites, whose spine is the *ṛc* verses;
‖1‖ (9.6.2’) Whose body hairs are the *sāmans*, whose heart is said to be the *yajus*, and whose sacrificial strewing is the oblation. ‖2‖
When the host of guests looks upon the guests, he gazes upon the place of sacrifice.
When he greets them, he enters the consecration; when he asks for water, he leads forward the waters.
Those very waters that are led forward in the sacrifice are these same ones.
(9.6.6) That which they bring as a libation is indeed that very animal victim bound for Agni and Soma.
(9.6.7) When they prepare the guest-quarters, they are thereby preparing the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds.
(9.6.8) What they spread out is the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) itself.
When they bring a raised couch, by that he wins the heavenly world.
(9.6.9) When they bring a coverlet and a pillow, these are the enclosing sticks.
(9.6.10) When they bring ointment and salve, that is indeed clarified butter. (9.6.11)
(9.6.12) Those two which they bring for tasting before the serving [of the food] are indeed the two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).
(9.6.13) When they call out "one who has prepared the meal," they are indeed calling out "one who has prepared the oblation" (*haviṣkṛt*).
(9.6.14) Those rice grains and barley grains that are poured out are indeed the *aṃśu* stalks.
(9.6.15) Those which are the mortars and pestles are indeed the pressing-stones.
(15) (9.6.16) The winnowing-basket is the filter; the husks are the dregs, and the waters are those for the pressing.

(16) (9.6.17) The offering-ladle is the spoon, the stirring-stick is the mixing-vessel, the wooden troughs are the jars, the Vāyu-cups are the vessels, and this very earth is the black antelope skin. (17) {15}

When the host of guests looks at the things to be brought forth, saying, "Let this be more! Let that be more!", he thereby performs the role of the *yajamāna-brāhmaṇa*. When he says, "Bring out more!", he thereby makes his vital breath (*prāṇa*) more abundant.
He brings the oblations near and sets them down.
When they have arrived as guests, he offers them into his own self.
(21) With the *sruc* as the hand, into the breath as the sacrificial post, with the *sruk-kāra* as the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
(22) These indeed—whether dear or not dear—are the officiating priests who cause one to go to the heavenly world, namely the guests. (23)
He who, knowing this, does not eat while feeling aversion, nor eats the food of one who feels aversion toward him, nor of one who is suspected, nor of one who is currently suspecting—
every such person has indeed consumed all evil, for they eat the food of one whose evil has been devoured.
(9.6.26) Or rather, he whose food others do not eat is entirely one who has not consumed evil.
(9.6.27) He who offers [food] is indeed always one whose pressing-stones are joined, whose strainers are moist, whose sacrifice is spread out, and whose sacrificial rite is brought forward.
(9.6.28) The sacrifice of him who offers is indeed extended as that of Prajāpati.
He who serves food follows the strides of Prajāpati.
He who is among guests is the Āhavanīya fire; he who is in the house is the Gārhapatya fire; that in which they cook is the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.
He who eats before the guest eats the merit of both the sacrifice and the charitable works of the household.
He who eats before his guest eats the milk and the essence of the household.
(32) He who eats before his guest eats the vigor and the abundance of the household.
(33) He who eats before his guest eats the progeny and the cattle of the household. (34)
He who eats before the guest eats up the fame and glory of the household;
he who eats before the guest eats up the prosperity and harmony of the household. A true guest is indeed one learned in the Vedas; therefore, one should not eat before him.
(9.6.38’) When the guest has eaten, he himself should eat for the sake of the integrity of the sacrifice and the non-interruption of the sacrifice; that is the vow.
(9.6.39’) Indeed, this is even more delicious: milk from a cow that has recently calved or meat; yet one should not eat that very thing.
(9.6.40’) He who, knowing thus, pours out milk and offers it—
(9.6.40.c) As much as one obtains by sacrificing with a well-performed Agniṣṭoma, so much does one obtain by this [offering].
(9.6.41’) He who, knowing thus, offers it after pouring clarified butter over it—
(9.6.41.c) as much as one obtains by sacrificing with a well-performed Atirātra, so much does one obtain by this [offering].
He who, knowing thus, offers honey after pouring it over [the food], wins as much as one wins by performing the Sattrasadya sacrifice when it is well-prosperous; so much does he win by this means.
He who, knowing thus, offers meat after pouring it over [the food]...
(9.6.43.c) As much as one obtains by sacrificing with a very prosperous twelve-day rite, so much does he obtain by this [offering].
(9.6.44’) He who, knowing thus, pours out water and presents it, goes for the procreation of offspring; he becomes dear to his offspring, he who, knowing thus, pours out water and presents it. (18)
For him, Uṣas makes the sound *hiṃ*; Savitṛ chants the prelude;
Bṛhaspati sings with vigor; Tvaṣṭṛ responds with nourishment; the All-Gods are the finale. 2.

(9.6.45.e) He who knows this becomes the final resting place of prosperity, progeny, and cattle. (9.6.46’) For him, as the sun rises, it makes the sound *hiṅ*; at the time of gathering [the cows], it chants the *prastāva*; at midday, it sings the *udgītha*; in the afternoon, it performs the *pratihāra*; and as it sets, it is the *nidhana*.
(9.6.46.e) He who knows this becomes the final resting place of prosperity, offspring, and cattle.
(9.6.47’) For him, becoming a cloud, he utters *hiṅ*; thundering, he performs the *pra-stuti*;
lightning, he performs the *pratihāra*; raining, he sings the *udgītha*; and ceasing to rain, he performs the *nidhana*.
(9.6.47.e) He who knows this becomes the final resting place of prosperity, progeny, and cattle.
(9.6.48’) For he looks toward his guests; he utters "hiṅ"; he addresses them; he praises them; he asks for water; he sings the *udgītha*;
he brings food near; he offers it back; the remnants are the *nidhana*.
(9.6.48.e) He who knows this becomes the foundation of prosperity, progeny, and cattle.
||48|| {19} (9.6.48’) When he calls the *kṣattṛ*, he is indeed causing [the announcement] to be heard. ||49|| (9.6.50’) When he responds, he is indeed causing the response to be heard. ||50||
Those who approach from the front and from behind with vessels in their hands as servers are indeed the *camasādhvaryu* priests. Among them, no one is the *hotṛ*.
When the master of the guests, having served the guests, goes toward his own house, he thereby enters the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
That which he shares out, he shares out as sacrificial gifts; that which he performs, he thereby concludes with the *udavasānīyā* offering.
(54) Invited, he partakes [of the Soma] upon the earth; invited, he partakes of whatever is of manifold form upon the earth.
(55) Invited, he partakes [of the Soma] in the intermediate space; invited, he partakes of whatever is of manifold form in the sky. (56)
Invited, he partakes in heaven; invited, he partakes in that which is of manifold form in heaven.
Invited, he partakes among the gods; invited, he partakes in that which is of manifold form in heaven.
Invited, he partakes in the worlds; invited, he partakes in that which is of manifold form in heaven.
(9.6.60’) He is invited; he is invited.
(60) (9.6.61’) He attains this world; he attains that world. (61) (9.6.62’) He who knows thus conquers the worlds of light. (62) {20}

Prajāpati and Parameṣṭhin are the two horns; Indra is the head; Agni is the forehead; Yama is the nape of the neck. (9.7.2) King Soma is the brain; the sky is the upper jaw; the earth is the lower jaw.
(9.7.3) The lightning is the tongue; the Maruts are the teeth; Revatī is the neck; the Kṛttikās are the shoulders; the Gharma is the back.

Vāyu is the universe, the heavenly world; Kṛṣṇadram is the supporter, the place to be entered. (4) Śyena is the purchased one, the intermediate space; Pājasya is Bṛhaspati, the hump; the Bṛhatī meters are the vertebrae. (5) The wives of the gods are the ribs; the Upasads are the side-flesh. (6)

Mitra and Varuṇa are the shoulders; Tvaṣṭṛ and Aryaman are the forearms; Mahādeva is the two arms. (9.7.8) Indrāṇī is the buttocks; Vāyu is the tail; Pavamāna is the hair. (9.7.9) Brahman and Kṣatra are the hips; strength is the thighs.
Dhātṛ and Savitṛ are the two knee-bones; the Gandharvas and Apsarases are the shanks; Aditi is the hooves. (10) The mind is the heart; wisdom is the liver; the sacred vow is the pericardium.
(11) Hunger is the belly; food is the rectum; the mountains are the kidneys. (12)
Anger is the two kidneys; indignation is the testicles; progeny is the penis.
(13) The river is the urethra; the lords of rain are the breasts; thunder is the udder. (14) Viśvavyacas is the skin; the plants are the body hair; the stars are the form. (15)
The divine folk are the intestines, human beings the entrails; here, the belly is the waters.
(16) The Rakṣases are the blood, the people of the other world the undigested food in the stomach. (17) The cloud is the fat, the marrow is the Nidhana. (18)
Agni is seated; the Aśvins are standing.
Indra stands facing east; Yama stands facing south. Dhātṛ stands facing west; Savitṛ stands facing north.
(9.7.22’) Soma the King has reached the grass.
(22) (9.7.23’) Mitra, looking on, has turned back as bliss.
(23) (9.7.24’) Being yoked, he belongs to all the gods; when yoked, he is Prajāpati; when released, he is everything. (24)
(9.7.25) This, indeed, is the omniform, the all-formed, the form of the cow.
(9.7.26) Multiform and all-formed cattle attend upon him who knows thus.
{21} (9.8.1) [The remedy for] headache, for disease of the head, for earache, and for blood-letting.

(9.8.1.c) We drive out by means of sacred speech all disease from your head. ||1|| (9.8.2’) From both your ears, from the hollows of your ears, the ear-ache and the piercing pain— (9.8.2.c) We drive out by means of sacred speech all disease from your head. ||2||
For whose sake the wasting disease departs from the ear and from the mouth—
every ailment of yours that is located in the head, we charm it away to the outside.
That which makes a man deaf, which makes him blind—
(9.8.4.c) We drive forth from you all disease of the head with our sacred spell.
(9.8.5.a) The breaking of the limbs, the fever of the limbs, the ailment that pervades every limb, the creeping sore—
(9.8.5.c) we drive forth from you all disease of the head with our sacred spell.
(9.8.6) That which, resembling Bhīma, causes a person to tremble—
that *takman* which is all-autumnal, we exorcise outwards with our spells.
(9.8.7) That which creeps along the thighs and likewise goes to the groins—
(9.8.7.c) We drive the consumption away from within your limbs to the outside.
(9.8.8’) If it arises from desire, from lack of desire, or from the heart— (9.8.8.c) we drive the swelling from the heart and from the limbs to the outside.
(9.8.9) We drive the jaundice from your limbs, the swelling from within your belly; we banish the seat of consumption from within your self to the outside.
(9.8.10) Let the *āsas* become *balāsa*; let it become urine; let it become disease.
(9.8.10.c) I have uttered forth from you the poison of all consumptive diseases. 10 (9.8.11’) Let the *kāhābāha* run out through the external opening from your belly.
(9.8.11.c) I have uttered forth from you the poison of all consumptive diseases. 11

From your belly, from your lungs, from your navel, and from your heart— from you, I have uttered forth the poison of all consumptive diseases. Those [diseases] which shatter the suture of the skull and flow toward the head.
(9.8.13.c) Let them flow out through the opening, unharmed and healthy.
||13|| (9.8.14’) Those that flow toward the heart and spread along the ribs— (9.8.14.c) Let them flow out through the opening, unharmed and healthy. ||14||
Those that flow along the sides and descend upon the ribs—
let them, non-violent and free from disease, flow out through the external opening.
Those transverse channels that flow into your flanks— let them flow forth.

(9.8.16.c) Let them flow out from the hole, harmless and free from disease. (9.8.17’) Those worms that crawl along the intestines and cause confusion in the entrails— (9.8.17.c) Let them flow out from the hole, harmless and free from disease.
Those [worms] which suck out the marrow and tear apart the joints—
let them flow out through the opening, harmless and healthy.
Those wasting diseases (*yakṣmāsaḥ*) of yours that cause suppuration and madden the limbs— [let them flow out...]
(9.8.19.c) I have uttered forth from you the poison of all consumptive diseases.
19 (9.8.20’) Of the spreading sore, of the abscess, of the wind-swell, and of the eruption;
(9.8.20.c) I have uttered forth from you the poison of all consumptive diseases. 20
From your feet, from your knees, from your hips and from your loins,
from your spine, from your channels, and from the *uṣṇihā* joints of your head— I have destroyed the disease.
May the fragments of your skull and whatever disorder is within your heart be gathered together.
(9.8.22.c) Rising with your rays, O Āditya, you have destroyed the disease of the head; you have stilled the pain in the limbs.
‖22‖ {23} (9.9.1’) Of this lovely, gray-haired Hotṛ-priest, his middle brother is Aśna.
(9.9.1.c) His third brother has ghee upon his back; here I beheld the Lord of the People (*viśpati*) who has seven sons. ‖1‖
Seven yoke the one-wheeled chariot; a single horse, bearing seven names, draws it.
The wheel has three naves, is undecaying and invincible, upon which all these worlds stand.
Upon this seven-wheeled chariot stand the seven; seven horses draw it.
(9.9.3.c) Seven sisters cry out together toward that place where the seven names of the cows are deposited.
(9.9.4’) Who has seen the first-born, when the boneless one supports that which possesses bones?
Where indeed is the life-force, the breath, and the blood of the earth? Who shall go to the wise man to ask this? 4.
(9.9.5’) Let him who truly knows declare here the hidden track of this lovely bird.
From its head the cows milk forth milk; clothed in their covering, they have reached the water with their feet.
(9.9.6’) Being simple-minded and lacking understanding in my mind, I ask about these tracks laid down by the gods.
(9.9.6.c) Over the heifer and the calf, the seers have stretched out seven threads to be woven.

(9.9.7.a) Being myself ignorant, I ask here the wise seers who know, like one who knows not asking those who know: (9.9.7.c) "What indeed is that One, in the form of the Unborn, who has propped apart these six worlds?"

(9.9.8’) The mother shared in the Father according to the *ṛta*; for she first united with him in her mind. Loathing the flow of the embryo, she was pierced; then those full of reverence approached her with their invocation.
(9.9.9’) You were the Mother yoked to the pole of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); the embryo stood within the enclosures.
(9.9.9.c) The calf lowed; he beheld the cow of all forms in the three unions.

9 (9.9.10’) Bearing three mothers and three fathers, the one stood erect; they did not cause him to weary. (9.9.10.c) On the back of yonder heaven, those who know all converse in speech that is unknown to all. 10 {24}

(9.9.11) Upon the five-spoked wheel as it revolves, on which all worlds are supported—its axle, though bearing a heavy burden, does not grow hot; from of old its nave has never been severed. (9.9.12) They call him the Father, five-footed and twelve-formed, rich in moisture, dwelling in the highest half of heaven.
(9.9.12.c) Now others say it is fixed upon another, the far-seeing one, with seven wheels and six spokes.
(9.9.13.a) That wheel of Order rolls around the sky; it has twelve spokes and does not decay.
(9.9.13.c) Here, O Agni, seventy-two pairs of sons have taken their stand.
The unaging wheel, with its rim, has rolled forth; ten yoked [horses] carry it upon the outstretched [earth].
The eye of Sūrya moves through the mid-air, encompassing that in which all beings have taken their stand.
Though they are women, they call them men to me; he who has eyes sees, yet the blind man does not perceive.
(9.9.15.c) He who is the son, the seer, has perceived this; he who understands these things shall be the father of his father.
(9.9.16’) Of those born together, they say the seventh is born alone; the six are called twins, the seers born of the gods.
Their desired abodes are established according to their stations; though transformed, they tremble in their various forms.

Beneath the upper realm, above this lower one, the Cow has risen, bearing her calf upon her foot. Whitherward has she gone? To which region has she departed? Where indeed will she bring forth her young, for she is not in this herd?
Beneath the upper realm, he who knows his Father—beyond the upper, above the lower.
(9.9.18.c) Who here, acting as a seer, has declared from whence the divine mind was born?
(9.9.19’) Those which they call "hitherward," they call "thitherward"; those which they call "thitherward," they call "hitherward.
O Indra and Soma, those things which you two have fashioned carry [the world] like yoked horses at the pole of the firmament.
Two birds, united as companions, cling to the same tree.
Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating.
On that tree where all the honey-eating birds settle and nest, they abide.
(9.9.21.c) As for that which they call the sweet fig at the top, it shall not reach him who does not know his father.
(9.9.22’) Where the birds, partaking of the food of immortality, ever-vigilant, sing together in the assembly—therein this wise guardian of the entire world has entered me, the simple one.
(9.9.22.c) Therein this wise guardian of the entire world has entered me, the simple one. {25}
That which is the Gāyatra placed upon the Gāyatra, or the Triṣṭubh fashioned from the Triṣṭubh;
or that foot of the Jagatī which is placed upon the Jagatī—those who know this have attained immortality.
With the Gāyatra he measures out the hymn (*arka*); with the hymn, the Sāman; with the Triṣṭubh, the word (*vāka*).
With the *vāka* they measure out the *vāka*, with the two-footed and four-footed, and with the syllable; they fashion the seven voices.
(9.10.2.c) With the *jagatī* he propped up the celestial river, and in the *rathantara* he beheld the sun.
They say there are three kindling-sticks of the *gāyatrī*; therefore it excels by its greatness and its majesty. (9.10.3)
I invoke this well-milking cow; may the skillful milker milk her.
May Savitar impel for us the most excellent impulse. The Gharma has been heated; let him proclaim that clearly.
Lowing, she who is the mistress of treasures has come toward us, seeking her calf with her mind.

(9.10.5.c) May this inviolable cow yield milk for the Aśvins; may she prosper for our great good fortune. (9.10.6’) The cow has lowed toward her blinking calf; she has made the "hiṅ" sound at his head to measure him out. Lowing toward the warm milk, she utters her cry; she yields milk with her streams of milk.
(9.10.6.c) Longing for the warm milk, she bellows her lowing sound; she yields milk with her streams of milk.
This is that which bellows, by which the cow is encompassed; she lowing like a wild beast rests upon the cleft of the earth.
By her thoughts she has indeed surpassed mortals; becoming lightning, she cast off her covering.
The swift-moving one has gone to rest; the living, the throbbing, the firm one lies in the midst of the dwellings.
(9.10.8.c) The immortal life-force of the dead moves on by means of funeral offerings; it shares a common womb with the mortal.
(9.10.9’) The grey-haired one has swallowed the young moon as it hastens across the back of the waters. Behold the poetic wisdom of the god in its greatness: he who died today was alive yesterday.
He who made this does not know it; he who saw it is far removed from it.
Enveloped within his mother’s womb, he who has many offspring—Nirṛti has entered him.
I beheld the Herdsman, who never rests, moving hither and thither along his paths.
Wearing garments that flow together and those that spread apart, he revolves repeatedly within the worlds.
Heaven is our father, our progenitor; here our navel is fixed. This great earth is our kin, our mother.
Between the two upturned bowls lies the womb; therein the father deposited the seed within his daughter.
I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth; I ask about the seed of the stallion.
I ask about the navel of the entire world; I ask about the highest heaven of speech.
This altar is the furthest limit of the earth; this Soma is the seed of the stallion.
(9.10.14.c) This sacrifice is the navel of the entire world; this Brahman is the supreme vault of speech.

(9.10.15’) I do not discern what this is that I am; hidden and girt with the mind, I move about. When the first-born of Order come to me, then indeed I obtain a share of this speech. (9.10.15.c) When the first-born of Order come to me, then indeed I obtain a share of this speech.
Moving westward and eastward, he goes, held by his own power; the immortal one shares a common womb with the mortal.
These two, eternal and moving in opposite directions, pass along; people perceive the one, but they do not perceive the other.
Seven half-embryos, the seed of the world, abide in the supporting structure by the command of Viṣṇu.
(9.10.17.c) They, through their insights and with their minds, being wise and all-encompassing, surround everything on every side.
(9.10.18’) In the syllable of the Ṛgveda, in the highest heaven, upon which all the gods have settled;
he who does not know that—what will he do with the Ṛgveda? But those who know it, they sit together here. (9.10.18.c) 18.
Fashioning the word of the *ṛc* by means of its measure, they formed with the half-verse all that moves.
The three-footed Brahman, assuming many forms, has spread itself abroad; by it the four quarters of space live.
(19) O blessed one, may you indeed have good pasture; and may we likewise be blessed. (20)
(9.10.20.c) Eat grass, O inviolable one, at all times; drink pure water as you come hither.
(9.10.21’) The Cow has lowed, fashioning the waters; she is one-footed, two-footed, four-footed;
she has become eight-footed, nine-footed, possessing a thousand syllables—the fivefold array of the world. From her the oceans flow forth.
The bay steeds with beautiful wings, clothed in water, fly up to heaven along the black path.
They have returned from the seat of Cosmic Order; indeed, they have spread the earth with ghee.
22 She who is footless goes forth as the first among those that have feet. O Mitra and Varuṇa, who among you perceives this? 23
(9.10.23.c) The embryo bears the burden; indeed, it fulfills his *ṛta* and guards against *anṛta*.
(9.10.24’) Virāj is speech, Virāj is the earth, Virāj is the intermediate space, Virāj is Prajāpati.
Virāj became Death, the sovereign lord of the Sādhyas. Under his control are the past and the future; may he bring the past and the future under my control.
I saw from afar the smoke of Śaka, rising straight upward above the lower regions.
The heroes cooked the dappled bull; those were the first ordinances. 25.25.25–26ab (9.10.25–26ab)
Three long-haired ones appear in due season; one of them shears his hair within the year.
Another beholds the universe with his powers; the speed of the third is seen, but not his form.
Speech has been measured out in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them.
(9.10.27.c) Three [aspects] hidden in the cave do not stir; mortals speak only the fourth part of speech.
(9.10.28’) They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni; and he is the divine, fair-winged Garuḍa.
Being one, the sages call him by many names; they call him Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan. (28)
That which the healers fashion like a bride on her bridal litter— multiformed, wrought by hand—
that we drive away from its very essence.
Headed, nose-possessing, ear-possessing, fashioned as a sorcery, assembled, multiformed— [we drive it away].
(10.1.2.c) Having reached her core, let us drive her away!

(10.1.3’) Whether wrought by a Śūdra, wrought by a king, wrought by a woman, or wrought by Brahmins—let her, like a wife driven away by her husband, seize the doer as her kinsman! (10.1.3.c) Let her seize the doer as her kinsman! 3.
By means of this herb, I have caused all sorceries (*kṛtyā*) to fail—those which they have performed in the field, those in the cattle, or those in your men.
Let there be evil for the evildoer; let the curse recoil upon him who utters the curse.
(10.1.5.c) We send it back against [them], so that it may destroy the one who performed the *kṛtyā*.
(10.1.6’) Facing westward, the descendant of Aṅgiras, our overseer and domestic priest, (10.1.6.c) [sends] the *kṛtyās* back; strike down those performers of the *kṛtyā*.
(10.1.7’) But as for him who said to you, "Go away," speaking contrary to what is right—turn against that one in your purpose; do not seek us, who are innocent.
(10.1.8’) He who has joined together your joints with wisdom, like a craftsman [forges] a chariot—
(10.1.8.c) Go to him; there is your path. This person here is unknown to you.
(10.1.9’) Those wise practitioners of sorcery who, having seized you, bound you— (10.1.9.c) With this auspicious remedy for neutralizing magic, which turns back and follows after, we bathe you.
Whatever ill fortune we have encountered from one who has been bathed for purification, or from one whose offspring has died—let all that evil depart from me; let wealth abide with me!
Whatever name they have taken for you when giving to the ancestors or at the sacrifice—[may it be auspicious].
(10.1.11.c) May these plants release you from every sin that has been designated.

‖11‖ (10.1.12’) From sin against the gods, from that against the ancestors, from that which is named, from that which is designated, and from that which is manifest—(10.1.12.c) may the plants release you by their power, by the sacred word, by the *ṛc*-verses, and by the milk of the seers. ‖12‖
Just as the wind shakes the dust from the earth and the cloud from the atmosphere,
even so shall all ill fortune driven away by the *brahman* depart from me.
Step aside, crying out like a tethered she-ass!
(10.1.14.c) Strike down the doers; they have been driven away by the heroic Brahman.
(10.1.15’) “This is the path,” we lead you [saying], toward the one sent forth; we send you against her.
(10.1.15.c) With that, go forth, breaking through like a wagon-drawing train—multiform and full of activity.

(10.1.16’) Far away is your light; turn your path hitherward. Make for us a way other than this. (10.1.16.c) Go beyond the ninety navigable rivers; pass over the difficult streams; do not harm us; go away!
(10.1.17’) Like the wind to the trees, crush them down and bring them low. Spare neither cow, nor horse, nor man among them.

(10.1.17.c) Turn back the sorcerers from this rite; awaken them to childlessness! (10.1.18’) Whatever spell or secret charm they have buried for you upon the sacrificial grass, in the cemetery, or in the field; or whatever they have practiced against you in the *gārhapatya* fire—those more clever ones, while you were innocent and simple-minded. (10.1.18.c) [May they be turned back. (10.1.18’) Whatever spell or secret charm they have buried for you upon the sacrificial grass, in the cemetery, or in the field; or whatever they have practiced against you in the *gārhapatya* fire—those more clever ones, while you were innocent and simple-minded. (10.1.18.c) [May they be turned back. (10.1.18’) Whatever spell or secret charm they have buried for you upon the sacrificial grass, in the cemetery, or in the field; or whatever they have practiced against you in the *gārhapatya* fire—those more clever ones, while you were innocent and simple-minded. (10.1.18.c) [May they be turned back. The enmity that was brought forward, recognized, buried, and driven deep—we have found the one who wrought it.
Let it go back to where it was brought from; let it turn back like a horse and slay the offspring of the sorcerers.
In our house there are axes with iron blades; we know your joints, O sorcery, in all their many ways.
(10.1.20.c) Arise! Go away from here! O Unknown One, what do you desire here?
‖20‖ (10.1.21’) I shall cut off your necks, O Kṛtyā, and your feet as well; run away!
(10.1.21.c) May Indra and Agni protect us, they who are the progenitors of living beings. ‖21‖
May King Soma, the sovereign, and the gracious lords of all beings be merciful to us.
May Bhava and Śarva cast their lightning bolt, the weapon of the gods, upon the evildoer, the performer of sorcery, and the doer of wickedness.
Whether you have come as a two-footed or a four-footed creature, fashioned by magic, gathered together, and possessing every form—
becoming eight-footed, O bringer of misfortune, go back again! Anointed, smeared, adorned with beauty, and carrying all evil away, go back!

(10.1.25.c) Know that the doer of a service is like a daughter toward her own father. (10.1.26’) Go away, O service; do not stay. Follow the track of one who has been pierced, as if it were a deer. He is the hunter and you are the deer; he ought not to harm you.
(10.1.27’) Moreover, one archer, taking up his bow, strikes down another who was shooting first;
(10.1.27.c) or even as the first is striking, the other strikes him back.
(10.1.28’) Listen indeed to these words of mine: go now, for you have come from somewhere!
(10.1.28.c) But against him who made you! ‖28‖ (10.1.29’) Terrible indeed is the slaughter of the innocent; O sorcery, do not kill our cow, horse, or man!
(10.1.29.c) Wherever you are laid down, from there we raise you up; become lighter than a leaf! ‖29‖
(10.1.30’) If you are shrouded in darkness, as if caught in a net,
we destroy all these sorceries and send them back to their maker.
(10.1.31’) [We destroy] the offspring of those who practice sorcery, who are treacherous, and who bring forth [evil spells].
(10.1.31.c) Destroy the sorcery! Release us from it! Strike down these practitioners of black magic!

(10.1.32’) As the sun is released from darkness, as the night leaves behind the signs of dawn, so do I cast off all that is ill-fated, wrought by the makers of sorcery; like an elephant shaking dust from itself, I shake off misfortune. (10.1.32.c) 32 {3}
(10.2.1’) By whom were the heels of man brought together? By whom was the flesh gathered? By whom the two ankles?

(10.2.1.c) By whom the well-formed fingers? By whom the cavities? By whom the two collarbones? And who established the middle as the foundation? (10.2.2’) From what indeed did they fashion the two ankles below and the two knee-caps above for man?
(10.2.2.c) Having pulled out the shanks, they laid them down; where indeed are the joints of the knees? Who has understood that?

2 (10.2.3.a) Four [limbs] are joined together at their ends; above the knees, the trunk is loose. (10.2.3.c) As for the hips and the thighs—who brought those into being, by which the firm *kusindha* came to be? 3
(10.2.4’) How many were the gods, and who were they, that fashioned the breast and the neck of Puruṣa?
(10.2.4.c) How many assigned the two breasts, who [assigned] the two shoulders, how many built up the shoulder-blades, and how many the ribs?
(10.2.5’) Who brought together his two arms, saying, "Let them perform heroic deeds"?
(10.2.5.c) Who is that god who placed his shoulders upon the *kusindha*?
(10.2.6’) Who pierced the seven openings in the head— these two ears, the two nostrils, the two eyes, and the mouth— through which,
by the greatness of his victory, four-footed and two-footed creatures go their way in many directions?
For he placed the wide tongue within the jaws; then he fixed the great voice upon it.
He moves to and fro within the worlds, clothing himself in the waters—who indeed has understood that?
Who was the first to fashion his brain, his forehead, and his temples, who [first fashioned] his skull?
(10.2.8.c) Having piled up the funeral mound upon the jaws of the person, which god ascended to heaven?
8 (10.2.9’) Abundant pleasant and unpleasant things, sleep, distress, and exhaustion;
(10.2.9.c) from what cause does the formidable person carry joys and delights? 9

(10.2.10’) Whence come affliction, misfortune, destruction, and lack of understanding in man? (10.2.10.c) Whence come success, prosperity, failure, intelligence, and the dawns? ‖10‖ {4} (10.2.11’) Who placed within this [man] the waters that flow in all directions, moving in many ways, born for the rushing of rivers?
(10.2.11.c) Intense, ruddy, red, copper-colored, and smoky; upward, downward, and across within the person.
||11|| (10.2.12’) Who placed form in him? Who [placed] greatness and name?
(10.2.12.c) Who [placed] the path in him? Who the banner? Who the movements in the person? ||12||

(10.2.13’) Who infused the out-breath (*prāṇa*) into him, who the in-breath (*apāna*) and the diffused breath (*vyāna*)? (10.2.13.c) What god established the equalizing breath (*samāna*) within this person?
‖13‖ (10.2.14’) What one god placed the sacrifice (*yajña*) within this person?
(10.2.14.c) Who in this world is truth? Who is falsehood? Whence comes death? Whence comes immortality?
(10.2.15’) Who clothed him in garments? Who ordained his lifespan?
(10.2.15.c) Who bestowed strength upon him? Who fashioned his speed? (15)
By whom was the water stretched out? By whom was the day made for the sake of splendor? By whom was the dawn kindled? By whom was the evening state bestowed?
Who placed seed within it, saying, "Let the thread be spun out"?

By what does one follow Parjanya? By what, the far-seeing Soma?

By what both the sacrifice and faith? By what is the mind placed within this [body]? (10.2.19) By what does one attain the learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*)? By what, this Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*)? (10.2.20)
(10.2.20.c) By what means does a person obtain this Agni? By what means did he measure the year? ||20|| (10.2.21’) Through Brahman one attains the learned Śrotriya; through Brahman, this Parameṣṭhin.
(10.2.21.c) Through Brahman a person obtains this Agni; through Brahman he measured the year. ||21||
(10.2.22) By what does one dwell among the gods? By what [does one dwell among] the clans of divine origin?

By what is this other constellation [defined], and by what is true sovereignty (*kṣatra*) said to exist? (10.2.23) The sacred word (*brahman*) dwells among the gods; the sacred word [dwells among] the clans of divine origin.
(10.2.23.c) This other world is Brahman; Brahman is called both the true and the ruling power (*kṣatra*).
(10.2.24’) By whom was this earth established? By whom was the sky placed above? (10.2.24.c) By whom was this wide intermediate space, extending upwards and across, established?
By Brahmā the earth was established; by Brahmā the higher heaven was placed above.
By Brahmā this expanse—the atmosphere—was established, both upwards and across.
Having sewn together his head and his heart, Atharvan [performed the rite].
(10.2.26.c) From the brain upward, Pavamāna impels [the breath] from the head.
(10.2.27’) That indeed is the head of Atharvan, the divine casket closed up; (10.2.27.c) Prāṇa protects that head, as do food and the mind. (27)
(10.2.28’) Was he created upright? Was he created crosswise? The Puruṣa has pervaded all directions.
(10.2.28.c) He who knows the city of Brahman, of which the Puruṣa is said to be the name— (10.2.29’) He who indeed knows that city of Brahman, which is enveloped by immortality...
To him, both Brahman and the Brāhmaṇas granted sight, vital breath, and progeny.
(10.2.29.c) Indeed, neither sight nor vital breath abandons him before old age, who knows the city of Brahman, of which he is called the person. (10.2.30)
The city of the gods, Ayodhyā, has eight wheels and nine gates;
within it is a golden treasury, heaven enveloped in light.
Within that golden treasury, upon a three-spoked, triple-supported [throne], ||31||
(10.2.32.c) That which is the conscious spirit within it, the knowers of Brahman truly know that as Brahman.
(10.2.33’) Radiant, golden, and completely surrounded by glory, Brahmā entered the unconquerable golden city. (10.2.33.c) {6}
This amulet of mine, Varana, is a bull that destroys rivals;
with it, seize the enemies and crush those who plot evil. Pierce them through, crush them, and seize them; let this amulet be your forerunner from the front.
(10.3.2.c) By means of the *varaṇa* plant, the gods warded off the daily assault of the Asuras.
(10.3.3’) This *varaṇa* amulet is a universal remedy; it is thousand-eyed, green, and golden.
(10.3.3.c) May it cast your enemies down; first, subdue those who hate you.
This *varaṇa* tree shall ward you off from the sorcery spread against you, from this human fear,
and from every evil;
this divine lord of the forest (*vanaspati*) shall be your protector.
(10.3.5.c) Whatever wasting disease has entered into him, that the gods have driven away.

||5|| (10.3.6’) If, having fallen asleep, you see an evil dream—such as a wild beast fleeing along an unpleasant path—from the sneeze, from the ill-omened cry of a bird, this *varaṇa* amulet shall ward it off. ||6||
From ill-will, from destruction, from malevolent magic, and likewise from fear—
from the deadly blow of more powerful death— may the *varaṇa* tree ward you off.
Whatever sin my mother, my father, my brothers, or my own kin have committed, and whatever sin we ourselves have committed.

(10.3.8.c) Then this divine lord of the forest shall ward us off. I am uninjured, my protector is uninjured; may I be long-lived and a man among all men. May this *varaṇa* jewel protect me from every direction.
This *varaṇa* on my chest is a king, a divine lord of the forest.
(10.3.11.c) May he drive away my enemies, as Indra [drove away] the Dasyus and the Asuras.
||11|| (10.3.12’) I carry this Varaṇa tree, may I be long-lived for a hundred autumns;
(10.3.12.c) may it bestow upon me sovereignty, dominion, cattle, and vital strength. ||12||

Just as the wind shatters the lords of the forest, the trees, with its might, so do you shatter my rivals—those born before and those born after. May the *varaṇa* tree protect you. Just as the wind and the fire consume the trees, the lords of the forest.

(10.3.14.c) So, devour my rivals—those born before as well as those born after; may the *varaṇa* tree protect you. (10.3.15’) Just as trees, withered by the wind, lie cast down, so do you wither my rivals and cast them down.
(10.3.15.e) May the Varaṇa protect you from those born before as well as those born after.
‖15‖ (10.3.16’) O Varaṇa, cut them down for him—before their destined time, before the end of his life—those who seek to harm him among his cattle and those who seek to harm his kingdom. ‖16‖

Just as the sun shines intensely, just as splendor is deposited within it, so may the Varuṇa amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity. May it sprinkle me with brilliance; may it anoint me with glory. 17.17.17e–f.

Just as glory resides in the moon and in the sun, the beholder of men, so may the Varuṇa amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity. May it sprinkle me with splendor and anoint me with glory. 18.3.18.18′–18.e.

Just as there is glory upon the earth, and just as there is [glory] in this Jātavedas, so may the Varuṇa amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity. May it sprinkle me with splendor and anoint me with glory. 19.3.19.19.
As glory is in a maiden, as it is in this prepared chariot, so may the Varana amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity. May it sprinkle me with splendor; may it anoint me with glory. 20.3.20. {8}

As there is glory in the Soma-drinking, as there is glory in the honey-mixture, so may the Varana amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity. May it sprinkle me with splendor; may it anoint me with glory. 21.
As glory resides in the Agnihotra, as glory resides in the Vaṣaṭ-call, even so may the Varuṇa amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity.
May it sprinkle me with splendor; may it anoint me with glory. 22.
Just as glory rests with the sacrificer, and just as it is established in this sacrifice, so may the Varuṇa amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity. May it sprinkle me with splendor;
As glory resides in Prajāpati, as it resides in this Parameṣṭhin, so may the Varuṇa amulet bestow upon me renown and prosperity.
May it sprinkle me with splendor; may it anoint me with glory. 24.24.24(e)

Just as immortality is established among the gods, and just as truth is placed within them, so may the Varana amulet bestow upon me fame and prosperity. May it sprinkle me with brilliance; may it anoint me with glory. 25. {9}
Indra’s is the first chariot; the gods’ is the second chariot; Varuṇa’s is the third.
The lowest chariot of the serpents has reached the pillar and then sped away.
Darbha is the flame, the young shoot; the horse’s tail-hair, the tail-hair of the speckled one.
(10.4.2.c) The seat of the chariot. (10.4.3’) Strike down, O White One, with your foot, both from the front and from behind!
Like wood floating upon the water, render the serpents' poison sapless—the fierce liquid! (10.4.3.c) 3.
Araṅguṣa, having dived down and emerged again, spoke:
"Like wood floating upon the water, the serpents' poison is sapless; their fierce venom is like water.
Paidva slays the kasarṇīla snake; Paidva slays the white and the black.
(10.4.5.c) Paidva split the head of the Ratharvi and of the Pṛdāku serpent.
(10.4.6’) O Paidva, go forward as the first; we shall follow after you. Drive the serpents away from the path by which we travel.
(10.4.6.c) Drive the serpents away from the path by which we travel.
(10.4.7’) Here Pedu was born; here is his place of departure.
(10.4.7.c) These are the tracks of the horse, of the one possessed of strength, who strikes down the serpent. 7.
(10.4.8’) What is joined together, let him not unbind; what is opened wide, let him not close.
(10.4.8.c) In this field there are two snakes, a female and a male; both of them are sapless.
(10.4.9’) Sapless are the snakes here, those that are near and those that are far away.
With a club I strike the scorpion; with a staff, the snake that has approached. (10.4.9.c) 9.
This is the remedy for Aghāśva and for both Svaja as well.
Indra has delivered for me the serpent who sought to harm; Paidva has subdued that serpent. We meditate upon Paidva, the steadfast one whose foundation is firm.

(10.4.11.c) These vipers sit brooding behind us. (10.4.12’) Their life-breath is gone, their poison is gone; they have been struck down by Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt. Indra has slain them, and we have slain them.

(10.4.12.c) Indra has struck them down, and we have struck them down. (10.4.12’) Their life-breath is gone, their poison is gone; they have been struck down by Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt. Indra has slain them, and we have slain them. (10.4.12.c) Indra has struck them down, and we have struck them down. 12.
(10.4.13’) The cross-striped snakes are slain, the vipers are crushed. Strike down the white leech that has made itself a ladle, the black one among the *darbha* grasses!
(10.4.14’) The young maiden Kairātikā digs for the healing herb.
(10.4.14.c) With golden hooves upon the ridges of the mountains.
(10.4.15’) This youth, the physician, has arrived—the speckled-slayer, the unconquered;
he is indeed the crusher of both the *svaja* and the scorpion. (10.4.15.c) 15.
Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa have made the snow subject to me;
so too both Vāta and Parjanya.
Indra has made the snow subject to me, as well as the viper and the adder.
(10.4.17.c) Svaja, Tiraścirāji, Kasarṇīla, and Daśonaśi—(17) Indra struck down the first progenitor of you, O serpent. (10.4.18.c) Of those being torn apart, what indeed was their essence? (18)
For I have seized their heads, as a fisherman seizes a large fish;
having gone into the middle of the river, I have washed away the poison of the serpent.
Let all the rivers carry away the poison of every serpent.
(10.4.20.c) The cross-striped snakes are slain; the adders are crushed.
{11} (10.4.21’) From among the plants, I choose them as I would fertile fields with skill. I lead them like mares; let the poison go forth! {21}
Whatever poison is in the fire, in the sun, on the earth, or in the plants; whatever stinging poison, whatever *kanaknaka*—let it go forth, let your poison depart!
Those born of fire, those born of plants, those of the serpents, and those born of the waters that have appeared as lightning—[let them depart].
(10.4.23.c) To those serpents whose offspring are many and great, we pay homage with reverence.
(10.4.24’) You are the maiden named Taudī, or you are indeed named Ghṛtācī.
With my foot, I place my step upon yours, [thereby] neutralizing the poison.
(10.4.25’) Shake it from limb to limb; avoid the heart!
(10.4.25.c) Whatever fiery power belongs to you, O poison, let that go downward away from you. (10.4.26’) Poison has gone far away; poison has roared; even poison has not reached [us].

(10.4.26.c) Agni has deposited the poison of the snake; Soma has led it away. (10.4.26.e) The poison has followed after the fang; the snake is immortal. 26 {12} (10.5.1’) You are the vigor of Indra; you are the endurance of Indra; you are the strength of Indra; you are the heroism of Indra; you are the manly power of Indra.
(10.5.1.c) For victorious application, I join you with the applications of the Brahman.
||1|| (10.5.2’) You are the vigor of Indra; you are the endurance of Indra; you are the strength of Indra; you are the heroism of Indra; you are the manly power of Indra.
(10.5.2.c) For victorious application, I join you with the applications of the Kṣatra. ||2||
(10.5.3’) You are the vigor of Indra; you are the power of Indra; you are the strength of Indra; you are the heroism of Indra; you are the manly courage of Indra.
(10.5.3.c) For the victorious union, I yoke you with the yokes of Indra.
(10.5.4’) You are the vigor of Indra; you are the power of Indra; you are the strength of Indra; you are the heroism of Indra; you are the manly courage of Indra.
(10.5.4.c) For the victorious union, I yoke you with Soma-unions.
(10.5.5’) You are Indra’s vigor; you are Indra’s endurance; you are Indra’s strength; you are Indra’s heroism; you are Indra’s manly power.
(10.5.5.c) For the victorious union, I yoke you with water-unions.
(10.5.6’) You are the vigor of Indra; you are the endurance of Indra; you are the strength of Indra; you are the heroism of Indra; you are the manly power of Indra.

(10.5.6.c) For the victorious harnessing, may all beings wait upon me; harnessed for me, you are the waters. 6 (10.5.7’) You are the portion of Agni; you are the brightness of the waters. O divine waters, bestow splendor upon us!
(10.5.7.c) By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I set you down for this world.
||7|| (10.5.8’) You are the portion of Indra; O divine waters, bestow upon us the brilliance of the waters.
(10.5.8.c) By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I set you down for this world. ||8||
(10.5.9) You are the portion of Soma; you are the brilliance of the waters. O divine waters, bestow splendor upon us!
(10.5.9c) By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I set you down for this world.
(10.5.10) You are the portion of Varuṇa; you are the brilliance of the waters. O divine waters, bestow splendor upon us!
(10.5.10.c) By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I set you down for this world.
||10|| (10.5.11’) You are the portion of Mitra and Varuṇa; you are the bright essence of the waters. O divine waters, bestow splendor upon us!
(10.5.11.c) By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I set you down for this world. ||11||
(10.5.12’) You are the portion of Yama; O divine waters, bestow upon us the brilliance of the waters.
(10.5.12.c) By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I set you down for this world.
(10.5.13’) You are the portion of the Fathers; O divine waters, bestow upon us the brilliance of the waters.
(10.5.13.c) By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I set you down for this world.
||13|| (10.5.14’) You are the portion of the god Savitṛ; you are the brilliance of the waters. O divine waters, bestow splendor upon us!
(10.5.14.c) By the ordinance of Prajāpati, I set you down for this world. ||14||

(10.5.15’) Whatever portion of the waters is within the waters, fit for the *yajus* and for the sacrifice to the gods—(10.5.15.c) this I release upon him; do not let it fall upon me. (10.5.15.e) By means of that, we release it upon him who hates us and whom we hate.

(10.5.16’) Whatever of the waters is the wave of the waters, within the waters, fit for sacrifice, a place for the worship of the gods—(10.5.16.c) this I release upon him; do not let it fall upon me. (10.5.16.e) By means of that, we release it upon him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.17’) He who is the waters, the calf of the waters, within the waters, worthy of sacrifice, the place of divine worship—(10.5.17.c) him I release here; do not cast him down upon me.
(10.5.17.e) With him we release that one who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.18’) He who is the bull of the waters, within the waters, worthy of sacrifice, the place of divine worship—(10.5.18.c) him I release over this; do not cast me down upon him.
(10.5.18.e) With him we release over him who hates us and whom we hate.

(10.5.19’) He who is the golden embryo (*hiraṇyagarbha*) of the waters, within the waters, worthy of sacrifice, the place of worship for the gods—(10.5.19.c) him I cast away from here; do not let him sink down upon me.
(10.5.19.e) By means of him, we cast away him who hates us and whom we hate.

(10.5.20’) That stone of the waters, the speckled, celestial one, which is within the waters, fit for sacrifice, the place of divine worship—(10.5.20.c) this do I release against him; do not cast it upon me.
(10.5.20.e) With it we release against him who hates us and whom we hate.

(10.5.21’) Or whoever is the fire of the waters, within the waters, worthy of sacrifice, the place of divine worship—(10.5.21.c) this one I release past him; do not cast me down upon him. (10.5.21.e) By means of him, we release past him who hates us and whom we hate.
Whatever falsehood we have uttered within the last three years—may the Waters protect me from all that evil and distress.
(22) I send you forth to the ocean; enter your own source.
(10.5.23.c) May we be unharmed, with all our life-force; let nothing whatsoever cause us distress.

(10.5.24’) May the waters, free from blemish, carry away the blemish from us; may they, of auspicious countenance, carry away from us sin, misfortune, evil dreams, and impurity. (10.5.24.c) May they carry it far away. 24.
(10.5.25’) You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by the earth, with the brilliance of Agni.
(10.5.25.c) Following the earth, I stride forth; from the earth we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.25.e) May he not live; may breath abandon him! ‖25‖

(10.5.26’) You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by the intermediate region, with the brilliance of Vāyu. (10.5.26.c) I stride across the intermediate region. From the intermediate region we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.26.e) May he not live; may breath abandon him! ‖26‖
(10.5.27’) You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by heaven, possessing the brilliance of the sun.
(10.5.27.c) Following the path of heaven, I step forth; from heaven we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.27.e) May he not live; may breath abandon him! ‖27‖
(10.5.28’) You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by the quarters, with the mind as your brilliance.
(10.5.28.c) Following the quarters, I stride forth; from the quarters we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.28.e) May he not live; may breath abandon him! ‖28‖

(10.5.29’) You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by hope, with the brilliance of the wind. (10.5.29.c) I stride along the quarters; from the quarters we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.29.e) May he not live; may breath abandon him! ‖29‖
(10.5.30’) You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by the Ṛgveda, and radiant with the Sāmaveda.
(10.5.30.c) Following the Ṛgverses, I step forth; from the Ṛgverses we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.30.e) May he not live; may breath abandon him! ‖30‖ {15}
(10.5.31’) You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by sacrifice, possessing the splendor of Brahman.
(10.5.31.c) Following the sacrifice, I stride forth; from the sacrifice we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.31.e) May he not live; may the vital breath abandon him! ‖31‖
(10.5.32’) You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by the plants, possessing the splendor of Soma.
(10.5.32.c) Following the plants, I stride forth; from the plants we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.32.e) Let him not live; let the vital breath abandon him! ‖32‖
(10.5.33’) You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened in the waters, possessing the brilliance of Varuṇa.
(10.5.33.c) Following the waters, I step forth; from the waters we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.33.e) May he not live; may breath abandon him! ‖33‖

(10.5.34’) You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by the plough, possessing the luster of food. (10.5.34.c) Following the plough, I stride forth; through the plough we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.34.e) May he not live; may breath abandon him! ‖34‖
(10.5.35’) You are the stride of Viṣṇu, the slayer of rivals, sharpened by breath, possessing the splendor of Puruṣa.
(10.5.35.c) Following after breath, I step forth; from breath we exclude him who hates us and whom we hate.
(10.5.35.e) May he not live; may breath abandon him! ‖35‖
(10.5.36’) Conquered is ours, won is ours; I have overcome all hostile armies.

(10.5.36.c) Here do I encircle the luster, the brilliance, the breath, and the life-span of the son of such-and-such a lineage and such-and-such a mother; here do I cast him down beneath my feet. ‖36‖
I turn following the turning of the sun, following the southern turning.
May she grant me wealth; may she grant me the luster of sacred knowledge.
I turn toward the luminous quarters.
(10.5.38.c) May they grant me wealth; may they grant me the luster of Brahman. 38.
(10.5.39’) I turn toward the Seven Seers. (10.5.39.c) May they grant me wealth; may they grant me the luster of Brahman. 39.
(10.5.40’) I turn toward Brahman; may they grant me that wealth, may they grant me that Brahman-splendor.
(40) {16} (10.5.41’) I turn toward the Brāhmaṇas.
May they grant me wealth; may they grant me the luster of sacred knowledge (*brāhmaṇavarcasa*).
(41) Him whom we seek, him we shall strike down with our weapons.
Into the wide-open mouth of Parameṣṭhin, we have cast him by means of the sacred word (*brahman*). (42)
(10.5.43) With the two tusks of Vaiśvānara, let the weapon strike him down.
(10.5.43c) May this oblation, this divine and most powerful kindling-stick, devour him.
(10.5.44) You are the bond of King Varuṇa.

(10.5.44.c) So, bind this man, the son of such-and-such a lineage and such-and-such a mother, to food and to breath! (10.5.45’) O Lord of the Earth, that food of yours which overflows across the earth— (10.5.45.c) grant that to us, O Lord of the Earth, O Prajāpati!
I have honored the celestial waters; we have been united with their essence.
Rich in milk, O Agni, I have come hither; endow me with splendor.
O Agni, endow me with splendor, with progeny, and with long life.
(10.5.47.c) May the gods know this of mine; may Indra know it together with the seers.

(47) (10.5.48’) O Agni, whatever curse the pair utters today, or whatever harsh speech the singers produce—(10.5.48.c) that arrow which is born from the fury of the mind, with that pierce the sorcerers in their hearts. (48)

(10.5.49) Crush the sorcerers with your heat; O Agni, crush the *rakṣas* with your flame. Crush the worshippers of false gods with your radiance; crush those who delight in the breath of others as they burn away. 49 (10.5.50) For him, I, the knowing one, hurl the four-edged thunderbolt of the waters to split his head.

(10.5.50.c) May he shatter all her limbs; may all the gods acknowledge this for me. (50) {17} (10.6.1’) The head of the enemy, of the rival, of the ill-disposed hater— (10.6.1.c) I cut it off with my might. (1)
(10.6.2’) This amulet, born from the plowshare, shall provide armor for me.
May it come to me full with the stirred offering, together with sap and splendor.
(10.6.3’) That which the skillful carpenter fashioned for you with his hand and his axe—
(10.6.3.c) May the waters, the life-giving and pure ones, purify you, who are pure, from that [impurity].
||3|| (10.6.4’) This amulet, adorned with golden garlands, bestowing faith, sacrifice, and greatness— (10.6.4.c) may it dwell as a guest in our house. ||4||
To him we offer clarified butter, wine, honey, and food upon food.
May he, like a father for his sons, provide for us what is better and better; may the jewel, coming day after day from the gods, grant us prosperity more and more.
The jewel which Bṛhaspati bound on—the plowshare that drips with ghee, the fierce, healing amulet for the sake of vital power—
Agni fastened it on; it milked for him clarified butter more and more, day after day. With that, do thou slay those who hate us!
The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound on—a ploughshare dripping with ghee, fierce, a *kadhira* for the sake of vigor—Indra fastened it on for the sake of vigor and heroic might.
(10.6.7.e) Thus it yields him strength ever more and more, day after day; with that, do thou slay our enemies.
(10.6.8’) The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound on—the plowshare dripping with ghee, the fierce *kadhira*—for the sake of power;
(10.6.8.c) That Soma fastened upon himself for great hearing and sight.
(10.6.8.e) Thus it yields him luster more and more, day after day; with that, do thou slay thy enemies.

(10.6.9.a) The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound on—the plowshare dripping with ghee, the fierce one made of khadira wood for the sake of vigor— (10.6.9.c) That Sūrya fastened upon himself; with it he conquered these quarters.
(10.6.9.e) Thus it yields prosperity for him, more and more, day after day; with that, do thou slay those who hate us.

(10.6.10’) The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound on—the plowshare dripping with ghee, the fierce one made of khadira wood for the sake of vigor—wearing that bright amulet, the Moon conquered the citadels of the Asuras, the golden strongholds of the Dānavas.
(10.6.10.e) Thus it yields him fortune more and more, day after day; with that, do thou slay thy enemies. 10.
(10.6.11’) The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the swift wind— (10.6.11.c) That yields him vigor more and more, day after day; with that, do thou slay thy enemies. 11.
The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the swift wind— with that amulet the Aśvins protect this cultivation.
Through those two physicians, it yields great abundance more and more, day after day; with that, do you strike down your enemies. 12.6.12.12‖

The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the swift Wind, wearing that amulet, Savitṛ conquered this heaven. It milks for him a wealth of truth, more and more, day after day; with it, do you slay your enemies. 13.
The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the swift wind—carrying that amulet, the waters flow on forever, inexhaustible.

The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the swift wind, that auspicious amulet King Varuṇa fastened on himself. It yields him nothing but truth, more and more, day after day; with it, do thou slay thy enemies. 15.

The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the swift Vāta—wearing that amulet, the gods conquered all the worlds in battle. It yields them victory again and again, day after day; with it, do thou slay thy enemies. 16.

The jewel which Bṛhaspati bound for the swift wind—this auspicious jewel the deities fastened on again. It milks all this for them, more and more, day after day; with it, do thou slay thy enemies. 17.
The seasons bound him; the seasonal periods bound him.
Having bound him, the year guards all that has come to be.
The intermediate quarters bound him; the cardinal directions bound him.
The amulet created by Prajāpati has cast my enemies beneath me.

With it, do thou slay thy enemies.

(10.6.28.c) May this jewel come to me together with all forms of prosperity.
(10.6.29’) May the deities grant me this jewel for nourishment—this jewel that is victorious, that increases dominion, and that crushes rivals. (10.6.29.c) 29.
(10.6.30’) Together with the splendor of Brahman, I cast off what is inauspicious for me.
(10.6.30.c) Without rivals, a slayer of rivals, he has cast my rivals beneath me.
‖30‖ {20} (10.6.31’) May this jewel, born of the gods, place me above those who hate me.

(10.6.31.c) He whose milk these three worlds drink as their nourishment— (10.6.31.e) may that jewel ascend upon my head for preeminence. (10.6.32’) That which the gods, the ancestors, and human beings always depend upon for life...
(10.6.32.c) May this amulet ascend me for preeminence, from the very summit.
(10.6.33’) Just as seed grows in a ploughed field by means of the plow,
(10.6.33.c) so may offspring, cattle, and food upon food grow within me.
O amulet, increaser of the sacrifice, for whomsoever I have fastened you on as a blessing—do you, O amulet of a hundredfold efficacy, quicken him to preeminence.
(34) O Agni, graciously accepting this well-prepared fuel, welcome it with these oblations. (35)
(10.6.35.c) In that kindled Jātavedas, may we worship with prayer for wisdom, well-being, progeny, sight, and cattle.

||35|| {21} (10.7.1’) In what limb of his does austerity abide? In what limb is truth placed? (10.7.1.c) Where does his vow and where does his faith abide? In what limb is his reality established? ||1||
From which limb does his fire blaze forth? From which limb does Mātariśvan blow? From which limb does the moon measure itself out, measuring the limb of the great Skambha?
In which limb does his earth stand? In which limb does the intermediate space stand?
(10.7.3.c) Upon which limb does the established heaven rest? Upon which limb does that which is above the heaven rest?
(10.7.4’) Seeking what does the fire blaze upward? Seeking what does Mātariśvan blow? Tell me of that Skambha toward whom the encompassing winds go seeking; who indeed is he?
(10.7.5) Where do the half-months go? Where do the months go, in harmony with the year? Tell us of that Skambha where the seasons go and where the seasonal periods go; what indeed is he?
(10.7.6) Where do the two young women of different forms, Day and Night, hasten together in pursuit, being in harmony?
(10.7.6.c) Tell me of that pillar toward which the waters flow, seeking to reach it; what indeed is it?
(10.7.7.a) That pillar upon which Prajāpati, having fixed himself, supported all the worlds—tell me of that pillar; what indeed is it?
Whatever supreme, lowest, and middle [forms] Prajāpati created, possessing every form—how much of that did Skambha enter there, and how much was it that he did not enter?
8 How much of the past did Skambha enter, and how much of the future does he lie within? 9
When he divided that one limb into a thousand parts, how much of him did Skambha enter there?
(10.7.9.c) Where people know the worlds, the treasuries, the waters, and Brahman—where non-being and being meet their end—tell me of that Skambha; who indeed is he? (10.7.10)
Where asceticism, having exerted its power, maintains the highest vow;
where truth and faith, the waters, and the Brahman are concentrated—that Skambha, tell me, who indeed is he?
In whom the earth, the intermediate space, and the sky are placed; in whom [all things] are established.
(10.7.12.c) Tell me of that Skambha upon whom fire, moon, sun, and wind stand supported; who indeed is he?
(10.7.13’) Tell me of that Skambha in whose limb all the thirty-three gods are contained; who indeed is he?
Where the seers, the first-born, and the great Ṛc, Sāman, and Yajus [are found]; where the Single Seer is established—tell me of that Skambha; who indeed is he?
Where both immortality and death are contained within the Puruṣa.
(10.7.15.c) He in whom the channels are gathered together like the ocean—tell me of that Skambha; who indeed is he?
(10.7.16’) He in whom the four primary directions stand as channels, and wherein the sacrifice has exerted its power—tell me of that Skambha; who indeed is he?
Those who know the Brahman in the person know the Parameṣṭhin.
He who knows the Parameṣṭhin and he who knows Prajāpati—
those who know the eldest Brāhmaṇa, they have fully known Skambha.
(10.7.18’) He whose head is Vaiśvānara, whose eyes were the Aṅgirases, (10.7.18.c) whose limbs were the Yātus—tell me of that Skambha; who indeed is he?
(10.7.19’) They say that his mouth is the *brahman*, and his tongue is the honey-stalk.
(10.7.19.c) They say its udder is the Virāj; tell me of that Skambha—what indeed is he?

(10.7.20’) From whom they carved out the Ṛg-verses, from whom they drew forth the Yajus-formulas, whose hairs are the Sāmans, and whose mouth is the Atharvāṅgirases—tell me of that Skambha—what indeed is he?
People regard this branch that rests upon the unreal as if it were supreme;
yet those who worship this branch consider themselves superior.
Wherein the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus are gathered together—
(10.7.22.c) That upon which the past and the future, and all the worlds, are established—tell me of that Skambha; who indeed is he?
(10.7.23’) Whose treasure the thirty-three gods always guard— who today knows that treasure which you gods protect?
(10.7.24’) Where the gods, knowers of Brahman, worship Brahman as the eldest—
(10.7.24.c) whoever indeed should know them directly, he would be a knower of Brahman, a true Brahmā.
(10.7.25’) Those gods who were born from the non-existent are called the "Great Ones" (Bṛhantaḥ).
(10.7.25.c) They say that one member of Skambha exists beyond the people.
(10.7.26’) Where Skambha, generating, turned toward the ancient;
(10.7.26.c) they have understood that one member of Skambha as the ancient.

(10.7.27) Those who know Brahman truly recognize that those thirty-three gods whom [the body] divided among its limbs as its members are indeed those thirty-three gods. (10.7.28) People know Hiraṇyagarbha to be supreme and unsurpassed.
(10.7.28.c) In the beginning, Skambha poured forth that gold within the world.

(10.7.29’) Upon Skambha the worlds rest; upon Skambha austerity; upon Skambha the cosmic order (*ṛta*) is established. (10.7.29.c) O Skambha, I know you directly: in you, Indra, everything is contained.
In Indra are the worlds; in Indra is heat; in Indra is the *ṛta* established.
I know you, O Indra, face to face: upon Skambha everything is supported.
(30) One invokes name by name before the sun and before the dawn.
(10.7.31.c) That which was born first as the Unborn, it indeed attained that sovereign rule over which no other being exists as superior.
||31|| (10.7.32’) To him whose measure is the earth and whose belly is the mid-air, who made heaven his head—to that eldest Brahman, homage! ||32||
To him whose eye is the sun and the moon is ever-renewing,
who made fire his mouth— to that eldest Brahman, homage!
To him whose out-breath and in-breath are the wind, and whose eyes became the Aṅgirases.
(10.7.34.c) Homage to that Supreme Brahman who made the quarters intelligible.

(10.7.35’) Skambha has supported both these, heaven and earth; Skambha has supported the broad intermediate region. (10.7.35.c) Skambha has supported the six wide directions; Skambha has entered this entire universe.

Salutation to that eldest Brahman, who was born from the toil of austerity and has pervaded all worlds, and who made the Soma his own alone. (10.7.36) How does the wind not cease? How does the mind not find rest? (10.7.37)
(10.7.37.c) Why do the waters, seeking truth, never cease their flowing?
(10.7.38’) A great spirit dwells in the midst of the world, having ascended into the heat upon the surface of the water.
Upon it rest all those who are gods, just as branches spread out around the trunk of a tree. (10.7.38.c) 38.

To whom the gods always offer tribute with their hands, their feet, their speech, their hearing, and their sight—in that immeasurable one, tell me, who is that Skambha? 39 The darkness of him has been struck away; he has turned back from evil.
(10.7.40.c) Within him are all the lights that are in Prajāpati.
(10.7.41’) He who knows the golden reed standing in the water—
(10.7.41.c) he indeed is the secret Prajāpati.
(10.7.42’) Two young women of different forms weave a web with six threads, stepping upon it.
(10.7.42.c) One stretches out the warp-threads, the other holds them; they do not withdraw, nor do they reach the end.
(10.7.43’) Of these two, as if they were dancing around, I cannot discern which one is further on.
(10.7.43.c) A man weaves this; they sing it aloud; a man has brought it forth upon the firmament.
(10.7.44’) These pegs have propped up the sky; they have made the *sāman* hymns the warp for weaving.
(10.8.1’) He who is the past and the future, and he who presides over all—
(10.8.1.c) And to that noble one alone, the eldest Brahman, be homage!
(10.8.2’) By the Skambha these two are propped apart; heaven and earth stand firm.
The Skambha is all this that possesses a self, both that which breathes and that which blinks. (10.8.2.c) 2.
Three generations have passed beyond; others have settled around the *arká*.
The lofty measurer of the region has stood firm; the tawny one has entered the tawny mares.
Twelve are the spokes, the wheel is single, and there are three hubs—who indeed has understood that?
(10.8.4.c) Therein are three hundred and sixty stakes and wedges that are unshakable and immovable.
(10.8.5’) O Savitṛ, understand this: there are six Yamas, each born from one. (10.8.5.c) In him they desire their own state—he who among them is the one born from one.
Manifest yet hidden in the secret cave, wearing out its name, is the great station;
therein all this is placed—the moving, the breathing, the firmly established.
(10.8.7) It rolls with a single wheel and a single rim; it has a thousand syllables, extending forward and backward.
(10.8.7.c) With one half he generated the entire world; where has that other half of his gone?

(10.8.8’) This five-horsed chariot carries them at the head; the side-horses are yoked and follow along. Neither its coming nor its going is seen; it is neither near nor far, neither beyond nor below.
The ladle has its opening horizontal and its base turned upward; in it is deposited glory of every form.
There sit together the seven seers who were the guardians of this great one.
That which is yoked in front and that which is yoked behind, that which is yoked on all sides and that which is yoked everywhere—
(10.8.10.c) That by which the sacrifice is extended forward—that, I ask you, which among the *ṛc*s is it?

‖10‖ (10.8.11’) That which moves, that which falls, and that which stands; that which breathes and that which does not breathe, and whatever exists with closed eyes— That has supported the earth in all its forms; having come together, it becomes one alone. ‖11‖

Infinite and spread out in many places, the infinite appears as if finite within the limits; he, the guardian of the firmament, moves about discerning what has been and what is to be, for he is wise. Prajāpati moves within the womb, invisible, yet he is born in manifold ways.

The two wings of this golden swan, Hari, as he flies to heaven, extend across the sky for a thousand days.
Resting all the gods upon his breast, he travels beholding all the worlds.
Through truth he shines upward; through the sacred word (*brahman*) he looks downward.
(10.8.19.c) By means of breath he breathes across; in him the supreme is established.
(10.8.20’) He who indeed knows your two fire-sticks from which wealth is churned out—he, being wise, would consider himself the eldest; he would know the great Brāhmaṇa. (20) {27}
(10.8.21) At first he came into being footless; in the beginning, he brought forth the light. Having become four-footed, he became an object of enjoyment and took all food for himself.

(10.8.22.c) Whoever shall worship the eternal God who possesses the higher realm;

A hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million—countless wealth of his own is deposited in this [body].
While he looks on, they destroy it; therefore, this god shines thus. One [part] is subtler than a hair; yet another is not seen at all.

May that which is your head, that which is your mouth, your two ears, and your two jaws—
may they yield for the giver *āmikṣā*, milk, clarified butter, and honey. May those which are your two lips, your two nostrils, your two horns, and your two eyes [yield the same].
(10.9.14.c) May they yield for the giver curdled milk, milk, clarified butter, and honey.
(10.9.15’) Whatever lung you have, whatever heart, and the pericardium together with the throat—
may they yield for the giver curdled milk, milk, clarified butter, and honey.
Whatever liver you have, whatever two kidneys, whatever intestines and whatever bowels you have— let them yield for the giver curds,
milk, ghee, and honey. Whatever membrane you have, whatever rectum, whatever two flanks, and whatever skin you have— let them yield for the giver curds, milk, ghee, and honey.
